title: Tunisia bars family, lawyers from seeing Ghannouchi after prison collapse
summary: No word on jailed Tunisian opposition leader Ghannouchi for 11 days, his son tells Al Jazeera.
full_text:
Tunisia bars family, lawyers from seeing Ghannouchi after prison collapse
No word on jailed Tunisian opposition leader Ghannouchi for 11 days, his son tells Al Jazeera.
The son of jailed Tunisian opposition leader Rached Ghannouchi says his family and lawyers have been unable to see or contact the 85-year-old for 11 days since he was hospitalised after collapsing in prison.
In an interview with Al Jazeera on Monday, Moadh Ghannouchi said the last time lawyers saw his father was days before he temporarily lost consciousness on July 17, and that requests to visit him in hospital, including one submitted to the public prosecutor, had been refused, leaving the family with no confirmation of his whereabouts or condition.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Jailed opposition leader Ghannouchi faints in Tunisian prison due to heat
- list 2 of 3Tunisians mark fifth year of emergency rule with calls for Saied to go
- list 3 of 3Thousands rally against Tunisia’s president five years after power grab
“It is like a situation of enforced disappearance,” he said.
Ghannouchi said his father, who has high blood pressure and difficulty breathing, had been left exposed to a severe heatwave in a prison with no air conditioning.
“We hold the authorities fully responsible for his condition,” he said, alleging that his father’s confinement in a stiflingly hot prison was intended to worsen his health.
“It was not enough to imprison him – they want to torment him further,” Moadh told Al Jazeera.
“This is stressful for us and certainly for him as well because he’s used to always having a number of visits every week from lawyers and from family – so it has been 11 days cut off from everything, from every visit, from everyone.”
Ghannouchi said conflicting rumours had spread on social media, with some placing his father at the Rabta public hospital in Tunis, others at a military hospital, and some claiming he had suffered a heart attack. But the family has received no official information, he said, with the authorities refusing to communicate.
In a statement on his official Facebook page on Monday, Ghannouchi’s defence team demanded information on his condition. An Ennahda party spokesperson told Al Jazeera that it did not know which hospital he is in or his state of health.
The former speaker of parliament and most prominent figure detained in President Kais Saied’s crackdown on opponents has been jailed since April 2023 after receiving a life sentence that his supporters say was politically motivated. Saied’s government denies that prosecutions of opponents are politically driven.
Rached Ghannouchi lost consciousness last week as temperatures inside Mornaguia prison climbed, according to Haifa Chebbi, daughter of another imprisoned opposition figure. She said she witnessed the incident and that the temperature reached 52C (126F). His lawyers said on Thursday that his condition was “critical.”
The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention previously found that Ghannouchi’s detention was arbitrary and called for his immediate release, a ruling his son said authorities ignored.
On Sunday, the National Salvation Front, a broad opposition coalition, urged the authorities to issue an immediate statement on his health and Amnesty International called for the protection of prisoners during the heatwave.

title: Honduras’s Hernandez returns home after Trump pardon: How it happened
summary: Sentenced to 45 years in the US, Hernandez returns home to his family, party and supporters after Trump pardons him.
full_text:
Honduras’s Hernandez returns home after Trump pardon: How it happened
Sentenced to 45 years in the US, Hernandez returns home to his family, party and supporters after President Trump pardons him.
Nearly four years after being extradited to the United States for a drug-trafficking trial, former Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernandez returned home after a pardon by US President Donald Trump at the end of last year.
Trump claimed the trial was a “set up” orchestrated by former President Joe Biden’s administration.
Hernandez still faces corruption charges in Honduras but returned on Sunday after an arrest warrant against him was cancelled.
Human rights activists and lawyers fear a trial on home soil, where his party holds the presidency, would be a sham.
So why did Trump pardon and release the former president of Honduras despite abducting and arresting Venezuela’s Nicolas Maduro on drug and gun charges in January?
Why did Hernandez return to Honduras?
Hernandez was able to return after being pardoned by Trump, released from a US prison and then having an arrest warrant against him suspended last month.
He arrived at Palmerola International Airport, where he was greeted by his family and supporters of his National Party.
Hernandez led his country from 2014 to 2022, during which, according to US prosecutors, he once boasted he would “shove the drugs right up the noses of the gringos”, referring to Americans.
Shortly after leaving office, he was extradited to the US, where he was found guilty by a federal jury and sentenced to 45 years in prison for involvement in a scheme to export cocaine to the US.
Prosecutors described the scheme as “one of the largest and most violent drug trafficking conspiracies in the world”. He was convicted of accepting millions of dollars in bribes from violent drug-trafficking organisations over 18 years, which he was alleged to have used to fuel his rise in politics.
“During his political career, Hernandez abused his powerful positions and authority in Honduras to facilitate the importation of over 400 tons of cocaine into the US,” the US Department of Justice said after he was sentenced last year.
During his trial, Hernandez denied taking bribes from drug dealers, arguing he in fact cracked down on the narcotics trade and citing his administration’s cooperation with the US military.
“I cannot deny the profound emotion and joy I feel in my heart to be returning home,” Hernandez wrote on social media earlier this month, saying he was counting down the days to see his family.
“It wasn’t easy. The process has been extremely difficult … and what I experienced in prison, I truly wouldn’t wish on anyone,” he added.
Hernandez is expected to appear in court on August 3 to face the Honduran corruption charges.
Why did Trump pardon him?
Under the US Constitution, a president may offer two types of clemency for federal crimes: pardons, which forgive defendants their federal charges and restore their civil liberties, and commutations, which reduce people’s punishment without addressing their convictions.
Hernandez was pardoned by Trump in December. The US president said Hernandez had not received a fair trial and had been “set up” by the Biden administration.
Trump added that Hernandez was “treated very harshly and unfairly”.
At the same time, Trump also threw his weight behind right-wing candidate Nasry “Tito” Asfura, a member of Hernandez’s party. He ran in November’s presidential election and was declared the winner a month later in the close race after delays and allegations of fraud. He took office in January.
A Pandora Papers corruption investigation also accused Hernandez of diverting nearly $11m in state funds to political campaigns from 2010 to 2013.
Why a pardon for some but jail for others?
The Trump administration has faced criticism at home for pardoning the Honduran leader while at the same time abducting former President Maduro of Venezuela and his wife, Cilia Flores, in January on similar charges.
Maduro and Flores were seized in Caracas by the US military and flown to New York, where he is facing a range of guns and drugs charges and accusations of being a “narcoterrorist”.
At the time of Maduro’s abduction and since then, the Trump administration has targeted small boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific that it claims, without providing evidence, are involved in drug trafficking. More than 220 people have been killed in more than 60 such strikes on small boats in what many lawyers and activists have deemed extrajudicial killings.
Since taking office for a second term in January 2025, Trump has ordered more than 1,800 acts of clemency benefitting a range of personalities, including cryptocurrency billionaires, disgraced politicians and hundreds of political allies.
Some of the most controversial beneficiaries are supporters of his Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, including hundreds of rioters who attacked the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, in a bid to prevent the certification of Biden’s electoral victory over Trump two months earlier.
Legal experts have argued that while the president’s clemency power is broad, using it for allegedly corrupt purposes, such as to protect political allies or obstruct justice, could form the basis for impeachment proceedings.
US constitutional expert Bruce Fein told Al Jazeera that the US Constitution’s framers “understood the abuse of the pardon power to shelter political or personal friends to constitute an impeachable high crime and misdemeanour justifying the removal of the president through the impeachment process”.
“If Democrats gain control of Congress in the midterm elections, Trump will be in impeachment jeopardy for pardoning Hernandez,” Fein said, referring to elections in November.

full_text:
If you ever thought branch stacking was a harmless game played by young, ambitious political operatives seeking to advance within the party, think again.
On Monday, on the first day of the corruption watchdog’s inquiry into operation Rosny, an investigation into allegations of “possible offences under the Electoral Funding Act”, we heard boasts on secret tape recordings from a developer that he had “my hands on the state government” and he had “fucked” the career of a state politician by “taking his seat”. As for the state’s building commissioner, David Chandler, who was a thorn in the developer’s side, he was going to “fuck him sideways”.
In another call, in September 2021, the developer, Jean Nassif, reflects on the “fucking bitch”, the then premier Gladys Berejiklian. “Mate, we thought we’re gonna change her,” he says to the other person on the call, Charles Perrottet.
The opening address of counsel assisting the New South Wales Independent Commission of Inquiry, Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC laid out the allegations in horrifying detail. She said that Nassif, now a fugitive in Lebanon, had used his millions to engage the services of a group of Liberal operatives, known as the Reformers, as consultants.
These young men, Dwyer alleges, ran a major branch stacking operation that was designed to take over the Liberal party and promote their conservative agenda, while at the same time using their influence to deliver the outcomes their benefactor sought.
It was not just idle boasting by Nassif. Soon after that taped call, he got what he wanted: the Baulkham Hills MP, David Elliott, lost his preselection. Kevin Anderson, the minister responsible for the building commissioner, was replaced and Chandler, under enormous pressure, resigned.
The Reformers, Icac heard, included two of the former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet’s brothers – Jean-Claude and Charles – as well as the principals of two public relations firms, Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood.
Dwyer alleges Ellis and Greenwood took consultancy payments over a period of three years between 2019 and 2022, from Nassif and others.
These were “sham” payments, she says, and no real work was provided for these payments.
Instead the money was, she alleges, an illegal donation to the Reformers, and the consultancies an elaborate scheme to avoid either caps on the amount of donations or to funnel donations from banned donors – such as developers and those from the liquor and gaming industry – or both.
The alleged amounts are staggering: $2m from Nassif, more than $250,000 from the Catholic Schools Association and $125,000 from lawyer turned publican Michael O’Hara, who also happens to be the former law partner of right-wing Liberal powerbroker and upper house MP, Damien Tudehope. Tudehope stood down from the frontbench after being called as a witness to the inquiry.
Dwyer also gave hints of the evidence the Icac might have: a huge trove of “encrypted messages” between the young men who are central to this investigation. It appears they are now decrypted.
Icac also has evidence of the fundraisers the Reformers held, at which high-profile members of the Liberal party and others, including Tudehope, Tony Abbott and Alan Jones, were speakers.
Dwyer stressed that what she has outlined are at this stage allegations, not evidence, and that it was for the Icac commissioner, Fabian Gleeson SC, to decide the nature of the payments and crucially, the intentions of the key actors.
She urged the public not to get despondent at the sheer scale and breadth of the alleged schemes.
But it will be hard for those who follow this inquiry not to feel very alarmed about the state of our democracy, and what it may imply about how both major parties select candidates and determine policy and priorities.
For the first time we are seeing the internal ideological war within the Liberal party laid bare.
Dwyer read from a dossier – the Reformers’ sales pitch- which was prepared to recruit donors and members.
It says they planned to recruit 5,000 members by 2022 and take back the NSW Liberal party for conservatives, aimed to deliver 75% of the seats in the NSW parliament to conservatives by 2023, and sought control over the Liberal party’s peak body, the NSW state executive.
Their agenda? More conservative policies on same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia.
But branch stacking requires significant funds, both to pay the fees of the members who are stacked and the time of the stackers. They needed cash – and that meant finding covert donations.
“Money in politics as in other spheres has the potential to corrupt,” Dwyer told the inquiry.
Just how she alleges it corrupted in NSW remains to be seen. But her opening address hinted that it may have infected decisions on developments, Liberal party preselections, and led to attempts to unseat the building commissioner, David Chandler, to name a few.
Before the ALP gets too smug about the tsunami of horrible news that is going to engulf the NSW Liberals, there is a third allegation of blackmail and corrupt conduct involving Labor councillors at Strathfield council.
They appear to have caught, on the phone taps uncovered during operation Rosny, allegedly planning blackmail of a fellow councillor.
For all major political parties facing an ascendant One Nation, who markets itself as anti-establishment, this inquiry could not have come at a worse time.
Trust in our major parties is low. It’s about to get much lower.

title: Pauline Hanson and Malcolm Roberts deride family law system, calling DV a ‘weapon’ and court a ‘slaughterhouse’
summary:
Exclusive: Resurfaced comments by the One Nation leader underline her criticism of paid family violence leave and domestic violence support groups

Pauline Hanson told a podcast last year she believed “your employer should not be responsible” for providing paid domestic violence leave, while her colleague Malcolm Roberts recently referred to the family court as the “slaughterhouse of the nation”, in the latest One Nation comments critical of the family law system to emerge.

Hanson claimed on a 2021 podcast that domestic violence was being “used as a weapon” in court proceedings, and criticised domestic violence groups for focusing on support for women.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Pauline Hanson told a podcast last year she believed “your employer should not be responsible” for providing paid domestic violence leave, while her colleague Malcolm Roberts recently referred to the family court as the “slaughterhouse of the nation”, in the latest One Nation comments critical of the family law system to emerge.
Hanson claimed on a 2021 podcast that domestic violence was being “used as a weapon” in court proceedings, and criticised domestic violence groups for focusing on support for women.
“I feel for the children, I feel for the parents and I’m sick of these feminists who are trying to take over this whole thing and who are actually driving their own agenda. I’m sick and tired of hearing that men are the only perpetrators and they’re denied the right to see their children,” Hanson told the Dad Talk Today podcast in 2021.
Hanson’s past comments on domestic violence have drawn renewed scrutiny after a 4BC radio interview last week in which she said family violence was “wrong” but “it’s also a two-way street”.
In an interview with the Broken Fathers podcast last year, Hanson described paid leave for those experiencing family and domestic violence as “ridiculous”, calling it “domestic violence holiday leave”. She also suggested domestic violence was taking police away from “real crime” and called for the family law system to be “wound back”.
Hanson later claimed her 4BC comments had been taken “out of context” and denied she had downplayed domestic violence.
But the newly unearthed comments show the full breadth of One Nation’s criticism of the family law system.
In an interview with Hanson for a podcast titled Unemployable Media in January 2025, during a discussion about challenges facing business owners, the podcast host brought up the issue of domestic violence leave.
“Nobody in Australia would say domestic violence isn’t a horrible thing, but you’ve got 10 days,” the host began saying, before Hanson interjected.
“It should not be tied up in your employment. Your employer should not be responsible,” Hanson said.
The federal Labor government in 2022 legislated for 10 days of paid family and domestic violence leave annually as a workplace entitlement in the National Employment Standards, upgrading the previous five days’ unpaid leave. The cost is borne by employers.
Some businesses raised concerns when the change was legislated, but the social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, said only “a tiny number of people” used the leave.
“But they use it to get medical help, report to police, move to a safer home or go to court”.
The ACTU president, Michele O’Neil, said the scheme was “an essential lifeline available to workers facing some horrifically dangerous situations”.
In the 2021 interview, the One Nation leader criticised “feminist” groups in the domestic violence system.
“You have the domestic violence organisations, they’re getting millions of dollars in funding for it. You’ve got these refuges – and I can see that a woman needs to be protected if they don’t have a house to actually go to with the kids, a safe place to go … but you’ve got to offer the same to a man. You can’t just look after women,” Hanson said.
Later in the interview Hanson claimed domestic violence was “used as a weapon” in court.
“Domestic violence here is, the person can go in and say ‘I’m in fear’ and that can be domestic violence. If you text your partner a number of times ‘I want to see my child’, that’s harassment, that can be domestic violence. If you say ‘honey, sorry why’d you buy another pair of shoes? We’ve got the rent to pay’, that’s domestic violence.”
Roberts, whose advocacy of conspiracy theories has come under scrutiny, also criticised the family court system in a May interview with the rightwing podcast Cafe Locked Out.
“The family law court, a friend of mine describes the family law system as the slaughterhouse of the nation and he’s right,” Roberts said.
“It’s set up to divide. It’s set up to make money for lawyers. It’s set up to smash the family.”
One Nation and Hanson’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

title: ‘I knew what he had done to those boys’: murderer to stay in jail after journalist’s fight for justice
summary:
Gibraltar-based Ros Astengo inspired four men to report sexual assaults carried out by Allan Grimson in 1990s

Ros Astengo, a journalist based in Gibraltar who usually focuses on politics and social issues, had qualms when she began investigating the case of the suspected serial killer Allan Grimson as he neared release from prison after serving more than 20 years.

She worried that she might reopen the scars of survivors of Grimson – but also that she could be putting herself in the “crosshairs” of a dangerous man who had sexually assaulted and battered two young men to death in the late 1990s when he was a Royal Navy petty officer.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Ros Astengo, a journalist based in Gibraltar who usually focuses on politics and social issues, had qualms when she began investigating the case of the suspected serial killer Allan Grimson as he neared release from prison after serving more than 20 years.
She worried that she might reopen the scars of survivors of Grimson – but also that she could be putting herself in the “crosshairs” of a dangerous man who had sexually assaulted and battered two young men to death in the late 1990s when he was a Royal Navy petty officer.
“But the public interest overrode it,” Astengo said. “It would have been so easy for me to have just done nothing. But I thought to myself, how would I feel if as soon as they let him out he reoffended and harmed another young man. My motive was to keep the public safe.”
Because of Astengo’s work, four men came forward to report sexual assaults by Grimson carried out on them in the same era as the two murders.
On Monday, a jury at Winchester crown court found Grimson guilty of 13 sexual offences relating to the men, which may mean he remains in prison for years to come.
Judge Dugdale told Grimson he was an extremely dangerous man in the 1990s and asked for reports to be prepared to help him understand if he still posed a serious risk.
The judge also asked for victim personal statements to be taken from the men. He thanked the jury for hearing a “very unusual case” and invited them to return to court when he sentenced Grimson in November.
“The men were incredibly brave to come to court, bring all this back into their lives,” Astengo said.
Grimson was jailed for life in 2001 and told he would serve at least 22 years in prison for sexually abusing and murdering Nicholas Wright, 18, and Sion Jenkins, 20, in Portsmouth, both of whom had served in the navy. The sentencing judge described him as a “serial killer in nature if not by number”.
At the time, Grimson also admitted in police interviews sexual offences or contact with another four men – three young sailors and a teenage boy. He said he had thought of killing two of them but the Crown Prosecution Service did not pursue the allegations because he was going to serve a long jail term for the murders anyway.
While in prison Grimson was on best behaviour in the hope that he would be released after serving his 22 years and in November 2020 the Parole Board recommended he be moved to an open prison to prepare him for freedom.
At this time, Astengo was covering the search for the body of another sailor, Simon Parkes, who vanished in Gibraltar in 1986. Grimson was in the British overseas territory at the time. He has long been a suspect but denies involvement.
No remains were found and Astengo said she was deeply moved when Parkes’s elderly parents, Margaret and David, from south-west England, described it as their last chance to get justice. “It was a very lonely journey for them.” She promised them she would write a book about their son’s case to keep his memory alive.
She began her research and was disturbed to find he had made admissions over the four boys and young men but no action had been taken.
“I was astonished that he was never charged over them,” Astengo said. She was alarmed that Grimson seemed close to being released. “I knew what he had done to those boys. That really worried me. How could he be fully rehabilitated? I was worried he would go back into the community thinking he’s gotten away with it. I realised I was putting myself in the crosshairs of a killer but I thought something needed to be done.”
Astengo tracked down one of the four and travelled to the UK to speak to him. “I found a very angry man who was still hurt, angry and upset that he had never seen justice. He started talking about the fact that he was older now and a parent. He understands today what he didn’t back then – that was that he was groomed.”
Astengo told the man he could file a fresh complaint about Grimson. “I said to him, think very carefully about what you’re doing because you are going to open a can of worms for yourself.”
The man went ahead and spoke to police. Initially no action was taken so Astengo contacted the child sexual abuse review panel, which examines allegations of non-recent child sexual offences.
It agreed that the case was worth re-examining. Detectives interviewed the man and tracked down the three others. In February 2025, Grimson was charged over the attacks on the four.
The month-long trial highlighted how far the justice system had come in dealing with sexual crimes.
In the late 1990s and early 2000s it was not uncommon for serious sexual allegations not to be pursued if a defendant faced a long jail sentence for even more serious crimes. Now it is considered the state’s duty to do so.
It is also a reminder that until the turn of the century, gay people were not allowed to serve openly in the armed forces, meaning some of those assaulted by Grimson were keen not to talk about what had happened back then because they feared dismissal.
In court, Grimson’s legal team tried to argue that it was unfair for him to be charged with offences that the authorities had not pursued a quarter of a century ago. They made it clear he felt he was being prosecuted now as a tactic for keeping him in prison, to “stymie” his parole.
His legal team also criticised Astengo, suggesting she had been motivated by making money from her book, which is due to come out next year.
John Price KC, prosecuting, urged the jury to ignore “conspiracy theories” about Astengo’s involvement and said good was achieved by energetic journalists.
Astengo said it was not about money. Every time she travelled to the UK she has had to pay her own way, take leave – and could make very little, if anything, from her book. She said: “The defence tried to paint me as somebody who has exerted undue influence all because I’m writing a book. For me, it was about justice and to prevent a serial offender from being released.”

title: Mayo beat 75-year-old ‘curse’ to become Gaelic football champions
summary:
Team to return for euphoric homecoming after winning all-Ireland men’s final against Kerry, ending decades of defeats

The hex is broken, dispelled, banished, and a story that bewitched Ireland for decades has ended in fairytale: Mayo are all-Ireland champions.

Seventy-five years after a supposed curse condemned its Gaelic men’s football team to endless defeat, the county prevailed and uncorked a wave of emotion that engulfed even its rivals.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The hex is broken, dispelled, banished, and a story that bewitched Ireland for decades has ended in fairytale: Mayo are all-Ireland champions.
Seventy-five years after a supposed curse condemned its Gaelic men’s football team to endless defeat, the county prevailed and uncorked a wave of emotion that engulfed even its rivals.
The team will return to the west of Ireland for a euphoric homecoming on Monday evening after winning the senior football championship, a victory that thrilled Ireland and Mayo’s diaspora, including Joe Biden, Mark Carney and Noel and Liam Gallagher.
“Mayo 1-20, Kerry 1-17. Chisel it on the gravestones, scribble it in the sky,” the Irish Times exulted. “Croke Park untethered, the whole place afloat for an hour on a lake of the sweetest tears that were ever cried.”
Most pundits had favoured Kerry to win the 138th all-Ireland final and write another chapter of Mayo woe at Sunday’s contest at the Dublin stadium. Instead the underdogs triumphed and even some Kerry fans wept at the catharsis.
Few seriously believed in the curse – it was said no member of the last winning team from 1951 would live to see another – but there was no doubting the drought that followed, with 11 defeats in 11 finals since 1989. A book about Mayo’s quest was titled House of Pain.
Whenever the county made it to a final, a frisson gripped television viewers and the 82,000-strong stadium crowd: was this the day they would witness the end of the hex? On Sunday it was.
“To every young boy and girl across Mayo and our diaspora across the world, never stop dreaming, stick your chest out and be proud to be from Mayo,” the team captain, Jack Coyne, declared as he held aloft the trophy named after Sam Maguire, a legendary player. “The wait is over. Sam is home.”
Authorities had provisionally estimated a crowd of 40,000 would greet the team at McHale Park in the county town of Castlebar on Monday but that looks conservative, Gerry Bourke, the homecoming committee chair, told RTÉ. “After what I saw in Croke Park yesterday, I think we’ll have to revisit the plan.”
Mayo, a landscape of bogs, rocks and Atlantic cliffs, is the third biggest of the island of Ireland’s 32 counties. It is sparsely populated, with just 130,000 people, but players and supporters have a reputation for fervency in the Gaelic Athletic Association, the sport’s governing body.
According to lore, the young victors of 1951 were on their way home to celebrate when they passed through the village of Foxford and failed to pay their respects to a funeral, prompting the enraged priest to utter the fateful words: “For as long as you all live, Mayo won’t win another all-Ireland.”
Seven decades later, the last surviving member of that team, Paddy Prendergast, told friends he would willingly “roll over and die” if there was any truth to the curse, but that it was a myth.
“There was supposed to have been a funeral in the local church; I don’t know whether there was or not. I saw people standing around the church but we didn’t get off the truck because we couldn’t get off the bloody truck,” he told an interviewer in 2017.
Researchers who probed church records, press cuttings and other sources failed to find any verification of the supposed curse, which gained currency in the 1990s. The legend, however, is intact: Prendergast died in 2021, aged 95, two weeks after Mayo lost the final.
Biden – who concluded a 2023 presidential visit to Mayo with the rallying cry “Mayo for Sam!” – congratulated his ancestral home county. “Today, the dream becomes reality,” he posted. “You earned this victory. Enjoy every minute.”
Carney, the Canadian prime minister who made his own ancestral pilgrimage to Mayo last month, echoed the joy. “The curse is broken,” he posted. The Gallagher brothers of Oasis, who also have family ties to Mayo, expressed pride. “Finally!! Up Mayo!!” Noel posted.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Boy George has released a new song entitled We Will Dance Again, which voices support for Israel’s military action in Palestine.
Posted on X and Instagram with the Hebrew title עוד נרקוד alongside its English translation, the song features a pop-reggae backing. The opening lyrics are: “You say genocide, I say war / When you’re attacked, that’s what the army’s for / Does it get ugly? You bet it does / When I know you wanna kill every last one of us.”
Boy George cites the attack by Hamas at the Nova music festival in October 2023, saying the civilians killed there were “murder[ed] … for the crime of dancing”. A total of 344 civilians and 34 security personnel were killed and 44 people were taken hostage.
The overall Palestinian death toll since the war started is more than 73,000.
The title phrase We Will Dance Again, repeated for the song’s chorus, has been used by Israelis to express hope and solidarity in the wake of the 7 October attack, and was used as the title of an acclaimed documentary about it.
Elsewhere in the chorus, Boy George asserts: “There will be no war / But if you’re ever confused / I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human.”
He also criticises the pro-Palestinian movement, including musicians who have condemned Israel: “You condemn the Jews, with selective memory / Musicians holding flags, mouthing like sheep / Propaganda fuelled by the internet feels so weak.” Musicians who have supported Palestine include Stormzy, Damon Albarn, Clairo and Brian Eno, the latter of whom conceived an all-star charity single, Lullaby, which vied for Christmas No 1 in 2025.
Boy George, who is not Jewish, has recently voiced support for Jewish communities. In an interview with the Telegraph, when discussing his admiration for Jewish peers in the 1980s during his time fronting Culture Club, he said: “Over the years it’s been a really personal thing. It doesn’t mean that I don’t have compassion for Palestinians, it doesn’t mean that I agree with what’s going on in Israel, but I am always going to defend the people that I love. I have a lot of Jewish friends and there would never be a situation where I’d turn my back on them.”
He also voiced his support after the knife attack in Golders Green in April which left two Jewish men injured, saying: “We need to make our Jewish community know we support them.”
His new song marks an intensification of his support for Israel, having said earlier in the year that he didn’t have an opinion on the country.
Speaking ahead of an appearance with San Marino for their Eurovision song contest entry (which didn’t reach the contest’s final), he was questioned about the boycott of Eurovision from countries opposing Israel’s inclusion in the contest. “I have many Jewish friends, whom I’ve known since I was 15 or 16 years old,” he replied. “Are people asking me, as someone with principles, to turn my back on my Jewish friends? That is not going to happen – it will never happen. From the beginning of my career, I wore the Star of David … I feel very connected to the Jewish people. I’m not necessarily connected to Israel. I don’t really have an opinion on that. But the mission of music is to unite people.”
His characterisation of Israel’s action against Palestine as a legitimate military response rather than genocide runs counter to a United Nations inquiry, which stated in 2025 that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Israel’s foreign ministry called the report “distorted and false”. Last month, another independent UN inquiry found that Israel was continuing to commit genocide by targeting children. That report was dubbed a “libellous sham” by Israel.
Boy George was one of the most flamboyant and recognisable pop stars of the 1980s, with Culture Club scoring four UK Top 10 albums including 1983’s chart-topping Colour By Numbers. Hit singles include Do You Really Want to Hurt Me? and Karma Chameleon, which were both hugely successful in the US as well as UK, and have endured as staples on oldies radio.
The band also had a hit with an anti-war track, The War Song, which reached UK No 2 in 1984 and featured the chorus: “War is stupid and people are stupid / And love means nothing in some strange quarters.”
Last month, Boy George launched a new company called Artist Included, which will use AI to allow artists to create new versions of earlier songs which resemble the originals, as a way of wresting back control of master recordings. It launched with a new version of Karma Chameleon, which Boy George recorded then de-aged. “When I heard it, I was absolutely gobsmacked,” he told the Hollywood Reporter. “It sounds like another take from that original session.”

title: 15 Habits Infectious Disease Experts Swear By to Avoid Getting Sick
summary: They follow surprisingly simple rules to prevent illness.
full_text:
Dr. Daniel Griffin doesn’t like to get sick. The first reason why is obvious—the congestion, the aching, the cough that overstays its welcome, the unpleasant stomach symptoms.
The second is a matter of professional dignity. "It's almost like a gardener with dead plants," says Griffin, chief of the division of infectious disease at Island Infectious Disease Medical in Long Island, N.Y. and president of Parasites Without Borders. "I really don't want to be sick—because then the infectious disease doctor got sick.”
So what do infectious disease doctors and experts like him do differently than the rest of us when it comes to preventing illness? Not as much as you'd think. Infectious disease specialists aren't disinfecting every surface or hiding from the outside world. Instead, they've built a collection of practical habits into their daily lives—simple routines that reduce risk without making life less enjoyable.
We asked six infectious disease experts which habits they never skip.
Set up your kitchen so cross-contamination can't happen
Jill Roberts tries to take the guesswork out of food safety. "One of the major causes of foodborne illness is cross-contamination," says Roberts, a molecular epidemiologist and professor at the University of South Florida College of Public Health. "It's when you have something that's raw and you get microbes from the raw thing into the ready-to-eat thing."
Her favorite solution: color-coded cutting boards. Meat always goes on the red one; vegetables never do. "If your meat is always on the red cutting board, you're never gonna have your salad stuff on your red cutting board,” she says.
Order matters just as much. She makes the salad first, puts it in the refrigerator, and only then brings out the red boards and raw meat. Once she starts handling meat, she’s vigilant about sanitizing any surfaces she may have contaminated—from the counters and sink to the faucet handles and refrigerator door.
Wash your produce under running water—not in a bowl
Some people think rinsing produce means filling a bowl with water and letting everything soak. But that's not the best approach. "What you actually need is that little bit of friction to break the surface," says Dr. Heidi Torres, an infectious disease physician and assistant professor of clinical medicine at Weill Cornell Medical College. About 30 seconds under running water, while gently rubbing the produce with your hands, does far more than a passive soak.
The problem with a bowl is that you're washing everything in the same water. "If you have one piece that's contaminated, that water could contaminate the other vegetables," Torres says. Running water washes germs away instead of moving them from one piece of produce to another. It won't remove everything—Cyclospora, for example, doesn't simply rinse off—but it does reduce bacteria, viruses, and even some pesticide residue.
Microwave your kitchen sponge
A sponge is a nearly perfect habitat for germs: damp, warm, and studded with food particles, sitting next to the counter where you just set down raw chicken. "Sponges and wet dishcloths are really good at growing bacteria," says Kelley Steury, a clinical associate professor in the school of public health at the University of Nevada, Reno, who specializes in veterinary preventive medicine. Her routine: Rinse her sponge until no food particles come out, then microwave it for 20 seconds. Just make sure it's wet. "If you did it when it was pretty dry, you could start a fire,” she says.
Brush your teeth like it's infection control
Most people brush their teeth to prevent cavities. Torres brushes hers to prevent infections.
"At least 25% of infections that I see are related to dental disease," she says. Here's why: Every day, small amounts of bacteria slip into your bloodstream, and a healthy immune system clears them without you ever noticing. Cavities and gum disease change the equation. They allow more bacteria—and more aggressive bacteria—to leak into the blood, which Torres describes as "a highway to all your organs." In some cases, she says, doctors can trace an infection back to the mouth because the bacteria involved simply don't live anywhere else.
That makes brushing about much more than fresh breath. "Rinsing alone wouldn’t replace it, because you really need that mechanical brushing to break down that film of bacteria," Torres says. Hospitals have even started treating basic oral care as a form of infection prevention, she says—which is a pretty compelling reason to take it seriously at home, too.
Rethink the rug in your bathroom
Your bath mat outside the tub should be washable, hung to dry between uses, and tossed in the laundry about once a week. "We don't leave the wet stuff on the floor, because that's gross," Roberts says. A damp bath mat can also spread athlete's foot from one person to another.
As for the old-fashioned rug wrapped around the base of the toilet? Roberts would get rid of it altogether. Rubber backings don’t often hold up well in the wash, which means it probably doesn't get cleaned as thoroughly as it should. "Especially if you have kids, they don't aim well," she says. "You have splash-overs." In other words: Nothing around the toilet should be soaking anything up.
Leave your shoes at the door
Shoes pick up a lot more than dirt. Every sidewalk has been shared with other people, their pets, and whatever else has passed through. Dr. Cesar J. Figueroa Ortiz, an infectious diseases specialist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, would rather not track any of that across the floors where his family walks and spends time—so shoes come off at the door.
His job reinforces the habit. Hospitals are meticulously cleaned, but there's always "the risk of bringing pathogens with you on your shoes," he says.
Open a window before company comes over
Before guests arrive, most people wipe down the counters. Chin-Hong thinks they should be paying more attention to the air. "I respect air more than surfaces," he says. "You're probably going to have a bigger bang for your buck when you think about ventilation."
His solution is simple: crack a window. If the air conditioning is running, make sure it's bringing in fresh outdoor air rather than recirculating the same indoor air all evening, he adds.
Wash your hands like you're not in a hurry
Even infectious disease doctors don't always practice perfect hand hygiene. Griffin has watched colleagues race out of a public restroom because they were about to miss a lecture at a conference. "They're so anxious to get back out because they're missing whatever the lecture is, and they're not really doing proper hand hygiene," he says. "Even the people that should know better are rushing back out."
And when people do wash their hands, they're often rushing through that, too. "Nobody's singing 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' to time themselves," Griffin says (besides him).
His other rule is knowing when soap and water beat sanitizer. (Basically always.) Alcohol-based hand sanitizer doesn't kill everything: Norovirus—the highly contagious stomach bug behind many cruise ship outbreaks—is particularly resistant. Soap and water keep you safe, though, so if someone around you is vomiting or has diarrhea, Griffin says, head for the sink.
Use your shirt tail
Steury will happily look a little strange to save herself a bout with a germ. "Someone might look at me and think I'm crazy, but I'll use the bottom of a shirt, like my shirt tails," she says—or the hem of a cardigan, whatever's handy—around her hand when she has to touch certain surfaces.
She's selective about when she does it. What worries her are high-touch surfaces that are indoors and out of the sun: elevator buttons, soda fountain dispensers, and the door handle to a medical clinic, for instance. And if she does touch one of those surfaces directly, she waits until she can wash her hands before touching her eyes, nose, or mouth.
Decline the grocery-store sample
B

title: Amazon’s trying to launch a global satellite cellphone network in 2028
summary: Amazon filed an FCC application on Saturday to launch a new Leo satellite constellation that will provide direct-to-device satellite service for "voice, messaging, data, and emergency services." If approved, Amazon will begin deploying the new constellation of 5,105 satellites in 2028. It says it plans to partner with mobile network operators to offer direct-to-device satellite […]
full_text:
Amazon filed an FCC application on Saturday to launch a new Leo satellite constellation that will provide direct-to-device satellite service for “voice, messaging, data, and emergency services.” If approved, Amazon will begin deploying the new constellation of 5,105 satellites in 2028. It says it plans to partner with mobile network operators to offer direct-to-device satellite service, similar to Starlink’s partnership with T-Mobile.
Amazon’s trying to launch a global satellite cellphone network in 2028
The new constellation of over 5,000 satellites will offer direct-to-cell service using Globalstar’s spectrum.
The new constellation of over 5,000 satellites will offer direct-to-cell service using Globalstar’s spectrum.
Earlier this year, Amazon announced it’s acquiring Globalstar’s satellite network and taking over its deal to provide direct-to-device satellite services for Apple devices. Amazon says its new constellation will “use Globalstar’s spectrum,” adding that it plans to “collaborate with Apple on future satellite services using the expanded network.” Advanced Television points out that the FCC application also includes a request to use spectrum assigned to Iridium’s satellite network outside the US, even as Rocket Lab is in the process of acquiring Iridium with plans to expand.
The new constellation and direct-to-device service will “complement” the broadband services Amazon also plans to offer through its Leo platform. In addition to consumer satellite service, it would also be used for things like disaster response and emergency messaging.
Amazon says the new direct-to-device satellites “will process the signals in orbit before relaying them to improve performance.” The new constellation will be nearly double the size of Amazon’s initial Leo constellation, which is planned to include around 3,200 satellites. As of July 2nd, Amazon says “over 375” of those satellites have launched so far.

title: This is my new favorite laptop, but thanks to RAMageddon it already went up in price by $800
summary: Framework laptops always come with compromises in exchange for their unique DIY premise. Even though you pay extra for one compared to sleeker options from competitors, it's easier to excuse minor flaws for modular ports, easy repairs, and an impressive range of upgradeable parts. So what happens when Framework goes "Pro"? We get a one-of-a-kind […]
full_text:
Framework laptops always come with compromises in exchange for their unique DIY premise. Even though you pay extra for one compared to sleeker options from competitors, it’s easier to excuse minor flaws for modular ports, easy repairs, and an impressive range of upgradeable parts. So what happens when Framework goes “Pro”? We get a one-of-a-kind jewel among notebooks.
This is my new favorite laptop, but thanks to RAMageddon it already went up in price by $800
The Framework Laptop 13 Pro has it all. But RAMageddon spiked its price.
If you buy something from a Verge link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
The 13 Pro corrects and improves many shortcomings of the regular Laptop 13. It has a bright and sharp touchscreen, the best haptic trackpad not made by Apple, and an impeccable build and feel. Take all that and marry it to a great Intel chip and cutting-edge user-replaceable LPCAMM2 memory — both of which help to better balance performance and extra-long battery life — and you’ve got something really special.
But what if this all happens in the throes of RAMageddon, with ever-increasing tech prices? Well, it’s now expensive as hell, of course. Our higher-end prebuilt review unit of the Laptop 13 Pro with a Windows license was meant to cost $2,299 when it arrived at my door, but after fresh memory price increases it’s now a nausea-inducing $3,099.
An $800 price increase before reaching a single customer. We’ve seen lots of recent sticker shock, but this one especially hurts.
The Good
- Modular, repairable, and upgradeable, as we’ve come to expect from Framework
- Ultra X7 has very good performance (even for some 1080p gaming) and great battery life
- Excellent build quality and a great keyboard and haptic trackpad
- Nice IPS touchscreen with 3:2 aspect ratio
The Bad
- Very expensive because of RAM
- Chassis gets very hot under full load
- Slightly lackluster speakers
Component report card
- Screen: B
- Webcam: B
- Keyboard: A
- Trackpad: A
- Port selection: A
- Speakers: C
- Number of ugly stickers to remove: 1 on the Windows prebuilt (but only on the bottom)
The Laptop 13 Pro is an all-black machine with an exquisite matte finish. It actually looks black instead of some variation of dark gray, and it feels rigid and well crafted — far from the hodgepodge erector set of its bigger cousin, the Laptop 16, or the good but slightly lower-quality build of the standard Laptop 13. Inside the 13 Pro are new Intel Panther Lake chips with LPCAMM2 RAM, or it can be optioned with last-gen AMD processors and slower SODIMM DDR5 memory. Our prebuilt review unit has a 16-core Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU with a 12-core Arc B390 integrated GPU, 32GB of RAM, 1TB SSD, and four modular USB-C ports. Unlike other Frameworks, each port supports Thunderbolt 4, DisplayPort 2.1, and up to 140W charging so you can freely mount your modular expansion cards without any restrictions.
Everything here is really well put together. There’s no flex or give to the chassis or keyboard deck, even though everything’s easily disassembled with a handful of simple screws. The keyboard itself is great to type on. It maintains the nice 1.5mm key travel and tactility of the regular Laptop 13, but feels ever-so-slightly better thanks to a new one-piece aluminum frame. The 1080p webcam is a holdover from the regular model, maintaining its solid performance — it’s pretty sharp, if just a touch grainy in some lighting.
The big upgrades to the 13 Pro’s components are the new haptic trackpad and touchscreen LCD. This is the best non-Apple haptic trackpad I’ve ever used. It’s very responsive to “clicks” from corner to corner, and it feels and sounds just right. The new screen is still a 13.5-inch matte-finish 120Hz IPS panel with 2880 x 1920 resolution for that excellent 3:2 aspect ratio, but it’s brighter (700 nits) and touch-enabled. Until now, a touchscreen on a Framework was only found on the cheaper Laptop 12.
The 13 Pro’s audio comes from a pair of side-firing stereo speakers. The speakers were one of the weaker points of the standard Laptop 13, and they’re the 13 Pro’s biggest fault. The side-mounted orientation creates a tiny bit of a soundstage, but overall the speakers sound a little thin and treble-y with minimal bass. When I reviewed the Laptop 13, a savvy commenter pointed me toward open-source app FxSound to help with its audio woes. FxSound does help the 13 Pro sound noticeably better and fuller (with lots of EQ and boost options), but unfortunately for Linux users it’s Windows only.
The Intel chip and LPCAMM2 memory inside do a great job delivering on both performance and exceptional power efficiency. This newer style of compression-mounted memory is better for both of those factors, just like LPDDR5X, but without having to be soldered to the main board. The tradeoff for using LPCAMM2 is that it’s newer tech that’s generally pricier than DDR5 (gulp).
Thanks to this memory and the power sipping of Intel’s Panther Lake chip, the Laptop 13 Pro is a battery champ. Framework claims it lasts up to 17 hours during active web usage, but that’s with brightness at only 250 nits. Even at 80 to 100 percent brightness and keeping over a dozen Chrome tabs plus Slack and Signal open while occasionally streaming Apple Music, it took me around 10.5 hours to go from fully charged to 12 percent battery left in the tank. Compared to the Laptop 13’s AMD chip, the 13 Pro is outstanding.
Raw performance from the Ultra X7 358H is good too. While Framework bills the Laptop 13 Pro as “the MacBook Pro for Linux users,” it still doesn’t quite keep up with Apple’s much cheaper laptops. (At least on Windows. I’ll have to see about testing it on Linux in a potential follow-up like I did the Framework Desktop.) It’s not left in the dust, however, especially in graphics-heavy tasks like Blender. That’s where the 12-core integrated GPU, a major improvement over the regular Framework 13, shines brightest. I was slightly taken aback by its low scoring in the PugetBench test for Adobe Premiere, and I expected slightly faster rendering in our Premiere 4K export test (see our benchmark table below), but real-world usage hasn’t disappointed.
I was quite happy with how the 13 Pro handled Adobe Lightroom Classic. It took just over seven minutes to import a card full of nearly 2,000 66-megapixel RAW images (93GB of files), and about that long to render all the initial previews. It also performed well when bouncing around a large selection of those images and making various edits. I know firsthand that even a base M5 MacBook Pro is faster at this kind of stuff, but the Framework performed just fine.
While the Framework isn’t built specifically for gaming, running Windows 11 immediately gives it that strength over any Mac by default. And the 13 Pro’s potent integrated graphics are just fine for 1080p gaming at low to even medium settings — typically delivering 50 to 60fps on titles like Cyberpunk 2077, Battlefield 6, and Helldivers 2 when using Intel’s XeSS upscaling. It could even push to the panel’s full 2880 x 1920 resolution in Cyberpunk and use frame generation to maintain 60fps (natively rendering 30fps, which is fine for a single-player game like that).
This laptop does get hot under load or when playing demanding games. The chassis is about the same thickness as a 14-inch MacBook Pro, though a touch lighter, and it can feel like it’s going to light your lap on fire when under full load. Your fingers thankfully don’t get toasted on the keyboard in either the home row or WASD positions, but just beyond that, near the hinge, I measured it briefly hitting 57 degrees Celsius / 135 degrees Fahrenheit. It didn’t stay that hot for long, but thermals might be a slight concern for people looking to work this laptop hard for lengthy periods.
As nice as the Laptop 13 Pro is, there’s no escaping its new astronomical price and the turmoil surrounding its launch. Framework has raised prices on all of its device

title: Tariffs didn’t bring manufacturing jobs back to the US
summary: Today, I’m talking with Evan Smith, who is cofounder and CEO of Altana, a company that develops software tools to manage big, messy supply chain networks around the world. We last had Evan on in early 2025 to talk about how Trump’s first few waves of tariffs were starting to affect global trade and what […]
full_text:
Today, I’m talking with Evan Smith, who is cofounder and CEO of Altana, a company that develops software tools to manage big, messy supply chain networks around the world.
Tariffs didn’t bring manufacturing jobs back to the US
Altana CEO Evan Smith on the new normal of global trade.
We last had Evan on in early 2025 to talk about how Trump’s first few waves of tariffs were starting to affect global trade and what patterns Altana was seeing in all that macro-level data about shipping and trade. It was a very alarming and also very illuminating chat; Evan and I got into the existential weeds of international relations and economics almost immediately. It was a great conversation.
A year and a half later, and everything is somehow even more chaotic than it was the last time Evan and I talked — and that’s true both about trade and in the business world. And, as you’ll hear, we jumped right back into the weeds yet again.
Developments in agentic AI have changed what Altana can do, but like every software company, they’ve also changed how Altana can do it. You’ll hear Evan describe how AI is changing how they make software for a very demanding set of clients that manage billions in international trade — which is causing some big debates about how a software company even runs in 2026.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
And of course, what they do also needs to change more or less daily. Trade policy is changing rapidly around the world but likely nowhere faster than here in the US. Between the Trump administration’s whack-a-mole tariff policies and war in Iran, it’s very hard to keep up with the current rules.
That’s where Altana comes in. All that data coming from all around the world gives Evan a really high-level view of what’s actually happening. All those tariffs, for example, were supposed to bring manufacturing jobs back to the United States. So I asked Evan directly: Is that actually happening? Spoiler alert — you won’t be surprised to hear him say “no.” And while it’s clear the world still relies on global supply chains, the pressure placed on economic chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz is going to get higher than ever.
There’s a lot going on in this one — as you can tell, Evan and I really enjoy talking to each other.
Okay: Altana CEO Evan Smith. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Evan Smith, you’re the co-founder and CEO of Altana. Welcome back to Decoder.
It’s good to be here again. Thanks for having me.
I was looking over our last interview from about a year and a half ago, and boy, we got straight into the existential weeds of what it means to run the global economy and what was changing. People can go back and watch, read, or listen to that interview. It’s very good. I really enjoyed it.
The thing that strikes me about the past year and a half is that some of this stuff was theoretical the last time you were on the show. You founded Altana on the idea that globalization as we knew it — what you call, “globalization 1.0” — was going to come to an end, it was going to get more complicated, and the world needed software to solve it. The rubber has hit the road. It has gotten more complicated. It’s getting more complicated by the day. Even as we speak this week, it is getting more complicated. Even over the last year and a half it feels like it has gone from being a bet to being something very practical now. Is that how you see it?
Completely. One of our investors described Altana as, “an index bet on global dislocation.”
That’s a lot. Can I just ask you maybe a philosophical, emotional question about that? I get a lot of feedback from our audience. You have CEOs on the show and they talk about making bets in this way, and on the ground, it’s chaos. So, I get an index bet on dislocation. That sounds great on CNBC, right?
I understand exactly how that plays to that audience. How do you feel about that approach to the world, especially as a software company that kind of just makes a map for people, and how it plays out for regular people? title: Samsung’s 27-inch QD-OLED gaming monitor is priced right at $299.99
summary: The cost of QD-OLED gaming monitors is going down, even as many other PC components are still soaring above their normal prices. If your budget is locked at $300, Samsung’s 27-inch 1440p model costs exactly that much thanks to a recent $50 discount at Amazon. Finding a good QD-OLED monitor under $500 these days is […]
full_text:
The cost of QD-OLED gaming monitors is going down, even as many other PC components are still soaring above their normal prices. If your budget is locked at $300, Samsung’s 27-inch 1440p model costs exactly that much thanks to a recent $50 discount at Amazon. Finding a good QD-OLED monitor under $500 these days is pretty easy, but under $300 is pretty rare. Its G50SF debuted at $499.99, but has spent the past six months bouncing back and forth between $350 and $450.
Samsung’s 27-inch QD-OLED gaming monitor is priced right at $299.99
We also found deals on a $20 four-pack of Find My trackers, PS5 physical and digital games, and Logitech’s MX Vertical.
We also found deals on a $20 four-pack of Find My trackers, PS5 physical and digital games, and Logitech’s MX Vertical.
Despite being cheaper than Alienware’s awesome $350 AW2726DM and some competitors, the Samsung G50SF doesn’t make a ton of compromises. It has a thin design, variable refresh rate support, and the same fast .03-millisecond response time we expect from these panels. It has a DisplayPort port plus HDMI 2.0 and a headphone jack (most competing monitors have two HDMI ports). Unless you’re keen on getting a monitor that has a 240Hz or faster refresh rate, you may not mind that this one tops out at 180Hz (via DisplayPort), or 144Hz via HDMI.
Some other Verge-approved deals
- Maybe you knew that Best Buy’s in-house Insignia brand has its own AirTag-like Bluetooth trackers, maybe you didn’t. I recently found out, and they’re surprisingly affordable; You can get a four-pack of its Apple Find My-compatible trackers for $19.99 ($10 off). It’s a nice price if you just want some low-cost trackers with lanyard hooks to attach to luggage before a trip. The tracker’s coin battery can be replaced, and its 65-decibel alarm can help you find lost items nearby. Insignia advertises up to a 164-foot Bluetooth range outdoors (or 65 feet indoors), but connecting them with Find My will let you track them from greater distances.
- Sony is hosting a summer sale on physical PlayStation 5 games, and it includes fairly new and notable releases like Saros ($49.99, $20 off), Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 ($29.99, $40 off), and Death Stranding 2: On The Beach ($39.88, $30 off), plus several other great games worth considering. The sale is happening at Amazon, Best Buy, and GameStop. These are some of the biggest discounts we’ve seen on physical titles, and digital versions on the PlayStation Store are matching these prices.
- Those who work all day at a computer might be familiar with having sore wrists, particularly from using a mouse. A vertical mouse might help, and you can get one of the better wireless models out there — Logitech’s MX Vertical — for $46.80 at Woot with the code LOGITECH22 used at checkout (usually $77 elsewhere). The mouse recharges via USB-C and can last for months with a single charge, according to my colleague Victoria Song, who loves hers. It can connect to devices with its included 2.4GHz receiver, or Bluetooth.

title: SDCC 2026’s best trailers are heavy on cyberpunk and sci-fi
summary: San Diego Comic-Con took place over the weekend, and as per usual it was full of tidbits of news across film, TV, and gaming. Marvel revealed the next Ghost Rider (Ryan Gosling) and Black Panther (David Jonsson), while we also got release dates for God of War: Laufey (February 16th) and the fourth and final […]
full_text:
San Diego Comic-Con took place over the weekend, and as per usual it was full of tidbits of news across film, TV, and gaming. Marvel revealed the next Ghost Rider (Ryan Gosling) and Black Panther (David Jonsson), while we also got release dates for God of War: Laufey (February 16th) and the fourth and final season of Silo (summer 2027).
SDCC 2026’s best trailers are heavy on cyberpunk and sci-fi
Get your first look at Neuromancer, Blade Runner 2099, and more.
Get your first look at Neuromancer, Blade Runner 2099, and more.
But the best part of SDCC each year, at least for those following along at home, are the trailers. And 2026 did not disappoint: We got first looks at highly anticipated cyberpunk shows Blade Runner 2099 and Neuromancer, along with a new take on a Stephen King classic and the return of some animated favorites.
Here’s all of the best stuff in one handy place.
Amazon first revealed that it was working on a series set in the Blade Runner universe in 2022, but it took a few years before we got a glimpse at it. 2099 is set 50 years after the last film and stars Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer as a blade runner and replicant who are forced to work together. The show is a limited series — don’t expect a season 2 — and all episodes will be streaming on November 25th.
Mike Flanagan had a solid run at Netflix through series like The Haunting of Hill House and The Fall of the House of Usher, but Amazon poached him a few years back for its own streaming service. He’s starting out with a series based on Stephen King’s classic Carrie. This isn’t Flanagan’s first King adaptation — see also Doctor Sleep and The Life of Chuck — and it starts streaming on October 7th.
The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power
Elsewhere on Prime Video, the service’s big fantasy epic The Rings of Power is coming back for a third season on November 11th. Perhaps the biggest addition in season 3 is that Simon Pegg is joining the cast as the voice of a demonic Balrog creature.
Neuromancer
Apple TV has steadily become the preeminent home of streaming sci-fi, and so an adaptation of William Gibson’s seminal cyberpunk novel Neuromancer seems like a perfect fit. The new series stars Callum Turner as “a damaged, top-rung super-hacker,” and it starts streaming on January 22nd.
Dark Matter
Speaking of sci-fi on Apple TV, season 2 of Dark Matter starts streaming on August 28th, and a new trailer reveals just how complex its story is becoming, with a family searching for safety amd of multiverse of infinite worlds.
Futurama
Futurama’s latest revival has been hit or miss, but the next season — we’re at 14, if you’re counting — at least looks jam-packed with everything from pop stars to vampires. It starts streaming on Disney Plus and Hulu on August 3rd.
Common Side Effects
The first season of Adult Swim’s Common Side Effects was an excellent surprise, an animated series that both looked incredible and explored the real-world dangers of the US healthcare system. And season 2 looks like it’s going to continue that when it premieres in 2027.
Lanterns
If you ever wondered what True Detective would be like if it featured space cops, the DC universe has you covered. HBO’s Lanterns follows a pair of intergalactic investigators — played by Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler — who become “drawn into a dark, earth-based mystery with cosmic ties” while looking into a murder. It premieres on August 16th.
Onslaught
A24 isn’t exactly known for action movies, but that could change with Onslaught, the latest from Adam Wingard, director of the last two Godzilla vs. Kong movies. It’s about a mother trying to protect her daughter from “a rogue squad of genetically engineered super soldiers,” and it hits theaters on September 4th.
Queen of the Damned
The show formerly known as Interview With the Vampire (and The Vampire Lestat) is coming back for the next chapter of Anne Rice’s saga. Queen of the Damned introduces the vampire progenitor Akasha to the series, though there’s no word yet on when the new season will premiere.
Transformers: The Movie
Okay, this one isn’t actually new, but the classic animated film is getting a 4K re-release for its 40th anniversary. It’ll be in theaters on September 17th.

title: Chinese RAM company CXMT makes a $484 billion stock market debut
summary: The China-based memory firm ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) had a massive first day on the Shanghai stock exchange after its shares surged 466 percent, as reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal and CNBC. The stock market frenzy boosted CXMT's valuation to $484 billion, making it the most valuable Chinese company listed on the exchange. […]
full_text:
The China-based memory firm ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) had a massive first day on the Shanghai stock exchange after its shares surged 466 percent, as reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal and CNBC. The stock market frenzy boosted CXMT’s valuation to $484 billion, making it the most valuable Chinese company listed on the exchange.
Chinese RAM company CXMT makes a $484 billion stock market debut
Its shares soared 466 percent in the midst of a global memory shortage.
Its shares soared 466 percent in the midst of a global memory shortage.
CXMT looks to challenge Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix, which currently control the majority of the global memory market. But with demand from data-hungry AI giants straining the memory industry, device makers are searching for alternatives to keep costs low.
A recent report from the Financial Times has suggested that Apple asked the Trump administration for permission to purchase CXMT memory, which the Pentagon has blacklisted. Gigabyte has also announced that it’s adding support for CXMT RAM in some of its motherboards, while reports suggest Dell, HP, Lenovo, and Asus are exploring its products as well.
SK Hynix had a similarly big debut on the US stock exchange earlier this month.
Founded in 2016, CXMT revealed its first DDR5 RAM products last year, though they currently remain “roughly one generation” behind the top chips from Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron, the South China Morning Post reports. As of June 2026, CXMT held an 8 percent share in the global RAM market, according to Counterpoint Research.

title: Digital asset trading platform Uphold cuts 17% of global headcount as crypto winter bites
full_text:
Digital asset trading platform Uphold cuts 17% of global headcount as crypto winter bites
The crypto trading platform said the layoffs reflect a strategic shift toward its fast-growing enterprise business.
- Uphold has cut 17% of its global workforce as it shifts resources toward its rapidly growing enterprise business.
- The company said it is not closing any offices and will continue serving U.K., European and enterprise customers as normal.
- Weaker retail crypto activity accelerated the move, while demand from banks, fintechs and broker-dealers continues to grow.
Crypto trading platform Uphold said it cut roughly 17% of its global workforce as it reallocates resources toward its fast-growing enterprise business.
Eight five people in total were affected by the cuts, and this included permanent staff and contractors.
The layoffs, which hit employees across multiple regions, were driven by a strategic decision to double down on enterprise services as retail crypto trading activity softened during the recent market downturn.
“We’re recalibrating after several years of extraordinary growth, during which we nearly doubled our headcount, CEO Simon McLoughlin said in emailed comments. “Despite the current slowdown in crypto trading activity, we’ve never been more confident in the prospects for digital assets and blockchain technology.”
Founded in 2015, the New York City-based firm is a digital asset trading platform that lets retail and institutional customers buy, sell and hold cryptocurrencies, fiat currencies, equities and precious metals through a single account.
In recent years, it has expanded beyond its consumer trading app, building enterprise infrastructure that enables banks, fintechs and broker-dealers to integrate crypto trading and custody services into their own products.
The cuts come as the crypto industry grapples with a prolonged downturn. After three consecutive quarters of declines, the total cryptocurrency market capitalization fell to around $2.1 trillion at the end of the second quarter, while trading volumes weakened and retail participation slowed amid higher interest rates, geopolitical uncertainty and persistent outflows from crypto exchange-traded fund (ETF).
U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs recorded a combined $6.9 billion of net outflows in May and June. While flows have recovered in July, including a six-day streak of inflows, the rebound remains modest relative to the withdrawals seen during the broader market downturn.
Uphold stressed that it is not closing its U.K. operations or any of its international offices, adding that all locations remain fully staffed and operational.
The firm’s enterprise platform enables banks, fintechs and broker-dealers to integrate digital asset services for their own customers, an area the company said is seeing rapid growth.
The momentum in that business, combined with weaker retail demand, made the restructuring necessary as it shifts personnel and investment toward enterprise products. Further growth announcements are expected in the coming months, the company said.
The firm remains bullish on the long-term outlook for the retail market. “In 2026, we’re expanding our popular consumer app into a multi-asset, blockchain-enabled financial companion,” McLoughlin said. “By year end, the app will offer US stocks, tokenized securities, asset-backed lending, credit cards, prediction markets and enhanced DeFi yield opportunities on assets including XRP,” he added.

title: Tether’s XAUt gold token receives Shariah certification to expand Islamic finance access
summary: The certification could expand access to Tether’s gold-backed token among Islamic financial institutions and investors seeking Shariah-compliant exposure to physical gold.
full_text:
Tether’s XAUt gold token receives Shariah certification to expand Islamic finance access
The certification could expand access to Tether’s gold-backed token among Islamic financial institutions and investors seeking Shariah-compliant exposure to physical gold.
Tether’s gold-backed token XAUt has received Shariah certification from Amanah Advisors, a move that could expand access to the token among Islamic financial institutions and investors seeking Shariah-compliant exposure to physical gold.
The certification found XAUt’s structure complies with key Islamic finance principles, including full backing by physical gold, the absence of interest and leverage, and transparent reserves. Each XAUt token represents one troy ounce of physical gold stored in Swiss vaults, according to Tether.
The designation gives Tether a clearer pathway to market XAUt to Islamic financial institutions and investors that require Shariah-compliant investment products. Tether said it expects the certification to support adoption across markets where Islamic finance is widely used, including the Gulf Cooperation Council, South Asia and parts of Africa.
XAUt is one of the largest tokenized gold products in the crypto market. Tether’s latest reserves report showed the token was backed by more than 707,000 troy ounces of physical gold worth over $3.3 billion as of March 31.
According to RWA.xyz data, the token’s onchain asset value has climbed from about $700 million in July 2025 to roughly $2.5 billion.
Tether tokenized gold. Source: RWA.xyz
Related: Kraken moves closer to UAE launch after Dubai regulatory approval
Shariah-compliant crypto products gain traction
Cryptocurrencies have long divided Islamic scholars, with debates centering on whether digital assets comply with Shariah principles that prohibit excessive uncertainty, speculation and interest. As companies seek to address those concerns, Shariah-compliant digital assets have begun to emerge.
One early example came in 2025, when Bahrain-based AlAbraaj Restaurants Group adopted a Bitcoin (BTC) treasury strategy and said it planned to develop Shariah-compliant financial instruments to broaden access to Bitcoin across the Islamic world.
More recently, in April, Palm Azgar Finance expanded its Shariah-compliant PUSD stablecoin to ADI Chain, targeting the more than $3 trillion Islamic finance market. PUSD became the second stablecoin available on the network, allowing institutions to settle transactions using either a dollar-linked asset or a dirham-denominated token on the same infrastructure.
Meanwhile, Dubai has emerged as a leading crypto hub in the Middle East, continuing to expand its regulated digital asset market. Earlier this month, the emirate’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA) issued its 50th virtual asset service provider license, surpassing the number of licensed crypto firms in Hong Kong and Singapore.

title: Kraken parent Payward acquires Magic Labs’ wallet business
summary: The deal brings wallet technology to Payward’s enterprise platform, potentially reducing the number of infrastructure providers businesses need to integrate with.
full_text:
Kraken parent Payward acquires Magic Labs’ wallet business
The deal brings wallet technology to Payward’s enterprise platform, potentially reducing the number of infrastructure providers businesses need to integrate with.
Payward, the parent company of crypto exchange Kraken, has agreed to acquire the wallet-as-a-service business of Magic Labs, expanding its enterprise infrastructure offering as demand for onchain financial services continues to grow.
Payward said Monday the acquisition will allow it to integrate Magic Labs’ non-custodial wallet technology into Payward Services, its business-to-business platform for crypto trading, custody, tokenized assets and fiat on- and off-ramps. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.
The addition of embedded wallets allows businesses to offer self-custodied wallets directly within their applications instead of relying on third-party wallet providers, giving business clients a broader suite of blockchain infrastructure through a single integration.
Magic Labs said its infrastructure has been used to create more than 60 million non-custodial wallets for over 200,000 developers and has facilitated more than $10 billion in stablecoin transactions.
The companies expect the transaction to close in the coming weeks, subject to customary closing conditions.
Following the sale, Magic Labs said it will focus on Newton, a platform that helps users and applications securely authorize and verify onchain transactions without relying on centralized intermediaries.
