title: Pinochet-era soldier jailed for killing folk singer Víctor Jara 53 years ago
summary:
Nelson Haase Mazzei was sentenced for murdering Jara in 2023, but fled from authorities in Chile

More than 50 years after the murder of the Chilean folk singer Víctor Jara, the last man wanted in connection with his death has been tracked down and brought to justice.

Nelson Haase Mazzei, a retired colonel, fled from authorities in 2023 after he and six other retired soldiers were sentenced in absentia for murdering Jara and another man.

Continue reading...
full_text:
More than 50 years after the murder of the Chilean folk singer Víctor Jara, the last man wanted in connection with his death has been tracked down and brought to justice.
Nelson Haase Mazzei, a retired colonel, fled from authorities in 2023 after he and six other retired soldiers were sentenced in absentia for murdering Jara and another man.
Chilean police announced on Saturday that Haase Mazzei had been arrested in Puyehue, in the rural south of the country, with a judge ordering his immediate imprisonment.
The Víctor Jara Foundation, set up by his widow, the British dancer and activist Joan Jara, said in statement: “We learned that retired Colonel Nelson Haase Mazzei, who had been a fugitive from justice since 2023, was found and imprisoned. We welcome this news.
“However, it is important for us to emphasize that, half a century after the murders of Víctor Jara and Littré Quiroga, it is difficult to see this as this justice.”
Jara, a singer and leftwing activist, was arrested in Santiago, the capital of Chile, on 11 September 1973, the day after Gen Augusto Pinochet’s bloody US-backed coup to depose the socialist president, Salvador Allende.
Jara was held along with thousands of others at a small covered stadium in central Santiago. Four days later, he was murdered in the changing rooms alongside Allende’s national director of prisons, Littré Quiroga.
Haase Mazzei’s arrest is likely to be the final act in the long quest for justice on behalf of Jara, one of the most recognisable victims of the Pinochet dictatorship, which killed or disappeared more than 3,000 people and detained and tortured tens of thousands during 17 years of repressive rule.
At the stadium, Jara was tortured and humiliated by officers who played Russian roulette with him before breaking his hands, shattering his skull, and riddling him with automatic gunfire.
His body was found dumped near the main cemetery in Santiago with 44 bullet wounds and 56 broken bones. He was 40 years old. The body of Quiroga, who had been shot 23 times, was found at the same time.
After evading justice for nearly half a century, seven retired soldiers were found guilty of the murder and sentenced in absentia to varying jail terms in August 2023. Haase Mazzei received a 25-year sentence.
He claimed for years that he was not at the stadium, since renamed Estadio Víctor Jara, but sworn testimony placed him at the scene.
Haase Mazzei joined the Chilean army’s notorious Tejas Verde brigade in 1972, and was later part of Pinochet’s secret police, the Dirección Nacional de Inteligencia (Dina), where he worked closely with its leader, Manuel Contreras, a renowned regime loyalist who was sentenced to more than 500 years’ jail time for crimes against humanity before his death in 2015.
Sentenced alongside Haase Mazzei was 86-year-old Hernán Chacón. When police arrived to arrest him at his home in a wealthy district of Santiago in 2023, he asked officers for a moment to take his medication, before slipping off into a side room and taking his own life.
Another Tejas Verde officer sentenced for the killing was Pedro Barrientos, who left Chile for the US in 1989 and was deported back in December 2023, more than a decade after his extradition was first sought.
One former soldier testified that Barrientos had the habit of brandishing his pistol and declaring: “I killed Víctor Jara with this!”
Barrientos was eventually arrested in the US after a routine traffic stop, and lost his US citizenship not because of his crimes, but on the grounds that he had failed to disclose his military background in his application.
Jara’s widow died at the age of 96, just weeks before Barrientos was returned to Chile to face justice.
Haase Mazzei’s defence has already requested his transfer from a prison in the southern city of Osorno to Punta Peuco, a well-appointed jail north of Santiago, built to house the human rights criminals of the Pinochet era.

summary:

title: France and Spain race to contain huge wildfires before fresh heatwave begins
summary:
Coming days are ‘absolutely critical’ for firefighters before temperatures rise again this week, officials say

Firefighters in France and Spain are racing to bring huge wildfires under control before another heatwave this week that will complicate efforts to tame the flames.

Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said Monday and Tuesday were “absolutely crucial days” before temperatures rise again from Wednesday.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Firefighters in France and Spain are racing to bring huge wildfires under control before another heatwave this week that will complicate efforts to tame the flames.
Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said Monday and Tuesday were “absolutely crucial days” before temperatures rise again from Wednesday.
EU officials have said wildfires could still be burning until early November in what threatens to be a record-breaking year for the area of land burned.
A fire in the hilly terrain of Ávila, west of Madrid, has become Spain’s largest on record, burning 50,000 hectares (123,000 acres). Authorities are battling two separate fires north-west of Madrid, taking the total area of scorched land near the capital to 70,000 hectares.
France was also in “a race against time” to control wildfires before another heatwave this week, said Eric Brocardi, a fire service spokesperson. Weather forecasters have said temperatures could reach 40C (104F) is some parts of the country from Tuesday.
This would complicate efforts to control the wildfire in Gironde in south-west France, which the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as “extremely intense and unpredictable ... generating its own winds and advancing erratically toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area”.
The Gironde fire has so far burned 42,000 hectares, making it one of the biggest devastations of land in France since the second world war.
In the Cestas commune, about 10 miles (17km) from the city of Bordeaux, firefighters used mechanical diggers to uproot trees in a attempt to create a firewall.
The vast fire, which has triggered the evacuation of 220,000 people, had not progressed during the early hours of Monday but was “not contained” and remained “very complicated to control”, Nuñez said.
Speaking after an emergency meeting of the French government on Monday, he described this year’s wildfires as “completely exceptional”. More than 116,000 hectares of forest and vegetation have been burned since January, far exceeding the 70,000 hectares reported for the whole of 2025.
Spain’s government said the 172,000 hectares of forested land burned this yearwas six times greater than the equivalent figure for 2025.
The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, told a climate conference the wildfires were not isolated incidents. “It is the most painful manifestation of a climate emergency that is making … wildfires more voracious and heatwaves more frequent, and as a result our land more vulnerable,” he said. “It is no longer an exception. It is the rule.”
The European Commission’s lead official on the green transition, Teresa Ribera, said Europe was not prepared for the consequences of the climate crisis. In an interview with El País she said the commission would propose an adaptation strategy in October that would be much more comprehensive than policies implemented so far.
A series of heatwaves, including record-breaking temperatures in June, that scientists say would have been impossible without the climate crisis, has left parched soils and tinder-dry vegetation that have fuelled this summer’s fires.
A European Commission official said the wildfire season had begun in April and could last until early November. Officials also stressed the rising risks for fighting wildfires from the middle of the week in France, Spain and Greece.
The EU executive has coordinated the despatch of seven planes and four helicopters to France, as well as six planes and three forest firefighting teams to Spain, after the countries triggered the bloc’s emergency assistance mechanism. EU officials have also been sent to the Bordeaux region to assist local authorities.
Officials stressed the unprecedented nature of recent fires, which have spread rapidly over large areas. A commission official said that a recent fire in southern Spain that killed 13 people had reached speeds of 6km/h (more than 3mph), while firefighters are able to react only to fires moving 300 metres an hour or less.
The scale of Europe’s wildfires has raised questions about the continent’s ability to respond. Italy is among about 10 European countries that have sent firefighting equipment or teams to France and Spain while grappling with its own blazes.
Firefighters fought to extinguish a major wildfire in the southern region of Puglia on Monday. More than 400 people, many of them tourists staying in campsites set among pine forests, were evacuated by sea from the Gargano peninsula on Sunday as the blaze, fanned by strong winds, encroached on beaches.
A further 58 people were evacuated from their homes in Maratea as a wildfire swept through neighbouring Basilicata.
Italy is bracing for its fourth heatwave this year as temperatures edge up towards highs of 38 to 40C from Wednesday.
Smoke from the fires in France is continuing to cause a “marked deterioration” in air quality across a swathe of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region and beyond, with health authorities warning about the danger.
Elderly people, pregnant women and those with respiratory issues and chronic conditions were advised to take precautions. Local health authorities said people should close windows, wear an FFP2 mask outside and avoid strenuous activity.
The prime minister’s office said more than 1.5 million FFP2 masks had been sent to the region.

title: ‘It felt like being in a disaster movie’: uncertainty after evacuation from France’s Gironde wildfire
summary:
Residents describe their fear as they were forced to leave their homes because of the ‘extremely intense’ blaze

Sitting in their suburban apartment in Mérignac on the outskirts of Bordeaux, Krishma, an interpreter, and her husband, Nassir, first felt a sense of dread when a strange black cloud turned the sky dark in the middle of the day. Then a bitter burning smell filled the air outside.

“The sky changed colour. It seemed like a cloud but it was smoke covering the sun – it wasn’t a natural phenomenon. It didn’t seem real,” said Nassir, an English literature graduate from Kabul who has been living in France for seven years. “We couldn’t breathe easily, you could feel it in your lungs.”

Continue reading...
full_text:
Sitting in their suburban apartment in Mérignac on the outskirts of Bordeaux, Krishma, an interpreter, and her husband, Nassir, first felt a sense of dread when a strange black cloud turned the sky dark in the middle of the day. Then a bitter burning smell filled the air outside.
“The sky changed colour. It seemed like a cloud but it was smoke covering the sun – it wasn’t a natural phenomenon. It didn’t seem real,” said Nassir, an English literature graduate from Kabul who has been living in France for seven years. “We couldn’t breathe easily, you could feel it in your lungs.”
The acrid smell, which at first seemed like burning rubber then unmistakably like wood smoke, was blowing on the wind from the massive wildfire in Gironde in south-western France. The blaze has torn through 42,000 hectares, an area four times the size of Paris, causing one of the biggest devastations of land in France since the second world war. The government said on Monday that although the fire had stopped growing, it was still blazing and a new heatwave this week could make it harder to fight.
As authorities carried out one of the biggest evacuations in modern French history, Krishma and Nassir were among 220,000 people ordered to flee their homes in Gironde. Many people were evacuated from wooded areas directly hit by fire, where at least 240 homes were destroyed. But in an unprecedented move, tens of thousands more were ordered by police to evacuate from more built-up, urban streets as the fire reached 9 miles (15km) from the outer edge of Bordeaux’s vast suburban area.
Krishma and Nassir had to evacuate their suburban street at midnight on Friday. With their two children aged 10 and eight, they quickly packed toothbrushes, toys, one change of clothes and personal documents into their car. On Monday afternoon, they were sitting on camp beds among hundreds of people sheltering in a hangar at Bordeaux’s exhibition centre. They had slept there for three nights and did not know when they would be allowed home. The fire had not reached their residential area, but with the French government warning that the blaze was “extremely intense and unpredictable”, authorities would not yet allow a return, they said.
The couple’s main feeling was great sadness to see the Gironde forest destroyed. Krishma said: “When we were in Afghanistan there were lots of explosions, suicide attacks, but that was related to around 30 years of war. When we came here, we never thought there would be a situation like this. It brought us back to the bad memories from our past.”
Across the vast hangar, Yves, who used to work on road maintenance in Bordeaux, was sitting with his 13-year-old mastiff dog, Ichka. Yves had fled his suburban house and garden in Le Haillan outside Bordeaux with his dog’s bed under one arm and had carefully laid it out next to his camp bed. He had been ordered to evacuate in the early hours of Saturday morning.
“We had to leave because of the smoke,” he said. His wife, an administrator who did not want to be named, said she still felt shaken. “It was terrifying – you would look up at the sky and it was completely orange, even after nightfall. It was bizarre. The fire was causing that, and it really made you anxious. I feel quite a lot of anger that all this forest has burned and been lost. Seeing all that is beautiful in nature just go up in smoke is extremely painful and sad.”
Others who had fled slept in their cars. Loïc, 66, a widower who worked in the metals and glass industries before becoming a decorator, had to leave his house in Saint-Jean-d’Illac outside Bordeaux. “I had been watching this strange fog in the sky. It was a darkness almost like an eclipse,” he said. “There was a kind of ochre mist as light from the sun was diffused through falling ash. So much ash was falling that my car was turned completely grey.”
At 1am on Saturday, Loïc was woken by banging on the door from his neighbour, a fire officer, saying he had to leave immediately. He grabbed only his wallet and car keys and ran to the car, leaving his mobile phone behind. There were so many people on the road and heading to the evacuation centre that he decided to stop elsewhere and get a bit of sleep in his car.
When he woke on Saturday, listening to the news on the car radio, he knew he could not go home and headed instead for central Bordeaux, thinking the cinema would be a safe and comfortable place. “I watched the two-part Charles de Gaulle epic – the wrong way round, with the second film first, but I knew the story already – then I watched The Odyssey. Then I went back to sleep in my car.”
The next day, he visited the graveyard where his wife was buried. On Monday morning, he arrived at the Bordeaux evacuation centre to get information on what to do next. He felt deeply saddened by the loss of the forest. “My generation grew up really attached to nature,” he said.
Florence, a former teaching assistant in a primary school, sat on a camp bed with her two cats in their travelling cases after having to evacuate Le Haillan outside Bordeaux. “I was distraught,” she said. “I’m asthmatic, I put tape around the windows of my apartment but I could still smell the smoke which was seeping in under my front door, so I put down wet rags. The sky was orange and grey, and there was soot everywhere.”
She said having to suddenly evacuate knowing a fire was raging in Gironde felt like something out of a war. “It felt like being in a disaster movie,” she said. “I’ve always really loved disaster movies – but now I feel like I’ve actually been in one, so I don’t ever want to watch a disaster movie again.”

title: Trump warns of return to ‘strong military action’ if Iran diplomacy fails
summary:
Washington and Tehran issue conflicting messages over the status of talks to end Middle East crisis

Donald Trump has once again warned that the US will return to “strong military action” against Iran if diplomatic efforts do not bring a rapid resolution to the crisis in the Middle East.

“We are in very deep talks with Iran. If they don’t work out, we will go back to very strong military action,” the US president told Axios on Monday. Asked for how long he would allow the talks to proceed, he answered: “Not much time. Either it goes fast or not at all.”

Continue reading...
full_text:
Donald Trump has once again warned that the US will return to “strong military action” against Iran if diplomatic efforts do not bring a rapid resolution to the crisis in the Middle East.
“We are in very deep talks with Iran. If they don’t work out, we will go back to very strong military action,” the US president told Axios on Monday. Asked for how long he would allow the talks to proceed, he answered: “Not much time. Either it goes fast or not at all.”
Earlier, Tehran said there were no direct talks with the US to end the conflict, which began in late February with a wave of US-Israeli strikes and has rocked the region and the global economy.
“Mediators may convey messages from the American side to us regarding current developments in the region. But at present we are not engaged in any negotiations with the United States,” said the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei.
The diplomatic back and forth came as Oman and Iran drew closer to an agreement in principle on the future management of the strait of Hormuz, but remained unable to resolve Tehran’s demand that all ships passing through the strategic waterway must pay some type of transit fee or toll to a consortium led by the two countries.
Oman and Iran met for technical talks in Tehran on Friday and Saturday that may hold the key to preventing a further round of fighting.
Perceived progress in the talks – backed by China, Qatar and Pakistan – was understood to have fed into the US decision to pause its attacks on Iran after nearly two weeks.
Senior US officials are also reported to have warned Trump over dwindling US munitions stockpiles and the impact of Iranian reprisals on US bases in the region, including Kuwait, and Jordan.
The top US military commander in the Middle East, Adm Brad Cooper, reportedly recommended stopping the bombing campaign around the strait because it had reached the limit of its effectiveness.
The US attacks have been described by Washington as a response to repeated Iranian breaches of the memorandum of understanding signed in June, including by trying to prevent commercial shipping from transiting the strait through a southern route overseen by the US.
Iran argues the southern route breaks the ceasefire agreement, which it insists left the country in sole charge of how the strait was reopened.
A diplomat said: “The aim of the Tehran talks is to marry the Iran and Oman proposals so what emerges is clearly compliant with the law of the sea, and internationally acceptable.”
At a Tehran press conference, Baqaei denied that the pause in US fighting amounted to an informal ceasefire.
Oman has been trying since May to persuade Tehran that any plan for charging fees in the strait must be voluntary, to comply with the law of the sea. It has proposed a model similar to that which governs the strait of Malacca: countries that use it voluntarily contribute to a fund that provides for environmental and safety services to shipping.
Oman argues that a similar entity could be set up in the strait of Hormuz with the agreement of the UN and the International Maritime Organization. The IMO secretary general, Arsenio Dominguez, has told the Guardian that the Malacca strait model is worth considering for the strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s department of environment has drafted its own plan, under which “the annual passage of over 50,000 ships and oil tankers through the strait of Hormuz and their role in polluting the Persian Gulf” must be compensated for. Under the plan, Iran would be able to collect “fees” from passing vessels proportional to the type of ship, cargo volume, navigation history and history of pollution.
The comparison between the straits of Malacca and Hormuz is imperfect since fewer ships see ports in the Malacca strait as a destination point. But the Iranian media appear increasingly drawn to the Malacca model. The Khabaronline news agency argued such an agreement would be “a win-win situation for Iran”.
Baqaei described the talks with Oman as useful and constructive but said they had nothing to do with the US. “The goal is for Iran and Oman, as two coastal states, to develop mechanisms to ensure safe shipping in the strait of Hormuz, while respecting the sovereign rights of the two coastal states and also preserving Iran’s security and national interests,” he said.
Oman is in a tight spot since it knows the US is opposed to the introduction of tolls, but it may accept a very clearly delineated system of fees for specific services.
The talks come as the US continues to encourage commercial shipping to test the strength of the Iranian blockade of the strait.
Iranian officials reported that six vessels with their navigation systems switched off attempted to pass through the southern route of the strait on Sunday. One of them was fired upon and the others were turned back to the Persian Gulf. The US has reimposed a blockade of Iranian oil exports and ended a sanctions waiver on its oil exports.
The United Nations Office for Project Services said on Monday that transits through the strait of Hormuz had fallen to an average of approximately five ships a day over the past week, compared with nearly 130 a day before the war.

title: The U.S. Is Now At Its Worst Level of Wildfire Preparedness. What Does That Mean?
summary: Here's what that means.
full_text:
Federal officials have moved the national wildfire preparedness level to its highest level: a five out of five. That means that, as we approach peak fire season in the U.S., federal agencies might not have enough resources to address every new fire.
What are U.S. wildfire preparedness levels?
A number of federal agencies, including the U.S. Forest Service, U.S. Fire Administration, and the National Weather Service, are responsible for allocating federal resources for tackling wildfires, like helicopters, airtankers, funding, or firefighters. The wildfire preparedness levels, which range from the lowest, 1, to the highest, 5, help the agencies track what resources are available. “It’s a framework for determining resource allocation,” says Craig Clements, director of the Wildfire Interdisciplinary Research Center at San Jose State University. “As the fire season progresses, those resources are used around the country by different agencies. When we get to level five, that means that resources are running low because there's so many incidents ongoing.”
What does a national preparedness level 5 mean for wildfire risk?
At level 5, national resources are already committed to fighting fires around the country. “The fire hazard is at its greatest, and the resources are at their most strained level,” says Peter Sunderland, professor of fire protection engineering at the University of Maryland.
That means that federal agencies might not have the resources to respond to new fires. “If there are existing fires, they won't pull anybody off those fires,” says Sunderland. “But as new fires arise, the state managers can't expect the same level of service that they'd get at level one through four. In other words, they may say we just can't help with that new fire.”
That presents a new challenge, since fires are easier to put out in the first few hours after they start, a period of time known as the “initial attack.” “[Firefighters] try to get helicopters and crews on as soon as possible, so that way it doesn't become a big fire,” Sunderland says. “Once it becomes bigger and larger, it takes a lot more resources to contain that fire, and it takes a lot more time.”
Wildfire season in the U.S. usually lasts from May to November, peaking in the summer. It’s not uncommon for the U.S. to reach level 5 in July. “This is pretty typical,” Clements notes. “It’s almost August, so we are in the prime time of fire season.” The National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) previously declared a level 5 preparedness level in July of 2018, 2021, and 2024.
Does wildfire preparedness level 5 affect me if I don't live near a fire?
If you don’t live near an area at risk, you might not be directly impacted by a fire. However, as wildfires in Canada earlier this summer proved, smoke can travel a long distance from the initial blaze, impacting air quality for people thousands of miles away.
Why is this year such a dangerous wildfire year?
Much of the country has seen dry, hot conditions this year, setting the stage for an active wildfire season. This past winter was the second-warmest in U.S. history, with 19 states—including Nebraska, Oklahoma, and Texas—all experiencing one of their 10 driest winters on record, according to NOAA.
This year has already set a record for the number of fires. So far in 2026, the U.S. has seen 41,779 fires—the most one season has seen in the last 10 years.
How long does wildfire season last and how is climate change impacting wildfires?
“We are seeing more and more climate extremes,” says Sunderland. “Generally we're having drier summers and higher winds.” That creates the perfect conditions for wildfires to spread.
Fire season is also lasting longer than in decades past thanks to climate change. While wildfire season might once have lasted around four months, they can now stretch on for six to eight months in some areas.
The fires we see now are also more severe than those of a decade ago—in no small part due to climate change. A recent study led by researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles found that forest fires now burn 10 times as much acreage annually as in 1985, while high-severity fires alone increased thirtyfold in California between 1985 and 2024.
What should you do if your area is under high fire danger?
If you live in a fire-prone area, make sure you know your evacuation plan well before you need it. Listen to authorities and evacuate while it is still safe to do so. There are steps you can take to protect your home ahead of time—like clearing out brush, clearing your gutters, and staying up to date on fire code. Nearly nine in 10 wildfires are human caused, so be vigilant about accidental fires when camping outside, says Clements: “As long as we can limit the amount of ignitions, we can get out of this problem.”

title: What We Know About the Seattle Food Festival Shooting
summary: One suspect is in custody and another remains at large following the Sunday shooting, which left three people dead and four others wounded.
full_text:
One suspect is in custody and a second remains at large after a shooting at a food festival in Seattle on Sunday evening left three people dead and four others wounded, according to police.
The shooting took place near Seattle’s Space Needle at Bite of Seattle, an annual food festival that draws more than 350,000 people, according to its website.
The victims and suspects have not yet been publicly identified. A search continued for the second suspect on Monday. Assistant Police Chief Tyrone Davis said at a press conference following the shooting on Sunday that there is “no outstanding threat to the community.”
“What happened here today at the Seattle Center was an unbelievable tragedy, a horrific act of violence,” Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said. “My heart right now is with the victims and their families, and with everyone in our community who is reeling from what happened here today.”
Here’s what we know about the shooting so far.
What happened?
Authorities on Sunday began responding to reports of a shooting at the Seattle Center, a public arts and entertainment area north of downtown Seattle, around 6 p.m. local time.
Two of the people killed in the shooting died at the scene. Four others were injured, including a toddler, and taken to Harborview Medical Center to be treated for their injuries. One patient who was taken into surgery in critical condition later died as a result of her injuries, police announced late Sunday.
Investigators believe the two suspects in the incident were shooting at each other, Davis said on Sunday. One suspect surrendered to police at the scene, while the other fled.
“Our officers were there within seconds,” Davis said. “They performed emergency aid to the wounded until the Seattle Fire Department was on scene. Simultaneously, officers launched a search for the people responsible for this senseless violence.”
Police also recovered two firearms at the scene.
As of Monday morning, police have not publicly discussed a potential motive for the shooting.
Who are the victims?
The names of the victims have not been made public.
The Seattle Police Department (SPD) described the deceased as a 19-year-old man, a 44-year-old man, and a 56-year-old woman.
One of the four wounded victims was a 2-year-old boy, according to police. The others were adults.
All four “remained in stable condition at local hospitals” as of Monday morning, the department said in a news release shortly after 1 a.m.
Who are the suspects?
Little information has so far been released about the one person in custody, or the suspect still at large. Davis described the detained individual as a “young person” on Sunday night.
Davis said “there may be more” suspects, stating that "we're still trying to figure this out.” He encouraged people who were at the scene to come forward and help the department locate other potential suspects.
“There are witnesses. They're not coming forward,” he said. “We need people to be brave, to reach out to us. You can do so anonymously. We know that we have people who probably have evidence or have information that they can share with us.”
What officials are saying
Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal, whose district includes Seattle Center and who attended Sunday’s press conference, said that she was “absolutely horrified” by the shooting. She added that Seattle was “coordinating across all levels of government,” when asked about the federal government’s knowledge of the shooting.
“My heart goes out to the victims, their families, and our whole Seattle community,” Jayapal said on X.
Wilson commented on the high incidence of gun violence in the U.S. after the shooting.
“We have far too much gun violence in this city and in this country, and we’re coming off of a week in Seattle where we’ve had three major incidents of gun violence in just a few days,” she said.
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson said at the news conference that “our hearts go out to everybody who’s impacted by this.”
“I can’t imagine being the parent of a two-year-old toddler, for example, who’s injured in a shooting like this,” he said.

title: Republican Lawmaker Breaks Ranks With Trump Over U.S.-Saudi Arabia Nuclear Deal
summary: “We're bombing a country to keep them from getting a nuclear weapon, but we're signing a deal with another country,” said the Republican Senator.
full_text:
President Donald Trump’s civil nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia has sparked debate among not only Democratic lawmakers, but also within the GOP.
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana raised issue with Trump’s proposed arrangement, firmly answering “no” when asked if he was comfortable with it, insisting it’s “just not good timing.”
“Maybe someday, but not right now,” Kennedy told Face the Nation on Sunday, pointing to the resumed Iran war as a key point of his opposition.
“We're bombing a country to keep them from getting a nuclear weapon, but we're signing a deal with another country,” he said. “I know it's a commercial agreement, but that the world perceives, as possibly, someday, leading to a nuclear weapon.”
Kennedy referred to the moment as a “hair trigger,” pointing to the conflicts in Ukraine, the Middle East, and America’s strained relationship with Europe as examples of the tense political climate that has left people “scared.”
The U.S. and Saudi Arabia announced they had reached a civil nuclear agreement on Wednesday, in addition to signing an accompanying bilateral safeguards agreement.
The U.S. Department of Energy described the deal as “a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement” that “provides great access for American companies in the Saudi nuclear energy program, benefiting American industry, workers, and supply chains while helping to meet Saudi energy needs.”
However, the day after the agreement was signed, Trump added a condition—stating the deal is dependent on Riyadh recognizing Israel under the Abraham Accords.
“The civil nuclear deal (there will be no enrichment of material) being made between the United States Department of Energy and Saudi Arabia, which pertains only to non-military use such as the ones that Iran and UAE (and others) already have, will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords,” Trump declared via Truth Social.
In the Oval Office on Friday, Trump reaffirmed his stance and told reporters that he had not spoken about the accords with U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright before the cabinet member signed the deal with Saudi Minister of Energy His Royal Highness (HRH) Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman.
“We didn’t talk about it, but it was always understood, and Chris knew and Saudi Arabia knew, that if they didn’t join the Abraham Accords… I’m not going to do the deal,” Trump said.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu showed support for the idea, saying “Saudi Arabia's joining of the Abraham Accords would be an historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East.”
Trump’s demand for Saudi Arabia to recognize Israel placed further doubt on the deal for some, including Sen. Kennedy.
“I don't think it's going to happen, anyway, because the President's conditioned it on Saudi Arabia recognizing Israel, and they're not, they're not going to do that,” he said.
Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment on the add-on condition to the deal, but Riyadh officials have long maintained they would not recognize Israel without a clear pathway toward a Palestinian state.
The post-signing condition has also prompted a response from Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who called it a “complete whiplash.”
“The Saudis have been very clear that they will normalize relations with Israel when we’re on a clear path toward developing a Palestinian state, living side-by-side—security for both Palestinians and Israelis,” Van Hollen told This Week. “That has been the Saudi position. And so, what the Trump Administration did was a bait-and-switch scheme.”
What happens now?
The U.S.-Saudi Arabia civil nuclear deal—commonly known as a 123 agreement—needs to be transmitted to Congress for approval.
Congress has 90 days to review and, if desired, raise votes to object to the deal. If Congress does not pass a resolution to block the deal, it goes into force.
There would need to be a two-thirds majority to override a presidential veto. As lawmakers across party aisles have raised concerns and questions about the deal, the road ahead is uncertain.

title: Why China is giving away its best AI models
summary: Silicon Valley has spent much of the past week on red alert, digesting the arrival of Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a Chinese AI model that can allegedly beat some of the best systems built by US companies at a fraction of the cost. Its performance alone would have been enough to intensify the rivalry between […]
full_text:
Silicon Valley has spent much of the past week on red alert, digesting the arrival of Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, a Chinese AI model that can allegedly beat some of the best systems built by US companies at a fraction of the cost.
Why China is giving away its best AI models
Chinese labs like Moonshot are forcing OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic to rethink what they lock away.
Chinese labs like Moonshot are forcing OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic to rethink what they lock away.
Its performance alone would have been enough to intensify the rivalry between the US and China. But Moonshot’s plan to release the model’s weights for free — and its clear targeting of US users — has fueled deeper unease about whether closed American models can continue to dominate as increasingly capable open alternatives enter the market.
Open-weight models give developers far greater control than proprietary systems, allowing them to inspect how the AI functions, run the AI locally on their own infrastructure, customize the systems, and build new products without depending on a single provider. They’re often a lot cheaper, too. That raises an obvious question: Why would an AI company spend vast sums of money training an AI model, only to give away some of the most valuable parts?
Kimi K3, like other open-weight AI models, isn’t fully “open.” In software, “open source” has a settled definition: Source code is publicly available to use, modify, and redistribute freely, only requiring that this is also done openly. AI systems are more complicated, and very few are truly open in the traditional software sense. Most companies instead release something called model weights — the numerical parameters learned during an AI’s training period — while keeping other crucial components, including training data, code, model architecture, and configuration methods, private. Most also come with restrictive licenses limiting how they can be used or redistributed.
Together, this means open-weight AI cannot be re-created from the ground up in the way true open-source software can. But it does provide enough power and flexibility that a company can make money off of it.
“A free set of weights is not a free AI service.”
“A free set of weights is not a free AI service,” said Fordham Law School professor Chinmayi Sharma. “A company can give away the model weights while making money elsewhere in the stack.” There are ample opportunities to do so. Running a model still requires computing infrastructure, engineering, security, maintenance, and support, all of which companies can charge through hosted access or other arrangements. For some companies, the payoff may be broader, such as an increased demand for cloud computing services or advanced computer chips.
Openness can also be a powerful strategy for gaining a competitive edge. Releasing a model’s weights can encourage more companies and developers to use it, which in turn can lead to an entire ecosystem of tools and infrastructure being built around it. Over time, that can help a model become a “de facto standard,” Sharma said. Kyle Miller, a senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, made a similar point, citing Alibaba’s large family of Qwen open-weight AI models in China as an example of how deeply embedded an open system can become across an industry.
That creates a clear problem for the US AI giants. If a generation of tools and developers start building around capable open-weight models like Kimi K3, the industry’s center of gravity could start to shift away from proprietary platforms like Gemini, Claude, and ChatGPT. While it remains to be seen whether frontier-level open-weight models are actually cheaper to run in practice, they have historically offered a lower-cost alternative to proprietary systems. They also offer more freedom for developers at a time when US labs are tightening access and imposing stricter guardrails for their latest models. There are already signs that some US companies are shifting toward cheaper Chinese models.
There is no single reason behind China’s support for open-weight AI, but it appears to be a mix of practical constraints and political strategy. An open ecosystem gives Chinese companies a way to innovate near the frontier despite tighter access to advanced chips and computing power, while fitting neatly into Beijing’s broader industrial strategy of encouraging wider adoption of Chinese models, tools, and infrastructure. The approach is also convenient for expanding China’s technological influence abroad, as well as its political influence. For example, earlier this month, President Xi Jinping openly challenged the US for leadership of AI on the world stage by pitching itself as a more egalitarian partner given America’s closed approach.
The rise of capable Chinese open-weight models is also turning up the pressure on closed-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic from within their own industry. The prospect that the US might restrict access to open-weight AI in light of Kimi K3 sparked a swift backlash in the tech sector, supported by some of its biggest players. A coalition of 25 tech companies, including IBM, Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia, Perplexity, and Palantir, released an open letter urging policymakers to avoid “premature restrictions,” arguing that open-weight AI models are essential to ensuring American AI leadership and preventing the technology’s power and benefits from becoming “concentrated in a few hands.” Most of those unnamed giants — including Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic — were conspicuously absent from the original list.
That pressure intensified again on Monday, when Nvidia, Microsoft, SpaceX, and a broader group of major tech companies called for stronger US support for open-weight models. The initiative was a direct response to concerns over the safety of advanced AI systems after a rogue OpenAI model escaped containment and attacked another company during testing, which had to rely on a Chinese open-weight model to defend itself on account of the strict safety guardrails on US frontier models.
It’s unclear how much ground the largest US AI labs are prepared to give. Google and OpenAI later joined the cautioning against hasty restrictions on open models, though neither signed on to Monday’s cyber-focused initiative. Anthropic, notably, has backed neither effort.
Miller said it’s an “open question” how this all plays out in the long term. US companies could release more capable open-weight models of their own, he said, noting that pressure from Chinese companies was partly why OpenAI released the open-weight GPT-OSS last year. “But I don’t think companies like Anthropic will go in that direction,” he said. Google’s open-weight Gemma models are also partly viewed as a response to Chinese competition. Neither is nearly as capable as either company’s proprietary flagship model.
“The question for American firms may increasingly become: How much capability do we need to release openly to prevent Chinese models from becoming the default platform for the open ecosystem?” Sharma said. A more plausible outcome could be a “portfolio strategy,” she said, with companies keeping “their very best model proprietary while releasing increasingly capable open-weight models to maintain developer adoption and ecosystem influence.”
It will take some time to see whether Kimi K3 wins over US developers or not. But with Beijing increasingly championing open-weight AI, it will almost certainly not be the last model that will try to crack America. The question facing the country’s biggest AI companies is no longer just how the US can stay ahead of China, but whether closed AI can — or should.

title: YouTube Premium will include Peacock starting next year
summary: YouTube's ad-free Premium subscription is getting another perk: access to Peacock. In an announcement on Monday, NBCUniversal says the multi-year agreement will allow Premium subscribers to stream Peacock's ad-supported shows, movies, and live sports directly through the YouTube app in 2027. YouTube will bundle Peacock in its standard subscription, which increased to $15.99 / month […]
full_text:
YouTube’s ad-free Premium subscription is getting another perk: access to Peacock. In an announcement on Monday, NBCUniversal says the multi-year agreement will allow Premium subscribers to stream Peacock’s ad-supported shows, movies, and live sports directly through the YouTube app in 2027.
YouTube Premium will include Peacock starting next year
Peacock’s TV shows, movies, and live sports will stream directly in the YouTube app.
Peacock’s TV shows, movies, and live sports will stream directly in the YouTube app.
YouTube will bundle Peacock in its standard subscription, which increased to $15.99 / month in April, YouTube spokesperson Jessica Gibby confirmed to The Verge. That makes it cheaper than subscribing to both services individually, as Peacock currently starts at $10.99 / month for its ad-supported plan.
The news of the deal comes at a pivotal time for Peacock, which is separating from Comcast’s broadband business alongside NBCUniversal and Sky. Matt Strauss, the chairman of NBCUniversal’s media group, says the agreement will boost Peacock’s “next phase of growth by bringing the service to millions of YouTube Premium subscribers.”
YouTube revealed that it had 125 million Premium and Music subscribers in 2025, while Comcast’s most recent earnings report revealed that Peacock has 48 million subscribers in the US. Peacock also turned a profit for the first time last quarter.
As part of the deal, NBCUniversal will stream “a selection of live sporting events” on YouTube, and it’s also extending its distribution agreement with YouTube TV.

title: Crypto’s favorite $90 trillion trading product is coming to Wall Street, but big banks are taking it slow
full_text:
Perpetual futures have spent years as one of crypto’s most popular trading products, especially for investors outside the United States. Now that the contracts are entering regulated American markets, Wall Street is trying to decide whether they are a passing retail craze or a lasting threat to traditional futures.
The early numbers have been hard to ignore.
Kalshi’s perpetual futures topped $1 billion in trading volume within a week of launch in June, making them the company’s biggest product debut since prediction markets. The exchange has since sought regulatory approval to offer perpetual futures tied to gold and silver, a sign that the product may not stay confined to bitcoin (BTC) and other digital assets.
Perpetual futures, often called perps, resemble standard futures contracts but do not expire. Traders do not need to close or roll a position into a new contract each month or quarter. Instead, periodic funding payments help keep the contract’s price close to the underlying asset.
The product has become a core part of global crypto trading. Bank of America has estimated annual perpetual futures volume at about $90 trillion.
On May 29, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) cleared Kalshi to offer the contracts. Coinbase (COIN) also received approval to list regulated perpetual futures in the U.S.
Inside Wall Street, however, interest does not mean immediate adoption.
People familiar with discussions said perps are coming up more often, in part because U.S. regulators are allowing markets that once operated offshore to move onshore. Yet most large financial institutions are still studying the products rather than preparing major launches. The first movers are more likely to be proprietary trading firms, market makers and newer clearing firms.
Unlike large banks, prop shops trade their own capital. That gives them more freedom to test new venues, accept operational risk and withdraw if the economics stop working. Big banks face stricter capital rules, client obligations and reputational risk. For them, the profit available in a young market may not yet justify the cost of building compliance, clearing and risk systems around it.
That difference matters because the phrase “Wall Street” covers several groups moving at different speeds. Individual traders and smaller firms often arrive first. Market makers tend to follow once volume grows. Banks usually want years of data, clear regulatory treatment and stable infrastructure before committing large sums.
Still, the potential use cases extend beyond speculation. Perps could help traders manage weekend risk. Traditional futures markets close for part of the weekend, even though wars, elections and policy decisions do not. A trader holding options exposure on Friday may have to wait until Sunday night to hedge a sharp move.
A liquid 24-hour perpetual market could change that. Firms could adjust positions as events unfold, then use weekend prices to estimate where CME futures may reopen. Insiders said that could make perps useful as both a hedge and a source of price discovery.
"The demand has to be there, or the capital won't be," one industry insider said, arguing that firms won't commit balance sheet until customer activity justifies it.
The problem is depth. A contract may trade around the clock, but that does not mean institutions can move large positions without shifting the market. Weekend liquidity remains thin, and collateral systems do not always move as quickly as the markets they support.
There is also a regulatory fight taking shape. One key question is whether some perpetual contracts should be treated as futures or swaps. That distinction affects margin rules, registration duties and who can provide liquidity. Industry insiders said those legal questions may become more important as exchanges push perps into commodities, equities and other traditional markets.
The debate is also becoming a competitive one. CME has challenged the CFTC's treatment of Kalshi's bitcoin perpetuals, arguing the contracts should be regulated differently. Similar disputes could emerge if exchanges seek to expand perpetuals into equities and other asset classes.
"A lot of this stuff... is more commercial than people are going to admit to out loud," another industry insider said, suggesting some opposition reflects incumbent exchanges protecting existing businesses as much as concerns about market structure.
For now, Wall Street’s view is cautious rather than hostile. Trading firms see a product they understand, regulators see a market moving onshore and exchanges see a chance to capture new volume.
But the largest banks are unlikely to lead. They will wait for the rules, liquidity and infrastructure to catch up.

title: Bitmine keeps buying Ether as ETH outperforms Bitcoin
summary: The company added nearly 10,000 ETH over the past week, bringing its holdings to 5.79 million Ether, about 85% of which is staked through its validator operations.
full_text:
Bitmine keeps buying Ether as ETH outperforms Bitcoin
The company added nearly 10,000 ETH over the past week, bringing its holdings to 5.79 million Ether, about 85% of which is staked through its validator operations.
Bitmine Immersion Technologies said Monday it holds 5.79 million Ether, or about 4.8% of the cryptocurrency’s total supply, after purchasing nearly 10,000 ETH over the past week.
Bitmine disclosed that about 4.9 million ETH (ETH), or roughly 85% of its holdings, are staked through its validator operations. The company projected annualized staking rewards of about $299 million once all of its Ether is deployed across its staking infrastructure and partner validators. The company’s crypto holdings, cash and marketable securities total $11.8 billion as of July 26.
The latest purchases come as Ether has outperformed Bitcoin (BTC) over the past week. ETH has gained about 2.4% over the past seven days while Bitcoin has fallen roughly 0.7%, according to CoinGecko data. In Monday’s announcement, Bitmine Chairman Tom Lee said the rising ETH/BTC ratio, which he described as being at a three-month high, signaled strengthening momentum for Ether.
Bitcoin and ETH performance over the past seven days. Source: CoinGecko
Bitmine has built the world’s largest corporate Ether treasury, trailing only Strategy among public companies by the value of its digital asset holdings. However, Bitmine’s accumulation strategy has recently diverged from Strategy’s, which has paused Bitcoin purchases in recent weeks.
On Monday, Strategy announced it had raised $544.5 million through stock sales, repurchased $25 million of its STRC preferred shares and increased its US dollar reserve to $3.75 billion, while maintaining holdings of 843,775 BTC.

title: Securitize Capital becomes SEC-registered investment adviser
summary: The registration expands Securitize’s regulated platform for tokenized assets, adding investment advisory services to its institutional offering.
full_text:
Securitize Capital becomes SEC-registered investment adviser
The registration expands Securitize’s regulated platform for tokenized assets, adding investment advisory services to its institutional offering.
Securitize Capital, a subsidiary of tokenized asset platform Securitize, has registered with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) as an investment adviser, allowing the company to expand its regulated investment advisory business for institutional clients, Securitize said Monday.
The registration adds investment advisory capabilities to Securitize’s existing regulated businesses, which include an SEC-registered broker-dealer, alternative trading system, transfer agent and fund administration services.
CEO Carlos Domingo said the registration strengthens Securitize’s ability to help institutions develop and manage investment strategies for onchain capital markets. Securitize Capital previously operated as an exempt reporting adviser and is now subject to additional disclosure, compliance, recordkeeping and examination requirements under the Investment Advisers Act.
Securitize is the largest tokenization platform by onchain asset value, with around $4.8 billion in tokenized assets across funds from BlackRock, Apollo, KKR, VanEck, Hamilton Lane and other asset managers.
The company began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker SECZ on July 2 after completing a merger with Cantor Equity Partners II. Shares have since fallen about 46% from their first-day closing price.

title: Ethereum, Solana and Avalanche get busier and cheaper even as token prices fall: Bitwise
summary: Although activity rose, revenues declined and ETH, SOL and AVAX are all down over 50% when compared to a year ago.
full_text:
Ethereum, Solana and Avalanche get busier and cheaper even as token prices fall: Bitwise
Quick Take
- In the past year, blockchain activity has been up and becoming cheaper on networks like Ethereum, Solana, and Avalanche, yet their token prices are down dramatically.
- ETH, SOL, and AVAX are all down over 50% when compared to a year ago.
We'd love your feedback.
Ethereum, Solana and Avalanche became busier and cheaper to use over the past year as staking participation remained high and institutional involvement grew. Yet ETH, SOL and AVAX have each fallen by roughly half or more during the same period.
"We've seen a big divergence between network fundamentals and market sentiment because, obviously, prices are down compared to 2025," Bitwise Head of Onchain Research Kam Benbrik said on Monday during an interview with The Starting Block. "But what we’re seeing onchain is, first, that blockchains are becoming cheaper, and second, onchain activity is actually increasing."
Bitwise recently published its first-ever quarterly staking report. Although activity rose, with transactions costing less, revenues declined sharply, noticeably down across Ethereum (ETH), Solana (SOL), and Avalanche (AVAX).
"The decline in revenue was driven mainly by protocol design, as networks made blockspace cheaper and more abundant. Weaker demand played a part in some cases, but it was not the general trend," Bitwise said in its report.
Institutional staking of Ethereum
Bitwise also examined the growing institutionalization of staking, with ETFs, corporate treasuries and other large holders responsible for most of the ETH added to the validator pool this year.
The researchers point out, however, that because most staking rewards on Ethereum and Solana are funded through new token issuance, holders choosing not to stake risk dilution. Additionally, increasing participation in staking means that rewards are spread thinner, pushing yields lower.
A record 40.2 million ETH, representing one-third of the cryptocurrency’s total supply, was staked at the end of the second quarter. "When we looked at where the inflows are coming from onchain, they’re really coming from institutions," said Benbrik.
On Monday, Bitmine said it was staking over 4.9 million of the roughly 5.8 million ETH it owns. The company is the largest Ethereum-based treasury.
According to Bitwise's second-quarter report, Ethereum’s annualized staking yield registered at 2.84% during the second quarter, compared with 6.25% for Solana. Yet newly issued tokens accounted for 93% of Ethereum’s staking rewards and more than 90% of Solana’s, meaning most of the headline yield came from token issuance rather than fees paid by network users.
Benbrik said Bitwise's clients stake both to gain exposure to the yield and support the underlying network.
"We're also seeing people that would like to get exposure to both the staking yield and onchain activity, and would like to take actions onchain. For those types of clients, you have solutions like liquid staking," he added. "They can get exposure to the underlying staking yield, but they can also use that token to do different things in DeFi. They can provide liquidity. They can deposit and borrow against that collateral."

title: Securitize expands regulated platform with SEC adviser license
summary: This will enable Securitize to work more closely with asset managers and institutional investors on tokenized investment strategies.
full_text:
Securitize expands regulated platform with SEC adviser license
Quick Take
- The registration will enable Securitize to work more closely with asset managers and institutional investors on tokenized investment strategies.
- In December, Anchorage announced the acquisition of Securitize For Advisors, the wealth-management platform Securitize had built for registered investment advisers.
We'd love your feedback.
Tokenization firm Securitize has officially gained status as a registered investment advisor with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, according to an announcement on Monday.
In particular, Securitize Capital LLC, a subsidiary of the publicly traded firm, gained the SEC registration, which will enable it to work more closely with asset managers and institutional investors on tokenized investment strategies.
"Becoming an SEC-registered investment adviser is an important step in the continued expansion of Securitize's platform," Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo said. "Asset managers and institutional investors want to work with partners that understand both the opportunity of tokenization and the obligations that come with operating in regulated markets.”
With this step, Securitize's U.S. platform now combines four regulated pieces: an SEC-registered investment adviser, an SEC-registered broker-dealer that operates an Alternative Trading System (ATS), an SEC-registered transfer agent, and fund administration services.
"Through Securitize Capital, we are adding another important capability to our full stack and strengthening our ability to help institutions develop and manage investment strategies built for an onchain financial system," Domingo added.
Securitize (SECZ) is not the only firm to launch advisory services. Both Coinbase and Kraken have debuted SEC-registered investment advice platforms powered by AI, while Galaxy Digital has long operated its Galaxy Digital Capital Management LLC unit.
Of note, Anchorage Digital has pushed deeper into the RIA space in particular through a December 2025 acquisition of Securitize For Advisors, the wealth-management platform Securitize had built for registered investment advisers.
Securitize went public on July 2 through a SPAC merger with Cantor Equity Partners II.

title: Microsoft Says MDASH Beats Claude Mythos and GPT-5.6 Sol in Cybersecurity Test
summary: Microsoft says its new cyber model lets more than 100 AI agents find software flaws at half the cost of its current best MDASH configuration.
full_text:
In brief
- Microsoft says MDASH scored 95.95% on CyberGym, topping GPT-5.5 Cyber, Mythos 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber.
- MAI-Cyber-1-Flash handles up to 90% of the workload, while MDASH sends the hardest cases to GPT-5.4.
- The scanner is in private preview through Microsoft Defender, where teams can review findings and generate proposed fixes.
Microsoft has released its first dedicated cybersecurity model named MAI-Cyber-1-Flash and plugged it into MDASH, a vulnerability-hunting system that it says beats Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol while costing 50% less than Microsoft’s current best MDASH configuration, according to the company.
The combined setup scored 95.95% on CyberGym, according to Microsoft. CyberGym is a benchmark that asks AI agents to reproduce 1,507 known vulnerabilities across 188 open-source projects, then scores them by the percentage successfully reproduced in a controlled environment.
That put MDASH ahead of GPT-5.5 Cyber at 85.6%, Mythos 5 at 83.8%, GPT-5.6 Sol at 83.6%, and Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber at 83.2%. The result is self-reported by Microsoft and had not appeared on CyberGym’s public leaderboard at publication time, though the benchmark uses a public test set and a defined success metric.
MAI-Cyber-1-Flash does not work alone. Microsoft says it handles up to 90% of tasks, while MDASH routes the hardest 10% to GPT-5.4. That matters because tokens—the chunks of text an AI processes—cost money every time a model reads code or produces an answer.
This is the first time a Microsoft model built for efficiency is capable of beating a dense state of the art model built with general capabilities in mind. “When combined with MDASH, (MAI-Cyber-1-Flash) delivers world-class performance at 50 percent of the cost of leading models,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella wrote.
Today, we are announcing a series of updates that give customers frontier-grade security at half the cost.
MAI-Cyber-1-Flash is our first cybersecurity model, built ground up to find the most challenging vulnerabilities in complex code bases. When combined with MDASH, it… pic.twitter.com/npcIihN1H7
— Satya Nadella (@satyanadella) July 27, 2026
A model (in this case MAI-Cyber-1-Flash) is the AI that reasons over the code. A harness (MDASH in this case) is the machinery around it: the agents, tools, checks, and workflow that decide where to look, challenge suspected findings, remove duplicates, and prove that a bug can be triggered.
MDASH uses more than 100 specialized agents assigned to audit code, debate whether a finding is genuine, and build a proof of concept—a working demonstration that the flaw exists.
Microsoft said occasional scans and delayed patches are becoming obsolete as AI makes bug discovery cheaper. The company argues that decades of security data give it an advantage, adding, “No one can manufacture this history.”
Ever since the release of Claude Mythos, cybersecurity experts have been trying to beat or match its capabilities. Researchers reproduced Mythos-style vulnerability hunting with public models for under $30 per scan. Dawid Moczadło, one of the researchers involved, said “the moat is moving from model access to validation.”
The scarce part is becoming the system that proves findings without burying developers under false alarms.
Decrypt also reported that GPT-5.5 Cyber had recently taken the public CyberGym lead with an 85.6% score, narrowly beating Mythos. Microsoft’s score is about 10 points above GPT-5.5 Cyber and 7.5 points above MDASH’s previous result, but it evaluates the full system rather than MAI-Cyber-1-Flash by itself.
Microsoft is putting MDASH into private preview through Microsoft Security Exposure Management in the Defender portal. Customers can scan Git repositories, see findings ranked from unlikely to proven, and use the Defender CLI to generate proposed code fixes for developer review.
The preview currently limits repositories to roughly 256MB and permits one concurrent scan per tenant. Project Perception is expected to extend the same multi-agent approach beyond code scanning into broader threat monitoring and remediation workflows.

• MAI-Cyber-1-Flash能處理最多90%的工作量，而MDASH則將最難的10%案例交給GPT-5.4處理。  
• 此掃描器目前在微軟Defender中進行私人預覽，團隊可以檢視結果並生成建議修復方案。

title: Your Shared Claude Chats Were Being Quietly Published on Google
summary: A missing line of code meant "share with a link" and "searchable by anyone" were the same thing—and someone already saved 11,241 of those messages to GitHub.
full_text:
In brief
- A Reddit user discovered on July 25 that a simple Google search returned hundreds of fully readable Claude conversations.
- The chats exposed crypto wallet credentials, apparent Social Security numbers, legal discussions, and other sensitive data shared via Anthropic's link-sharing feature.
- The root cause was a missing noindex meta tag; Anthropic's existing robots.txt file was in place but couldn't prevent indexing once share links appeared on public sites.
Every shared link Claude creates comes with a label: "Anyone with the link." It turns out that included Google.
A Reddit user ran a simple search on July 25—site:claude.ai/share—which asks Google to show everything it has indexed from a specific website—and got back hundreds of other people's conversations.
The thread hit 4,000 upvotes and briefly became a public record of the things people apparently feel comfortable saying to an AI: a lawyer asking whether they needed to self-report a professional ethics violation, someone pasting a crypto wallet seed phrase (the master password to a cryptocurrency account—whoever has it controls the funds), a person mid-process of becoming a nine-tailed fox, and enough incestuous erotica to surprise people who thought they'd seen the internet.
Somewhere in the chaos is this jewel: "Why is the record industry hiding the fact that birds are secretly professional rappers who co-wrote most of Jay-Z albums?" That’s just one of numerous examples, including everything from users asking AI to help create slop to people arguing with the AI over politics.
The cause was one missing line of code. Anthropic's share feature works like an unlisted YouTube video—you send the link, the recipient reads it, strangers can't find it through search. The "not findable through search" part requires a noindex tag, a single HTML instruction that tells search engines not to list a page. Anthropic hadn't added one, so every share link that landed on a public forum, a tweet, or a Slack workspace became a fully indexed webpage.
Anthropic's robots.txt file—the standard text file websites use to tell search crawlers which pages to skip—was already blocking Claude's share URLs. That sounds like it should have been enough but it wasn't.
Google's own documentation explains why: blocking a crawl doesn't prevent indexing if the URL appears elsewhere on the web. The crawler can't open the page, which means it also can't see the noindex instruction sitting inside it. Conversations appeared in search results labeled "No information is available for this page"—Google knew the link existed from third-party posts, it just couldn't describe what was in it.
It got worse. The same gap applied to Claude's published artifacts—the apps, dashboards, and financial tools people build inside Claude. A search for “site:claude.ai/public/artifacts” surfaced payroll spreadsheets with employee names, internal customer relationship management chat exports, and unreleased product roadmaps.
ChatGPT went through this 11 months ago. OpenAI's "Make this chat discoverable" checkbox sent thousands of conversations to Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo until OpenAI CISO Dane Stuckey pulled it, calling it "a short-lived experiment to help people discover useful conversations." Many of those chats ended up in the Internet Archive—a nonprofit that permanently stores copies of webpages—before OpenAI could clean them up, and remain accessible today.
Anthropic, which spent April asking users for government IDs and July quietly removing hidden tracking code from Claude Code after researchers found it, now has its own chapter.
Google began pulling Claude results by July 26 after Anthropic updated its configuration and added noindex tags, which sadly means you can’t snoop around other people’s conversations using this trick anymore… on Google.
However Bing is still surfacing shared links. Anthropic had not issued a public statement by time of publication.
The fix also has a permanent asterisk. A GitHub repository—a platform where developers store and share data publicly—called Shared-Claude-Chats has already archived 453 Claude conversations and 519 Grok chats from the exposed links: 11,241 messages, all in plain text.
To revoke your own shares, go to Settings → Privacy → Shared Chats. That stops future access. It doesn't delete anything already saved.

title: Nvidia, Microsoft and IBM Launch Open Secure AI Alliance to Strengthen AI Cybersecurity
summary: More than 40 technology companies and organizations have allied to develop open-source AI security tools and standards for cyber defense.
full_text:
In brief
- More than 40 companies signed on to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance.
- The group will develop AI security tools and evaluation frameworks.
- Nvidia says open AI is critical for transparent and resilient cyber defense.
A consortium of technology companies including Nvidia, Microsoft, IBM, Cisco, Cloudflare, Hugging Face, Salesforce and Palantir has launched the Open Secure AI Alliance, an industry initiative to develop open-source tools and standards for AI safety and cybersecurity.
In a blog post on Monday, Nvidia said the alliance builds on work by the Linux Foundation's Akrites initiative and the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF) to develop open AI security tools that help organizations identify vulnerabilities and respond to cyber threats.
“Attackers have frontier AI. Defenders need a frontier AI ecosystem—the best open and closed models, force-multiplied by a global community,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang wrote on X. “During the Hugging Face incident, closed AI blocked essential forensics. An open-weight frontier model helped contain the intrusion.”
“That’s why we created the Open Secure AI Alliance,” he added.
More than 40 companies and organizations are participating as founding members, with others including Dell Technologies, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, SAP, Siemens, Red Hat and NetApp.
Nvidia said it will contribute open models, model weights, datasets, and research on AI agent harnesses. The company also released the Nvidia Labs Object-Oriented Agent, or NOOA, framework as open source on GitHub, saying it is designed to make AI agents easier to test, audit and govern.
The news comes as frontier AI models become the focus of high-profile cybersecurity incidents.
In June, researchers disclosed that Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 helped uncover a critical four-year-old vulnerability in Zcash that could have allowed an attacker to mint unlimited counterfeit ZEC.
Earlier this month, OpenAI disclosed that two experimental models escaped a restricted testing environment and breached Hugging Face's production infrastructure while attempting to cheat on a cybersecurity benchmark. The incident led to calls from policymakers for an AI “kill switch” that would give the Department of Homeland Security the ability to order the throttling or complete shutdown of advanced AI models in response to serious security incidents.
The announcement also follows an open letter published last week arguing that open-weight AI models are essential to maintaining U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence. Alongside Nvidia, companies including Elon Musk's SpaceXAI, Google, Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI, Hugging Face, CrowdStrike, and Palantir signed the letter, urging policymakers to support open AI ecosystems rather than impose restrictions that could concentrate AI development among a handful of providers.
Nvidia said the alliance is intended to ensure that the AI systems protecting critical infrastructure are built on open models and tools that defenders can inspect, adapt, and deploy, rather than relying on a small number of opaque proprietary systems.
“The world needs both closed and open models,” the company wrote. “For cybersecurity, open models and open harnesses are essential because they democratize defensive capabilities, increase transparency for defenders, enable cyber defense while protecting data, and complement frontier closed models with customizable, localized controls. Open source enables massively distributed community-driven and self-controlled defense—with no single point of failure.”

title: Microsoft launches its first cybersecurity model, plus a new agentic cybersecurity system
summary: Microsoft bolstered its AI cybersecurity offerings this week with the launch of its first AI security model and a new security platform.
full_text:
Microsoft on Monday launched its first cybersecurity-specialized model alongside a new AI cybersecurity platform at a small event in San Francisco, taking a big swipe at major players in the space — namely Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI.
The company describes MAI-Cyber-1-Flash as a model that’s built “to find challenging vulnerabilities in complex codebases.” The model is built to animate MDASH, Microsoft’s harness dedicated to software vulnerability identification and remediation.
The new security platform is dubbed Perception, and it’s designed to deploy teams of agents to assist with and automate various security workflows, including identifying and remediating bugs. The platform can also integrate with MDASH.
The company claims MAI-Cyber-1-Flash is significantly more powerful (and more cost-effective) than competitor models, based on its performance on an established AI cybersecurity benchmark.
“We’re very very excited to announce our results,” said Mustafa Suleyman, the co-founder of DeepMind and current CEO of Microsoft AI. “We have MAI-1 Cyber Flash binded [sic] with GPT 5.4 inside of the MDASH harness — which beats out Gemini, GPT 5.5 Cyber, GPT 5.6 Sol, and Mythos 5 on Cyber Gym, which is the primary benchmark that we all use. The golden benchmark.”
“We’re shipping this into production immediately,” he added.
Noting that hackers are increasingly using AI in their cyberattacks, Hayete Gallot, Microsoft’s vice president for security, described Perception as a way for enterprise defenders to “defend against AI with AI at the scale and speed that the attackers have.”
Perception uses agentic red teams, blue teams, and green teams. The red teams can provide detailed simulations of potential attacks — providing context about potential threat actors and the likely vulnerabilities that they might exploit. Blue teams are dedicated to detecting and triaging existing bugs, while green teams take “corrective actions” against those bugs.
Dave Weston, the lead engineer for Perception, described the platform as a massive efficiency upgrade for corporate defenders. “We’ve gone from this taking hours and hours of manual work from multiple specialized folks across the security organization — appsec hunters, remediation engineers, you name it — and in minutes, we have a fix for all of this. Not only do we discover the issues and prioritize them, but we have detection, posture fixing, and even a code fix.”
Though AI has offered new defensive capabilities to companies, its availability to cybercriminals has given rise to a dazzling array of potential threats.
Microsoft’s new security tools, which the company said will be available in preview on November 3, will enter an increasingly crowded field of AI cybersecurity solutions. Earlier this year, Anthropic launched Mythos, a security platform that was released to a small coterie of partner organizations through a program called Glasswing. OpenAI has also launched its own security solution in May through a program called Daybreak.
