title: Fourth heatwave grips parts of UK with 35C forecast
summary: A fourth heatwave of the year is now under way for parts of the UK, with temperatures expected to climb into the mid-30s Celsius later this week.
full_text:
Fourth heatwave grips parts of UK with 35C forecast
- Published
A fourth heatwave of the year is now under way for parts of the UK, with temperatures expected to climb into the mid-30s Celsius later this week.
This latest spell of heatwave threshold-level temperatures is expected to peak on Wednesday in the south-east and east of England.
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has warned the rising temperatures could increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.
It has issued amber heat health alerts, external for much of eastern England that come into force on Wednesday.
North-south split
The heatwave will not be felt in all parts of the country, with clouds and outbreaks of rain continuing in Northern Ireland, Scotland and northern England.
The hot weather will be focused on central, southern and eastern England on Tuesday thought it may spread slightly northwards and westwards into midweek.
Temperatures in England and Wales are forecast to rise to around 25-32C for the next few days with Wednesday likely to see the peak, with readings of 30-35C across the Midlands, southern and eastern England.
Scotland and Northern Ireland will generally remain cooler and showery with temperatures in the high teens or low to mid-20s Celsius.
Current forecasts suggest that the intense heat across southern and central parts of the UK this week will be short-lived compared to the three previous widespread heatwaves this summer.
Some isolated showers may arrive later in the week.
Heat health alerts issued
July 2026 has been notably hot. The Met Office says the UK mean temperature so far this month is 17.5C, which currently makes it the second hottest of any month on record, behind only July 2006 (17.8C).
The ongoing heat means the East Midlands, East of England, London, and the South East are all under amber alerts heat health alerts from 09:00 on Wednesday until 09:00 Thursday.
The UKHSA warns that significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures, especially as much of July has seen temperatures well above average by day and by night.
Yorkshire and the Humber, the West Midlands and the South West are all under less severe yellow alerts for the same period.
When will it rain?
An ongoing lack of rain means hosepipe bans are in force for millions of households and dry vegetation has provided fuel for wildfires to burn in a number of areas.
Though there was some rain this weekend, the driest locations - including central, southern and eastern England - saw little, if any, meaningful rainfall.
According to the Met Office, rainfall in England this month is at 4.4mm, one of the lowest levels on record, behind only February 1891 (3.3mm) and tied with June 1925 (4.4mm).
Rainfall levels in Wales, where drought was triggered last week in some parts, are so low that July 2026 is currently the fourth driest of any month since records began.
As this next spell of hot weather develops across England and Wales, the lack of significant rain means dry ground and low soil moisture levels are likely to become an increasing concern.
Wisley in Surrey has been one of the driest locations in south-east England with 40 days of no rain as of 27 July.
Though some isolated showers are expected later in the week, there is no significant rain in the forecast.
You can check the latest for your area on the BBC Weather website or app.

title: Hundreds of thousands of women get morning-after pill via free pharmacy service
summary: Since October, the morning-after pill has been made available free-of-charge at high street pharmacies under a new scheme in England.
full_text:
Hundreds of thousands of women get morning-after pill via free pharmacy service
- Published
Hundreds of thousands of women have used a new, free morning-after pill service at high street pharmacies in England, figures reveal.
The scheme launched in October to improve access and save women from having to book a GP or sexual health clinic appointment.
New NHS figures show that almost 305,000 doses were given out at pharmacies between October 2025 and March 2026.
Meanwhile, the number of women asking pharmacists about going on the regular oral contraceptive pill more than doubled, from around 50,000 to more than 115,000 in the 12 months to February 2026.
Easier to access
The morning-after pill, known as emergency contraception, external, is medication designed to prevent unwanted pregnancies. It usually has to be taken within three to five days of having unprotected sex. The sooner it is taken, the more effective it is.
It works by delaying or preventing the release of an egg, but will only prevent pregnancy if ovulation has not already happened.
Alternatively, women can visit a doctor or nurse to have a coil or intrauterine device (IUD) fitted to prevent pregnancy at any time during their menstrual cycle. To be effective, it needs to be fitted within 120 hours or five days of unprotected sex.
The government said making the morning-after pill available free from pharmacies would end the "unfair" barriers and postcode lottery some women faced - with access varying dramatically depending on where they live.
Under the scheme, women can visit their local pharmacy and have a confidential consultation with a pharmacist or trained pharmacy technician, before receiving the medication on the same day.
Prior to this, women had to book an appointment with their GP, sexual health clinic or pharmacy to get the morning-after pill. Women could also access it privately, as they still can now.
In 2024/25, there were around 150,000 NHS prescriptions for the morning-after pill - far fewer than under the new service.
Dr Sue Mann, NHS National Clinical Director for Women's Health, said the pharmacy service was a "major step forward for women's health", with "no appointment, no waiting and no judgement".
"This service is already making a real impact, particularly for women living in more deprived communities, by making contraception easier to access closer to home," she added.
Women can check online, external to find their nearest participating pharmacy. All pharmacists and pharmacy technicians delivering the service have received specialist training to provide emergency contraception and wider contraceptive care.

title: Why attachment theory is everywhere right now and how it can help you
summary: Attachment theory is everywhere right now, but what is it and how can you use it to improve your relationships?
full_text:
Why attachment theory is everywhere right now and how it can help you
- Published
For Lizzy, relationships always seemed to end the same way. "I would get to a second or third date and find something wrong with them."
Just as things began to feel real, the connection she longed for would suddenly feel uncomfortable, even threatening. And she would pull away.
For years, she couldn't explain why - until she came across attachment theory.
And it was the description of a so-called fearful-avoidant - one of the four attachment styles - which felt strikingly familiar.
It describes someone who wants closeness, but worries that people in their life will eventually reject or abandon them.
"It was like I had found the missing piece to a puzzle that I've been trying to solve for years," Lizzy says.
She is not alone. Attachment theory has exploded into the public consciousness.
On TikTok, videos tagged #AttachmentTheory have racked up hundreds of millions of views.
And in popular culture it's used to explain everything from Marianne and Connell's relationship in the hit book and TV series Normal People to the lyrics of Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's record-breaking number one track Rein Me In.
"The first time I listened to it I started crying," Lizzy says.
For her, the song gave voice to both sides of avoidant attachment: the fear that can make love feel unbearable, and the confusion felt by the partner left behind.
What are the four attachment styles?
First developed in the 1950s by British psychiatrist John Bowlby, attachment theory suggests that the bonds we form with early caregivers shape our expectations of relationships.
If support is consistently available, you are more likely to see others as reliable. If care is unpredictable or emotionally distant, you may develop strategies designed to protect yourself from disappointment or distress.
There are four attachment styles - anxious, avoidant, fearful-avoidant and secure. In simple terms they are defined as follows:
- Anxious attachment is often associated with worries about rejection or abandonment. People with this attachment style may seek frequent reassurance from those close to them and struggle with low self-worth. They can be highly attuned to changes in other people's behaviour. 
- People with an avoidant attachment style prioritise their independence and find it difficult to open up emotionally or rely on others. They may subconsciously view intimacy as a threat to their autonomy and withdraw when relationships become too emotionally close. 
- Those with fearful-avoidant attachment (also known as disorganised) want close relationships but often struggle to feel safe in them. They may seek connection one moment and withdraw the next. 
- Someone who is secure is comfortable with both closeness and independence in relationships. They are generally able to trust others, communicate their needs and seek support when they need it. 
Research suggests that secure people tend to fare better not only in romantic relationships, but across life. They manage stress more effectively, cope better with setbacks like rejection or loss and are better colleagues and managers in the workplace.
And what began as a way to understand relationships is increasingly influencing how people navigate them.
Across social media, attachment styles are used to reassess friendships, make sense of family tensions or rule out potential partners.
And relationship coaches promise to reveal the hidden signs of emotional unavailability in a partner or the ways to heal anxious attachment.
The misconceptions around attachment theory
Dr Pascal Vrticka, an associate professor of psychology at the University of Essex, has spent nearly two decades studying attachment.
He says the theory offers "one of the best explanations" for the differences in how people seek support and connection with others.
And while he's glad to see it reach a wider audience, he worries the way it is interpreted can be "outdated, misinformed and, in the worst case, harmful."
"I think one problem is that people are overgeneralising it and using it in contexts where it might not be the best framework to explain our behaviour," he says.
Part of the issue, he explains, is that initial assumptions around attachment theory have evolved since it was first developed.
Vrticka says one of the biggest misconceptions is that attachment styles are fixed.
Although studies have found that they can show a degree of stability over time, Vrticka says change is possible.
"The good news is that the evidence shows that secure attachment is the most stable. Which means that once you become secure, you tend to stay secure."
He says attachment is often reshaped during periods of transition, particularly during adolescence, when young people begin forming close relationships beyond their family.
Later events in our lives, like entering a new relationship, experiencing a breakup or dealing with bereavement, can also be influential.
But Vrticka says that change is gradual and professional support is likely to be needed for people with more entrenched attachment patterns.
It's that nuance, Lizzy says, which is often lost in discussions of attachment theory.
She says some people can be "quick to assume the worst" and reduce others to labels.
However, while she says people with insecure attachment styles should be viewed with more empathy, she acknowledges the importance of self-awareness.
"For me, I know that my avoidant tendencies are toxic and it would be unfair for me to date someone right now," she says.
But, she adds, that doesn't mean people with insecure attachments are incapable of healthy relationships. "It is on you to acknowledge it and put in the work to heal."
How do you become secure?
Few have played a more influential role in bringing attachment to the mainstream than Dr Amir Levine.
His book Attached, co-written with Rachel Heller, was first published in 2010 and has since sold millions of copies around the world.
But in his latest book, Levine shifts the focus from identifying attachment styles to ask a different question: how do you become secure?
Part of the answer, he argues, lies in what he calls "SIMIs" - seemingly insignificant minor interactions.
A text from a friend asking about your weekend. A smile from a stranger.
"The brain monitors small interactions all the time," Levine says. "That's what attachment is about. It's a monitoring system for safety."
And he says these interactions gradually shape what the brain expects from relationships.
Positive experiences build evidence that people can be trusted and relied upon, helping move someone towards what he calls "secure mode".
But equally, a delayed response or a friend failing to follow through on plans can trigger subtle stress responses in the nervous system.
Importantly, Levine says it's possible to have different attachment styles with different people.
So he encourages people to identify the relationships in their lives that already make them feel safe and understood, and to use them "as a vehicle for becoming more secure overall".
And the idea that security can be built through current relationships reflects a broader shift away from seeing attachment as just the result of childhood experiences.
For some, discovering attachment theory can involve re-examining family relationships, which can potentially lead to resentment. But Levine says "it's not just about where you started, but what happens afterwards".
"If that way of thinking helps you understand yourself and move forward, that's useful," he says.
"But if it makes you feel stuck or damaged, then it's not accurate because people really can change."
Levine also argues that insecure attachments can in themselves be strengths.
He says anxious people are often acutely tuned into relationships, spotting subtle shifts in mood, tone and behaviour that others miss, while avoidant people can be fiercely independent and perform well under pressure.

title: China's new challenge as natural disasters strike - fake AI videos
summary: Storms and flooding incidents over the last few months have seen fake videos inundating social media.
full_text:
China's new challenge as natural disasters strike - fake AI videos
- Published
As China deals with the fallout of Typhoon Noul that made landfall over the weekend, officials will be painfully aware that they will likely have an additional challenge to deal with: dangerously misleading videos created with Artificial Intelligence (AI).
Powerful storms and flooding incidents over the last few months have seen fake videos inundating social media platforms – these include images of dead bodies floating in floodwaters, the false depiction of severe flooding in areas actually not affected and others with blatantly fake details of emergency response efforts.
In some areas, videos containing false information about power outages prompted residents to panic buy emergency supplies.
Other videos capitalise on real-life incidents.
Flooding in Hengzhou city, Guangxi in early July caused hundreds of snakes to escape from a breeding farm. Then fake images were also published showing crocodiles being released into a river.
In an already tense and dangerous situation involving mass evacuations and complex rescue operations, authorities want to avoid panic. Now they fear that AI technology - which China is pouring billions of dollars into - is providing simple, accessible tools that can be used to trick the public.
"Many of these content creators use disaster news to try to gain followers, knowing that more sensational or exaggerated content will garner more likes and more views. They are deliberately fabricating information to grab people's attention," Huang Zhihua, Deputy Chief in charge of online public security for Zhejiang Police Department told Chinese state media.
In recent weeks, there have been arrests and punishment – ranging from detention awaiting criminal prosecution to fines – for the creation of bogus reports and video content.
But experts are warning that an unprecedented crisis of misinformation could be looming.
In an article published by the newspaper of the Communist Party's Central Party School, Professor Chen Bin said, "AI dramatically lowers the technical barriers to producing false information. Individuals no longer require sophisticated technical skills. By simply prompting AI tools, they can rapidly generate convincing text, images, audio and video… which is highly realistic but entirely fabricated content, manufactured on a large scale."
Professor Gao Fuping, from the East China University of Political Science and Law, told the BBC that motivation for the publishing of such false content ranges from those who do it "to create something amusing without thinking about the consequences", to those who want to "generate traffic for personal gain" or those who wish to deliberately "cause panic or social unrest".
"Some users think the online world is anonymous and unregulated or that they cannot be traced," he said.
There have been calls for all AI-generated content to be clearly stamped but other users can then just re-edit the material removing the markings.
Professor Xu Xiaoke from Beijing Normal University told the BBC that greater efforts were also needed to verify geographic locations with timestamps and the checking of image sources.
"That said, I would also stress that detection technology still lags behind generation technology. We're in a constant cat-and-mouse game. So we should not assume that technology alone can identify AI-generated content with the click of a button," he warned.
The Chinese government is embracing AI in its bid to become the leading tech superpower.
In 2017, it announced that AI would be "the main driving force" of the country's progress.
Vast sums of money is pouring into AI businesses seeking more capital, fuelling domestic competition. The state-controlled wire service Xinhua reports that the country has over 6,000 "AI companies".
In this climate, Prof Xu believes that China needs to build "trusted information infrastructure". This could include official government early warning systems and disaster interfaces which news organisations can access.
But there have been instances of official sources, including government-controlled media, deliberately downplaying disasters, which has led to some public mistrust in this area.
Earlier in July, local journalists were asked to "soften" their language to describe a major breach in the wall of the Liulan Dam near Naning as an "opening" or "gap".
Officials appeared to be trying to make the breach sound less alarming but the consequences were deadly. Water bursting through the broken dam led to at least 26 deaths downstream.
And this is not an isolated incident.
In 2021, local officials were arrested, accused of concealing or underreporting 139 deaths in Henan province.
Incidents like these have resulted in a trust vacuum that has made it much easier for bad actors to spread fake content.
But police are imploring people to trust accredited sources during emergencies.
"When encountering disaster-related information from an unknown source, approach it with scepticism and rely on official announcements," Gao Kai from the Ningbo Public Security Bureau said.
He also tried to reassure the public that the creators of false information would be caught, saying that "the internet is not a lawless zone. Public security authorities will continue to intensify efforts to crack down on illegal online activity".
"We've created a specialised task force to monitor social media closely, especially short video platforms. They will investigate and handle these cases quickly, cracking down in a very strict manner".
Punishment could range from a fine to up to seven years in prison if the fallout of the misinformation is serious enough.
On 23 July, China's Cyberspace Administration also announced a nationwide crackdown on fake internet content related to floods and other disasters, ordering its local branches to focus on catching out fabricated data, malicious editing, staged scenes, misattributed historical events and those impersonating officials. In addition, it called on social media platforms to strengthen the review of the content they are publishing.
Prof Gao believes "the answer is public education combined with law enforcement", saying that there was a "need to publicise real cases where people have been punished."
He added that "the harm caused by AI-generated fake content is ultimately the result of how people choose to use the technology - not the technology itself", adding that existing laws were sufficient to deal with it.
However, others are not so confident. Professor Chen pointed out that "AI technology continues to evolve much faster than legal frameworks. As new legal questions emerge, AI misinformation remains a considerable challenge."
Shanghai and Washington based lawyer Peter Pang says lawyers around the world are seeing an explosion in the number of cases dealing with these issues.
He believes that the companies that create AI apps and the platforms used to publish fake videos and other material must be held legally accountable along with the people who create misinformation.
"The first line would be the platforms, because they're the ones that are the enablers. They're the ones that allow this to go out," he told the BBC.
He used a hypothetical example of a person who runs over a pedestrian following panic induced by a fake post on social media.
"The video creator might say 'you ran over somebody. That's your problem. I didn't do it.' But let's think it through. You created the foundation from which people reacted. If you created that panic, you need to have responsibility for consequences that occur."
And Professor Xu warns that "AI-generated misinformation is likely to increase not only in volume but in the speed with which it spreads."

title: Burnham appoints Phillipson as Labour Party chair
summary: She will work closely with Lucy Powell, having lost out to her in the deputy leadership contest.
full_text:
Burnham appoints Phillipson as Labour Party chair
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has appointed Bridget Phillipson as Labour Party chair.
A Labour spokesperson said Phillipson, who is also minister for women and equalities, will work closely with deputy Labour leader Lucy Powell to modernise the party ready for the next general election.
Phillipson and Powell went head to head for the deputy leader position last year, after a race triggered by Angela Rayner's resignation, with Powell emerging victorious following 54% support from the party membership, external.
Phillipson had been education secretary under Sir Keir Starmer but that job was also handed to Powell by Burnham when he appointed his cabinet last week.
Announcing Phillipson's appointment, Burnham said she would help the party focus on preparations for a new digital campaigning environment.
"She will play a vital role in ensuring the Labour Party is match fit for the next election," he said.
She replaces Anna Turley who was made a minister in the Home Office last week.
The leadership team, which also includes chief whip Anneliese Midgley, is expected to focus on culture change, and building the infrastructure and policy platform needed by 2029, which is the latest an election can be held.
Posting on X, Phillipson said she was honoured, external to take on the role.
"I joined our party as a teenager and saw first hand the difference a Labour government makes," she said.
"I'll work with members to build the election-winning machine that sees off Reform [UK] for good and secures a second Labour term."
Welcoming her, Powell said: "Working together, we will ensure the party continues to lead the way in campaigning, with the strongest ground operation in British politics as we prepare for the next general election."

title: How telehealth is helping close the healthcare gap in rural Zimbabwe
summary: Virtual consultations are replacing hours of travel, bringing affordable healthcare closer to rural Zimbabweans.
full_text:
How telehealth is helping close the healthcare gap in rural Zimbabwe
Virtual consultations are replacing hours of travel, bringing affordable healthcare closer to rural Zimbabweans.
Nyazura, Zimbabwe – Bright fluorescent lights reflect off polished floors as Anymore Kadzunge returns for a routine check-up at a telehealth centre that helped diagnose the illness she had struggled with for months.
The 38-year-old farmer sits quietly as a nurse wraps a blood pressure cuff around her arm. Moments later, the machine beeps with the reading.
Only months earlier, Kadzunge had been struggling to work her fields or prepare meals for her family. She had spent three months experiencing chest pains and dizziness before walking 14km (8.7 miles) from her village of Chimbondi after a friend told her about the facility.
A nurse found her blood pressure was elevated and connected her with a doctor through a video consultation.
“The nurse tested my blood pressure, but it was extremely high,” Kadzunge told Al Jazeera. “I then spoke to a doctor through a video call.”
She was diagnosed with hypertension and prescribed medication, which she continues to take daily. Within days, her condition improved.
Bringing doctors closer
Kadzunge’s experience comes as efforts grow to bring doctors closer to rural communities in Zimbabwe, where years of economic hardship have left the public health system facing shortages of medicines, equipment and medical workers.
The programme was launched in 2024 by ZimSmart Villages, a Zimbabwean technology and innovation organisation, in partnership with NetOne, the country’s state-owned telecommunications company, and Zimbabwe Posts (Zimpost), the state-owned postal and courier service.
The programme connects patients in remote communities with healthcare professionals providing digital consultations, reducing the need for long journeys to see a doctor.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), Zimbabwe had 1.7 doctors for every 10,000 people in 2022, compared with Africa’s average of 2.6.
For many rural residents, seeing a doctor in person requires expensive travel. Without the Nyazura centre, Kadzunge would have needed to travel 22km (13.7 miles) to Rusape, a town in eastern Zimbabwe, or 70km (43 miles) to Mutare, the capital of Manicaland province.
Ambulances are limited in many rural areas, forcing some families to transport sick relatives to health facilities using ox-drawn scotch carts, a common form of rural transport.
At the Nyazura centre, registered nurse Noreen Chimanya checks patients’ vital signs, including blood pressure, blood sugar levels and temperature, before arranging video consultations with doctors. She also provides prescribed treatment and refers serious cases to hospitals.
“When we opened in May 2024, telemedicine was something completely new in this community,” Chimanya told Al Jazeera. “People were used to speaking to doctors in person and being physically examined.”
Building trust required months of community outreach. Chimanya travelled to surrounding villages explaining how virtual consultations worked.
“They like it here because there are no queues,” she said. “At public health facilities, people spend hours waiting to be seen.”
The centre uses Starlink, the satellite internet service operated by United States aerospace company SpaceX, and a backup lithium battery to keep consultations running during frequent power cuts.
A lifeline for rural patients
According to ZimSmart Villages, by 2026 the organisation had established 28 telehealth centres across seven of Zimbabwe’s 10 provinces and conducted more than 28,000 virtual consultations, including about 25,000 diagnostic tests.
Tawanda Njerere, the organisation’s cofounder and chief operations officer, told Al Jazeera the programme was designed to create digital health access points within existing post office infrastructure.
“Rather than requiring rural patients to travel 50km or more to urban health facilities, the programme establishes digital health access points embedded within existing post office infrastructure,” he said.
The centres charge between $2 and $10 for consultations, compared with $15 to $20 at many private clinics.
For some rural households, that difference can determine whether they seek treatment or wait.
For Proud Chimene, a vendor from nearby Chimene village, it made seeking treatment possible.
In July 2024, after experiencing unexplained weight loss, extreme thirst and persistent fatigue, she visited the Nyazura centre.
“The situation had deteriorated,” Chimene told Al Jazeera. “The nurse tested my blood glucose level and it was high. After speaking to the doctor through a video call, they put me on an intravenous drip for several hours. He also prescribed medicine that I take twice a day.”
She was diagnosed with diabetes.
“If it was not for this nearby telehealth centre providing access to a doctor at affordable fees, I would probably not have sought treatment at all,” she said.
Njerere said the programme focuses on detecting illnesses earlier by bringing screening services closer to communities. Digital health records and follow-up consultations also help patients manage chronic conditions such as hypertension and diabetes.
The centres have also diagnosed sexually transmitted infections and referred patients needing specialised care.
Challenges remain
Despite its growth, telehealth cannot replace all the services provided by traditional healthcare facilities.
Specialist services, particularly for eye health, mental health and complex chronic disease management, remain limited across Zimbabwe.
“The programme addresses this through partnerships with established eye-care providers and specialist networks, but specialist capacity remains a systemic constraint,” Njerere said.
In some rural communities, unfamiliarity with virtual consultations means building trust remains an ongoing challenge.
For Kadzunge, the measure of success is simple: she can return to the fields and daily routines that illness had taken away.
“I am healthy again,” she said. “Now I can go to the farm without scaring my family.”

title: J&J offers $5.5bn settlement in lawsuits claiming talc link to cancer
summary: Johnson & Johnson agrees to pay $5.5bn to settle nearly 70,000 US lawsuits over talc-based baby powder cancer claims.
full_text:
J&J offers $5.5bn settlement in lawsuits claiming talc link to cancer
Settlement resolves thousands of US lawsuits, with a record UK case against the company under way.
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay $5.5bn to settle tens of thousands of lawsuits in the United States that allege its discontinued talc-based baby powder caused ovarian cancer.
The pharmaceutical giant made the announcement on Monday, saying it covers about 69,000 cases in US federal and state courts, accounting for 99.75 percent of outstanding talc-related cases in the country.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items- list 1 of 2How a study on hormonal contraception and breast cancer was distorted
- list 2 of 2Jury orders Johnson & Johnson to pay $966m in talc cancer case
The settlement will only be final once it is accepted by 95 percent of the claimants in state or federal courts.
Talc is a soft mineral and was once a staple ingredient in cosmetics and baby products, but its use has declined as concerns rose over its links to cancer.
In 2024, the World Health Organization classified talc as “probably carcinogenic to humans”.
J&J maintains that there is no evidence that talc causes cancer, but it stopped selling talc-based baby powder in the US in 2020 and worldwide in 2023.
In 2016, a US jury ordered J&J to pay $72m to the family of a woman who died of ovarian cancer, the first such case related to the use of the mineral in the country.
Though the case was overturned a year later, claims against the company have multiplied since, with juries across the US awarding the plaintiffs.
Erik Haas, J&J’s litigation head, said the agreement lets J&J “put this matter behind it”.
Lawyers representing the plaintiffs welcomed the settlement as a good resolution to a decade-long court battle.
The deal does not cover the United Kingdom, where the largest product liability case in UK history – covering more than 7,000 potential claimants – is being adjudicated.
Filed in October 2025, the UK case alleges that J&J knew that its talc could cause cancers, chiefly ovarian and mesothelioma, but continued to sell the product, a claim the company also denies.
The case has since gone before the UK High Court.

title: Houthis want to copy Iran’s Hormuz control in the Red Sea: Yemeni FM
summary: Speaking in Riyadh, Yemen's internationally recognised government warns global complacency has emboldened the Houthis.
full_text:
Houthis want to copy Iran’s Hormuz control in the Red Sea: Yemeni FM
Speaking in Riyadh, Yemen’s internationally recognised government warns that global complacency has emboldened the Houthis.
Houthis claim Saudi drone downed over northwestern Yemen
Yemen’s Houthi movement is aiming to replicate Iran’s strategy in the Strait of Hormuz by controlling shipping flows in the Red Sea’s Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the Yemeni government’s top diplomat warns.
“The Houthis want to copy the Iranian model , and this will shut down two main straits, the gateways into the Gulf and Red Sea,” the foreign minister-designate for the internationally recognised Yemeni government, Afrah al-Zouba, told journalists on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Houthis claim Saudi drone downed over northwestern Yemen
- list 2 of 3Saudi Arabia defends against drone strikes from ‘Iran-backed’ groups
- list 3 of 3Why a new war in Yemen could be different for the Houthis
Speaking at the Yemeni embassy in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, al-Zouba said the Iran-backed Houthis have been emboldened due to the insufficient international response to their activities in the region.
Bab al-Mandeb Strait connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean, and – much like the Strait of Hormuz – a significant portion of the global economy depends on the unimpeded flow of maritime traffic through it.
Approximately 30 percent of global container traffic passes through the Red Sea, and 12 to 15 percent of overall global trade.
Yemen’s geography gives whoever controls the country’s west a commanding influence over traffic through Bab al-Mandeb.
Data suggests that shipping through the Red Sea is already declining, with just 11 commodity vessels passing through it on Sunday.
Al-Zouba’s comments come as tensions between the Houthis on one side and Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognised government on the other escalate.
Earlier in July, the Houthis declared a maritime siege on Red Sea shipping to and from Saudi Arabia, and launched missiles and drones at the kingdom.
Riyadh has since launched air strikes on Yemen’s key port city of Hodeidah, held by the Houthis.
July’s escalation is the biggest since a truce was agreed to in 2022 and came amid a resurgence of US attacks on Iran.
Al-Zouba said Yemen’s government, which Saudi Arabia backs, is prepared for an escalation, and that fire was being exchanged along the front line where Houthi-controlled territory meets government-controlled areas, but that no offensive had been launched.
Nearly 20 fighters from both sides died earlier this month during clashes between the Houthis and government forces around Hodeidah.
Hundreds of thousands of people have died in Yemen since war broke out in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and then-President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi eventually fled to Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia led an Arab coalition in a campaign to dislodge the Houthis from 2015 up to the 2022 truce.
As of 2026, the Houthis remain in power in the capital and other parts of Yemen. Meanwhile, tensions between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, which Riyadh accuses of backing a southern separatist group in Yemen, have affected developments on the ground.
Yemeni civilians have paid the heaviest price, with an estimated 377,000 dying between 2015 and the beginning of 2022, most of them from war’s knock-on impacts, such as famine and disease.

title: US diplomats walk out as France addresses UN Security Council
summary: US diplomats walk out of UN meeting during France's speech amid tensions over human rights chief's reappointment.
full_text:
US diplomats walk out as France addresses UN Security Council
US accused France of “condescending” rhetoric over its human rights stances
United States diplomats walked out of a United Nations Security Council meeting on Russia’s war against Ukraine as France’s delegation took the floor.
The walkout on Monday came two days after an online exchange between US and French officials over Washington voting against renewing the four-year term of UN human rights chief Volker Turk.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items- list 1 of 2UN eyeing potential Israeli war crimes in Lebanon
- list 2 of 2How Volker Turk won new UN rights chief term despite US, Israel opposition
France’s UN Mission in Geneva wrote on Saturday that the US was no longer a “beacon of human rights” and stood isolated alongside North Korea, Nicaragua, Mali and Russia.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz replied on X that France had voted for a rights chief who “has been lecturing free, sovereign democracies like the United States, the UK, and Israel, while cozying up to the world’s worst oppressors”.
After the walkout, Dan Negrea, an alternate US representative, told the council that his delegation would keep walking out until France renounced its “condescending and disrespectful rhetoric”.
France’s ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, did not mention the walkout when he spoke, saying France was working to preserve the UN’s independence and its capacity to act.
Turk, who has criticised violations of international law by Israel and the US in Palestine and Iran, was reappointed by a UN General Assembly vote of 144 in favour, 10 against and 13 abstentions.
The administration of US President Donald Trump has cut funding to UN agencies and withdrawn from dozens of UN entities since 2025. It had also threatened to reassess its engagement over Turk’s mandate.
Washington and Paris have also clashed over NATO spending, trade policy and Trump’s threats to occupy Greenland, a territory of NATO member Denmark.
France, along with other European states, has also drawn Trump’s ire for refusing direct participation in the US-Israel war on Iran.

title: Rand Paul releases Anthony Fauci's pandemic-era diary notes. Here's what they tell us
summary: Sen. Rand Paul has released a tranche of Dr. Anthony Fauci's diary entries from the COVID-19 pandemic. Fauci is set to appear before a Senate committee Wednesday on the origins of the coronavirus.
full_text:
Rand Paul releases Anthony Fauci's pandemic-era diary notes. Here's what they tell us
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., published a tranche of diary entries over the weekend made by Dr. Anthony Fauci during the COVID-19 pandemic. The 1,141-page document, which was released over the weekend and was no longer available on the website on Monday, came ahead of Fauci's appearance before a Senate committee on Wednesday. The entries, and Paul's commentary on them, highlight the disagreement between the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) and some politicians over the origins of the coronavirus.
Paul and Fauci — who served as a key member of the White House's Coronavirus Task Force — have disagreed publicly for years over how the pandemic began. Even after Fauci stepped down from his position at NIAID at the end of 2022, Paul has continued to conduct an "investigation into the origins of COVID-19 and risky taxpayer-funded life sciences research."
On Saturday afternoon, as part of this ongoing inquiry, Paul published a thread on X describing the release of a string of what he called diary entries made by Fauci from December 2019 through December 2022. Paul commented on X at the start of the posts, "What [Fauci] wrote privately and what he told the country are two different stories."
Fauci and Paul did not respond to an NPR request for comment prior to publication.
Felicia Goodrum, a virologist at Dartmouth College who spoke to NPR from the American Society for Virology meeting in Minneapolis, says that it's possible that Fauci may have been less certain in private with his colleagues as they were racing to learn about the new virus than he was in public where he had to assure a population that was panicking over the rapidly emerging pandemic.
For stories of life in our changing world, subscribe here to the global health newsletter.
This thread emerges ahead of a scheduled hearing on Wednesday before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul chairs. Paul unilaterally subpoenaed Fauci to testify after he said that Fauci notified the committee that he wouldn't appear voluntarily. Lawmakers are expected to question Fauci about what he knew and didn't know as the pandemic was unfolding.
What is Rand Paul looking to hear from Anthony Fauci?
For years, Paul and Fauci have differed over the origins of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. Fauci has asserted that the scientific evidence points to a spillover — whereby the virus would have found its way from an animal into its first human host, and then spread at that point from human to human.
Proponents of this theory point to the wet market in Wuhan where potentially infected animals were waiting to be sold. "There's very good evidence that there are two lineages [of SARS-CoV-2] that emerged," according to Goodrum. "Both of those lineages were present at the market, and susceptible animals were present at the market."
Goodrum says the market was cleared before it was possible to take any samples. However, she says the genetic data "maps all initial cases to that market" and "none to, for example, the Wuhan Institute of Virology, where they have accused the virus of having been created or released."
Most scientists in the virology community share this view, according to a survey published in February 2024 by the Global Catastrophic Risk Institute, a nonpartisan U.S.-based think tank that studies potentially catastrophic events.
Paul has advocated for an alternative explanation. He says the possibility that the virus was engineered in a lab should not be discounted. Two years ago during a full Senate committee hearing, Paul said, "Do we know for certain it came from the lab? No, but there's a preponderance of evidence indicating that it may have come from the lab."
In late 2024, the Republican-led Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic published their final report that concluded a lab leak was the most likely explanation for the origins of SARS-CoV-2. They suggested that funds from the NIH may have helped support research by the Wuhan Institute of Virology to make a more potent or transmissible virus. Such viral enhancement is called gain of function.
But Robert Garry, a virologist at Tulane University, says he disputes this line of reasoning because there is "no actual evidence for it." And he says that no one, including the Wuhan Institute of Virology, had a precursor virus similar enough to SARS-CoV-2 to create the pathogen that ultimately caused the pandemic.
Still, Paul suggests that Fauci, his colleagues, and certain federal agencies may have covered up any evidence to support the lab leak theory. In his view, he said in that same statement, they "withheld and continue to conceal crucial information from both Congress and the public."
As noted, NPR reached out to Fauci about Paul's comments, but did not receive a response before publication.
What does Paul say these newly published diary entries reveal?
In his posts on X, Paul highlights a few select excerpts from Fauci's notes. For instance, he points to an entry on Jan. 26, 2020, not quite two months before the World Health Organization declared a global pandemic, where Fauci writes, "the first infection was in early December and was not connected to the market. … Now we know the market was not the source, it was the amplifier."
Paul notes in his post, "The wet market was already off the table in [Fauci's] own private notes."
But in that same journal entry, Fauci adds, "Having said that, somewhere the virus jumped from animals to humans."
Not quite a week later, in an entry penned on Feb. 1, 2020, Fauci listed the dozen researchers who participated in a conference call debating the origins of COVID-19. Specifically, they were talking about the plausibility that a key part of the SARS-CoV-2 genome could have evolved naturally.
According to his notes, only two of the scientists voiced support for a natural origin of SARS-CoV-2. "The rest felt that deliberate insertion was possible," he wrote, referring to the hypothesis that the virus was engineered in a lab.
In response to that passage, Paul wrote on X, "This was never a 50/50 room," suggesting that early scientific consensus considered a lab leak possible.
But Goodrum says that this meeting took place very early on, when scientists did not have as much data as they would later. The virologist points out that science is iterative and takes time to play out. What some of those scientists believed at the start gave way to a different consensus as more evidence emerged.
"We make the best conclusions we have with the data we have at the time, but then you're going to keep working," she says. "And then you're going to ultimately revise the original conclusions that you made. You will change your mind. That's absolutely fundamental to the way science is done. And it's something that Fauci wasn't really given any latitude to do."
Goodrum adds that it's possible that Fauci may have been less certain in private with his colleagues as they were racing to learn about the new virus than he was in public where he had to assure a public panicking over the rapidly emerging pandemic.
What happens next?
Fauci and Paul will again face off publicly on Wednesday when he testifies before the senator's committee. Paul is likely to ask Fauci about the contents of his notes and the specific lines of concern that he identified in his thread on X.
Fauci may respond to the questions as he has before, describing his thought process and that of his colleagues at different points throughout the pandemic.
Previously, Fauci has expressed disinterest in questions about unproven claims regarding the pandemic. title: China team unearths world’s oldest amber, hidden in ancient Xinjiang coal seam
summary:
Chinese scientists have uncovered the world’s oldest verified amber in the northwestern Xinjiang region, revealing that ancient plants were producing protective resin 385 million years ago, long before most animal groups had emerged to damage them.
The amber – discovered in coal seams in West Junggar, part of an ancient zone where tectonic plates collided, grew and merged – pushes back the record by roughly 65 million years and challenges some long-held assumptions about the origins of plant...
full_text:
China team unearths world’s oldest amber, hidden in ancient Xinjiang coal seam
Ancient plants were capable of producing resin to protect themselves 65 million years earlier than previously thought, study finds
Until now, the oldest known amber to have been isolated from rock and confirmed through chemical analysis dated to the Late Carboniferous period, around 320 million years ago, when the first herbivores also emerged.
The researchers, led by Luo Cihang, from the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology, detailed their findings in a paper published by the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances on July 15.
According to the paper, the palaeontologists were initially sceptical when they found hundreds of microscopic pieces of what appeared to be amber preserved in a coal seam dating from the Middle Devonian period around 393 million to 383 million years ago.
When Luo and his team travelled to Xinjiang in 2019, they did not expect the fossil samples they planned to examine and collect from the region’s unusual coal seam would yield the world’s oldest known amber, the paper said.

full_text:
What to see at the Shenzhen Natural History Museum, from dinosaur fossils to meteorites
The US$517 million museum opening on July 28 is a ‘living educational landscape’ covering space, dinosaurs, evolution and much more
The Shenzhen Natural History Museum will open to the public on July 28 as the first dedicated large-scale institution of its kind in southern China.
Spearheaded by the Shenzhen government with a total investment of 3.5 billion yuan (US$517 million) – excluding the cost of collecting artefacts – the museum, located in the Pingshan district in the northeast of the city, is among its “Ten Cultural Facilities of the New Era”.
The Shenzhen Natural History Museum is located on a 42,000-square-metre (450,000 sq ft) site, with a total floor area of 105,300 square metres. It was designed by Danish architectural firm 3XN, Canada-based B+H Architects and Chinese firm Zhubo Design in a consortium selected through a competition that drew more than 70 proposals from around the world.
Inspired by the form of a river delta, the building has a free-flowing, curvilinear structure that features a walkable green rooftop park and houses permanent and temporary exhibition galleries, research laboratories, a 1,100-seat nature theatre and three cinemas.

title: Asia ‘scraping the bottom of the barrel’ as Red Sea oil blockade worsens energy crisis
summary:
The Houthi threat to Saudi oil exports comes as Japan, South Korea and the Philippines are still reeling from the closure of the strait of Hormuz

Governments in Asia are scrambling to avoid their second major energy crisis in six months, as another maritime chokepoint in the Middle East faces a violent blockade, leaving only the Suez canal completely open for the free movement of gulf oil.

Countries like Japan, the Philippines, Thailand and South Korea – which rely on Middle East oil for up to 90% of their imports – are working to secure supplies after Yemen’s Houthis launched a blockade of Saudi Arabian shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, which forms the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Governments in Asia are scrambling to avoid their second major energy crisis in six months, as another maritime chokepoint in the Middle East faces a violent blockade, leaving only the Suez canal completely open for the free movement of gulf oil.
Countries like Japan, the Philippines, Thailand and South Korea – which rely on Middle East oil for up to 90% of their imports – are working to secure supplies after Yemen’s Houthis launched a blockade of Saudi Arabian shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, which forms the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Many countries in Asia are still reeling from Iran’s effective closure of the strait of Hormuz in March, which forced governments across the region to compete for increasingly dwindling supplies of Middle Eastern crude oil.
“They’re scraping at the bottom of the barrel in terms of global reserve capacity … there’s very little inventory now,” says Ahmed Helal, from the Asia Group thinktank.
Japan – along with neighbouring countries – is already spending billions on fuel subsidies to keep the cost of petroleum down, hitting government budgets hard. After the announcement from the Houthis, some like South Korea were quick to extend those fuel tax cuts.
Meanwhile, the spike in the cost of imports has led to a rise in inflation, piling pressure on the governments of regional giants such as Japan and Indonesia.
Now, the threat to Red Sea shipping is set to increase the pressure. In March, Saudi Arabia responded to the closure of the strait of Hormuz by rerouting oil exports from the gulf on the country’s east coast, to the west coast port of Yanbu in the Red Sea which now handles more than 70% of Riyadh’s crude oil exports.
That proved to be a lifeline for many Asian nations, like China – which is the largest buyer of Saudi oil – and India, Japan and South Korea, which follow close behind.
Some Japanese and South Korean refiners are reportedly seeking to circumvent the Houthi threat by rerouting cargos north through the Suez canal, to the Mediterranean and around Africa. But this lengthy detour comes with huge costs.
A VLCC, the largest size of oil tanker, is too big to pass through the Suez canal fully loaded, meaning cargos would need to unload up to half of their oil in the Red Sea, have it transported through Egypt’s Sumed pipeline to the Mediterranean coast, where they would then pick it up after transiting through the canal, adding costs and logistical complications to the journey.
Rerouting the oil via the Mediterranean and around the Cape of Good Hope would also more than double the voyage time for most Asian importers, further adding to freight and fuel costs.
For now, it’s a cost many may be willing to incur. The Houthis targeted at least two Saudi oil tankers exiting the Red Sea last week and launched attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure this week. The number of vessels transiting through Bab al-Mandab has fallen to the lowest level in months, with international shipping apparently paralysed by the Houthi threat.
“Changing behaviour by tankers tells us that they are taking the threats seriously,” says Matt Smith, a commodity research director at Kpler, a market tracker.
Insurers have responded in kind, with war risk premiums paid by tankers reportedly doubling in the last week, potentially adding hundreds of thousands of dollars to the cost of a voyage.
Those costs will inevitably be passed on to consumers in Asia, who are already reeling from the energy shock imposed by the US-Iran war.
“Businesses are going to have to close. You might have attempts to reduce consumption at peak hours. And you might have, in some extreme cases, higher risk of default,” says Helal.
A vulnerability exposed
After transits through the strait of Hormuz slowed to a halt in March, many countries in Asia rushed to mitigate the effects of the disruption. Coal-fired power plants blazed back into use, a four-day working week was imposed in Sri Lanka, while staff in Vietnam were urged to work from home. But now, resources and patience are running low.
The Houthi threat has inspired the Philippines, India and South Korea to all bolster their strategic reserves of oil and gas. Meanwhile across the region, the crisis has added a renewed urgency to the renewables transition.
But with no short-term solutions, Asian importers are reportedly looking farther afield for supplies, with Russia once again likely to benefit from chaos in the Middle East.
Earlier this year Japan and South Korea reportedly bought Russian oil for the first time since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. In the past week, Reuters reported that Chinese refiner ramped up purchases of sanctioned Russian crude oil to counter the latest disruptions.
The disruption and chaos points to a truth that experts say governments in Asia have ignored for too long: their energy systems remain far too vulnerable.
Helal predicts this crisis will force many governments to reckon with their supply chains and their capacity to store strategic reserves.
But for now, they simply have to secure supplies, he says, because “there’s very little in the tank for them to draw on.”

title: It’s the vibe: Australian comedy classic The Castle set to become a stage play
summary:
Working Dog team behind the 1997 film reuniting to write ‘new, fully updated’ version for the stage, which will premiere in Melbourne in 2027

An announcement that deserves to go straight to the pool room: the beloved Australian comedy The Castle is set to become a play, written by the team behind the original film.

Working Dog’s Rob Sitch, Tom Gleisner, Santo Cilauro and Jane Kennedy will write and co-produce the new theatrical production, which will again tell the story of the Kerrigan family and their fight against the Australian government to save their home from being bulldozed to make way for an airport expansion.

Continue reading...
full_text:
An announcement that deserves to go straight to the pool room: the beloved Australian comedy The Castle is set to become a play, written by the team behind the original film.
Working Dog’s Rob Sitch, Tom Gleisner, Santo Cilauro and Jane Kennedy will write and co-produce the new theatrical production, which will again tell the story of the Kerrigan family and their fight against the Australian government to save their home from being bulldozed to make way for an airport expansion.
The Castle, released in 1997, is regarded as one of the greatest Australian films ever made and is even studied in some Australian secondary schools. Starring Michael Caton as the affable patriarch Darryl Kerrigan, The Castle shaped the Australian vernacular with much-quoted lines including, “This is going straight to the pool room” – a place of pride in the Kerrigan household – “How’s the serenity?” and “Tell him he’s dreamin’.”
The play will premiere in Melbourne at Her Majesty’s Theatre in March 2027, to mark the 30th anniversary of the film.
In a joint statement Sitch, Gleisner, Cilauro and Kennedy said they had wanted to turn The Castle into a stage show for “the best part of 25 years” and said the production would not be “just a retelling of the story but a quarter of a century of funny updates”.
“We wrote this new, fully updated show in the same way that we wrote the film screenplay all those years ago – the four of us in a room trying to make each other laugh. Our goal was to capture the warmth and humour (dare we say, ‘the vibe’?) of the original story in a way that will hopefully resonate with new and long-term fans alike.”
Producer Michael Cassel said: “When the team at Working Dog first approached me about bringing The Castle to the stage, I knew we had to do this.
“The film miraculously captures the specificities of Australian life and yet feels so universally true; family love, the challenges change presents, and the warmth and humour and dignity of ordinary people standing up for what matters. It makes you laugh, and then, before you know it, it makes you cry.
“That is exactly what live theatre does at its best and why The Castle was always destined for the stage.”
Casting for the production has yet to be announced.

title: Ben Carroll to become next premier of Victoria after Jacinta Allan resigns
summary:
Premier stepped down from top job before expected spill, saying her deputy has her ‘unqualified support’

  • Live updates: Jacinta Allan quits as premier of Victoria

  • Who is Ben Carroll?

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Ben Carroll will become the next premier of Victoria, after Jacinta Allan resigned and a surprise rival for the Labor leadership emerged after a tumultuous 48 hours for Labor just four months out from the state election.

Speaking outside a party room meeting on Tuesday, Labor MP Juliana Addison announced that Carroll had been “unanimously endorsed by the state parliamentary Labor party as our next premier of Victoria”.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Ben Carroll will become the next premier of Victoria, after Jacinta Allan resigned and a surprise rival for the Labor leadership emerged after a tumultuous 48 hours for Labor just four months out from the state election.
Speaking outside a party room meeting on Tuesday, Labor MP Juliana Addison announced that Carroll had been “unanimously endorsed by the state parliamentary Labor party as our next premier of Victoria”.
The transport infrastructure minister, Gabrielle Williams, secured the party’s deputy leadership.
In a video shared on his social media accounts, Carroll said he was “honoured and humbled to have been elected unanimously by my colleagues to serve as the new premier of Victoria”.
“Yesterday, they asked me to put my hand up to lead our party, and I agreed,” Carroll said in the video.
“This was not an easy decision, but the stakes at this election are too high. Polling says Victoria is on track for Australia’s first Liberal-One Nation government.”
He said “only Labor could stop the risk” of such a thing, and promised to deliver a “new direction” for his government.
Carroll was expected to address the media on Tuesday afternoon.
Allan on Monday had vowed to contest a leadership ballot after a group of MPs told her she no longer had the support of caucus and urged her to stand down. Carroll, the deputy premier, also confirmed he would nominate for the Labor leadership.
But on Tuesday morning, Allan said on Tuesday morning that Carroll would have her “unqualified support”.
It was expected that Carroll would run unopposed for the leadership during Tuesday’s caucus meeting, avoiding a weeks’ long process to allow the broader party membership to vote.
But in a surprise move, Labor sources said frontbencher Sonya Kilkenny initially announced she would contest the leadership during the meeting, in which MPs could be heard shouting.
A contested leadership would have meant weeks of instability in the run-up to the election, as the party’s balloting process can take up to six weeks.
Speaking before the party room meeting on Tuesday, Allan said she had decided to step aside – despite believing she would have won a leadership ballot – because it was “the right thing” to do for Labor and Victorians.
“After speaking with my colleagues overnight, I have made the difficult decision to step aside as leader of the Victorian state parliamentary Labor party, and as premier of Victoria,” she said.
“I was prepared to put my record and my plan to a ballot of members as our rules allow. I believe I would have won. But doing this so this close to an election takes up valuable resources, including the most precious one – time.”
Allan said she would instead chair Tuesday’s caucus meeting to elect a new leader.
Speculation about a leadership spill had been swirling for months, and momentum had been building before parliament rose for the winter break in June. Poor polling and Allan’s weak personal approval ratings contributed to the push, along with rising support for One Nation.
Allan’s leadership has also been dogged by allegations of wrongdoing on the Big Build, as she was the minister responsible for transport infrastructure at the time. While she has apologised for criminal conduct that has been uncovered, she has also rejected calls for a royal commission. This is understood to have put her at odds with a number of MPs who believe the issue cannot be contained without one.
Carroll is understood to be in favour of a royal commission. He has also indicated that he believes he’d be better able to resolve the pay dispute between the government and public school teachers, improve the party’s economic credentials and do more to support businesses.
He had long been touted as a potential challenger for the leadership but consistently ruled out doing so. In June he looked Allan in the eye and declared he would not challenge her.
Under Labor’s rules, a contested leadership triggers an election process in which both the parliamentary caucus and rank-and-file Labor members vote, and can take a full six weeks to complete.
Arriving at parliament on Tuesday morning, Carroll made only a brief statement to reporters, saying his focus was on talking to his colleagues.
Before she announced her resignation, Steve Dimopoulos, a minister and key supporter of Allan, said: “I think the party has been good at sorting things out, this is what today will be.”
The former health minister Mary-Anne Thomas, who this year announced she would resign at the November election, said Allan had “served this state with real leadership. She’s always had the people of Victoria at the heart of everything that she does.”
The environment minister, Enver Erdogan, had told reporters on Tuesday morning there was a “case for change”. “I think we know some of these issues have been aired publicly but I think we need stronger action on crime and corruption in the state.”
Asked whether there needed to be a royal commission into allegations of corruption on Big Build construction sites, he replied: “Yes.”

title: Well-connected Melbourne man found guilty of raping former staffer
summary:
Jury finds that the man, who cannot be named, assaulted the woman at his home in March 2023

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A well-connected Melbourne man has been found guilty of raping a former employee.

The man, who cannot be named, faced two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault in the county court of Victoria, and pleaded not guilty.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A well-connected Melbourne man has been found guilty of raping a former employee.
The man, who cannot be named, faced two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault in the county court of Victoria, and pleaded not guilty.
After a three-week trial the jury found him guilty of all charges on Tuesday, after deliberating since late on Friday morning.
The man immediately had his bail revoked, and was taken into custody, but will be sentenced at a later date.
The assault occurred in March 2023, after the woman said she spent an evening drinking and taking cocaine with the man, while listening to music and watching the football at his friend’s home.
Both the prosecution and the defence argued that the most important witness was the alleged victim – the man’s former personal assistant – who gave evidence over more than four days before a closed court. The man did not give evidence during the trial.
The judge, Frank Gucciardo, thanked the jury after the verdict for their commitment during the trial.
“Those of us who have worked with juries for a very long time genuinely believe it’s the best system for determining matters like these,” he said.
“From time to time you hear people say that these cases should be judged by experts or lawyers or others, but those of us who have worked with juries know this is the best system we have.”
The prosecutor, Matthew Fisher, said given the man was likely to face a significant custodial sentence he should be taken into custody.
In his closing address to the jury, Fisher said some of the inconsistencies in the woman’s evidence had proved her credibility, as it showed she had not made it up.
But Dermot Dann KC, representing the man, described that as a “desperate submission”. He said the prosecution had asked the jury to swallow a “horrible mixture of lies, fabrications, inconsistencies [and] evidence that has been shown to be demonstrably untrue”.
Gucciardo told the jury in his final remarks before they retired to consider their verdict that the case was not about consent as the defence case was that no sexual contact had occurred.
‘I don’t want this’
At the start of the trial, Fisher said the offences had taken place when the woman was at the man’s house, where he tried to kiss her and sexually assaulted her.
She pushed his hands away and told him “I don’t want this”, Fisher told the court, to which the man responded with comments like “You’re so sexy”, “I can’t sleep, help me” and “I need this”.
The woman then felt the man rape her twice, Fisher said.
“She turned around to face him, and at that point she punched him with her fist to his face, to his nose,” Fisher told the court.
“He grabbed his face and said words to the effect of ‘you’ve broken my nose’.
“She got out of bed and said to him: ‘You’re a fucking rapist.’”
The woman went to another room and started taking notes of what happened on her phone, before texting her mother. Her mother called the police despite her daughter’s reluctance to involve them, the court heard.
The police arrived at the property about 3am on 24 March 2023.
Police then spoke to the woman, with the exchange recorded on a body-worn camera. The footage of that 35-minute conversation was shown to the jury.
Allegations denied in court
The trial heard that woman worked as the man’s personal assistant for several months during the previous year, and the pair had resumed contact to discuss other employment opportunities when he invited her to his property.
Dann told the court that none of the offences had occurred. He said the woman had claimed she continued to stay in the house after the alleged offences.
He also said she was reluctant to contact authorities because of a prior allegation involving police but that allegation had been found to be false.
Dann also questioned why she had raised the issue of “recompense” with her mother while she was still at the man’s house.
The court also heard evidence from two of the man’s friends, who saw him and the woman in the hours before the offences, along with another former personal assistant and a friend of the alleged victim.
Two men – a former colleague and a barrister who met the accused when they both served on the board of a prominent Melbourne organisation – also gave character evidence in the trial.

title: PM praises Sally McManus and Michele O’Neil as ‘giants’ as they resign from ACTU
summary:
Secretary and president of Australian Council of Trade Unions announced surprise departures on Monday evening

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The leadership of the trade union movement is set for a major shakeup after the secretary and president of the Australian Council of Trade Unions announced their surprise departures.

The ACTU’s secretary, Sally McManus, and its president, Michele O’Neil, revealed on Monday night they would be stepping down after eight years together. Anthony Albanese described both as personal friends and “giants of the labour movement”.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The leadership of the trade union movement is set for a major shakeup after the secretary and president of the Australian Council of Trade Unions announced their surprise departures.
The ACTU’s secretary, Sally McManus, and its president, Michele O’Neil, revealed on Monday night they would be stepping down after eight years together. Anthony Albanese described both as personal friends and “giants of the labour movement”.
The first all-female leadership team in the ACTU’s 99-year history, the influential pair played a major role in shaping the Albanese government’s workplace agenda.
They successfully campaigned for the right to disconnect law, same job, same pay protections, wage theft criminalisation and ensuring minimum pay, insurance and safety standards for gig economy workers.
The ACTU recently began targeting Pauline Hanson, in a clear sign the union movement now considers One Nation – rather than the Coalition – the biggest political threat to Labor and economic risk for working people.
McManus will depart in August while O’Neil will help the new secretary settle in before leaving before the end of the year.
In a farewell video posted to social media on Monday night, the pair said it was time for renewal.
“Union membership is growing and workers have over 47 new workplace rights,” McManus said. “But, of course, there are still big challenges with cost-of-living pressures, AI and billionaires who have too much wealth and power.”
In a statement, the prime minister said McManus and O’Neil’s “tireless advocacy and strong leadership” had put working families “in a stronger financial position today than they would otherwise be”.
“It is fitting that Sally and Michele announce they’re stepping down from their respective positions at a time when there have been significant wage increases in critical and long-undervalued sectors, the gender pay gap is at a record low and union membership is growing for the first time in decades,” Albanese said.
Speaking on ABC radio on Tuesday morning, O’Neil said the pair were “very trusting of each other”, and that the union was in good shape.
O’Neil ruled out seeking a career as a politician but would not reveal what her next move would be.
“I want to take a moment to breathe. I know more about what I won’t do than what I will do, but that’s OK,” she said.
“I’m very happy to take some time to think about it.”
The Greens’ leader, Larissa Waters, described them as a “powerful duo” and “strong voices for workers”.
“The union movement is strongest when it is bold, independent and willing to put workers’ rights ahead of vested interests. Sally and Michele have embodied that spirit in their leadership pushing the Albanese Labor government to implement a minimum 25% tax on gas exports and for action to address the housing crisis,” she said.
“We are entering what could be the most challenging period for Australian workers in recent history.
“It will be the task of the ACTU’s new leadership to hold governments to account, demand a good living for workers and refuse to allow political parties to tinker and capitulate to vested interests.”

title: Bitcoin slides 2% after U.S. close while Korea’s Kospi plunges 10%
full_text:
Bitcoin slides 2% after U.S. close while Korea’s Kospi plunges 10%
- Bitcoin fell about 2.7 percent to roughly $63,200, extending losses across major cryptocurrencies as Asian equities, led by South Korea’s Kospi, sold off sharply.
- The U.S. Senate has delayed action on the closely watched CLARITY Act to focus on a Russia sanctions bill, likely pushing any vote on crypto regulatory legislation to next week before the Aug. 8 recess.
- Analysts say bitcoin tends to move with stocks when macro and interest-rate stress is high, and they expect volatility across asset classes around the Federal Reserve’s rate decision Wednesday and key U.S. data on Thursday.
Bitcoin 
BTC has fallen to $63,200 from nearly $65,000, a 2.7% decline that has spilled over into the broader crypto market and dragged down the likes of ether (ETH), XRP (XRP), solana (SOL), and others. The drop ends the brief resilience the market showed earlier Monday as shares in NVDA tanked on Wall Street.
The Senate has shelved the CLARITY Act to prioritize a Russia sanctions bill, making a vote on the much-awaited legislation, touted to deliver regulatory clarity and unlock massive institutional buying for digital assets, unlikely before next week. This leaves only the final days before the Aug. 8 recess.
Asian stocks cracked sharply, with South Korea’s Kospi index falling 10% to its lowest level since mid-April. The index has now dropped 25% from its mid-June peak. The latest decline featured steep losses in heavyweights such as Samsung and SK Hynix. "The market is falling out of love with chipmakers at the moment and that's been a big driver of the bull market in South Korea," InvestingLive wrote.
BTC has a history of tracking equity-market volatility, but the correlation is not as straightforward as widely perceived.
"BTC trades with equities when the stress is macro and [interest] rates-driven, and decouples when the stress is idiosyncratic to the equity market. An earnings-and-capital-expenditure debate is precisely that, so on this data the correlation is overstated," analysts at Bitfinex said in a note to CoinDesk.
Looking ahead, Wednesday and Thursday could significantly move the needle and add volatility across asset classes. The Fed decides interest rates on Wednesday, while Thursday brings key data.
"The Fed decides rates Wednesday, with Core PCE and GDP following immediately Thursday. That makes Wednesday–Thursday the week's highest-volatility window for U.S. rate repricing," Dessislava Ianeva, analyst at Nexo, said.
