title: US launches another round of attacks on Iran
summary: Targets across southern Iran hit, including on strategic Qeshm Island.
full_text:
US launches another round of attacks on Iran
Targets across southern Iran hit, including on strategic Qeshm Island.
The United States Central Command (CENTCOM) says it has launched a “heavy wave of strikes against Iran”, following Iranian missile attacks on US forces a day earlier.
It claimed to have hit dozens of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets early on Thursday, according to a statement posted on X, including “military command centres, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defence sites, and maritime capabilities”.
The strikes came hours after US President Donald Trump promised to hit Iran, “very hard”, after it targeted a base in Jordan where US troops are stationed.
Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar said these latest strikes are “concentrated in Iran’s southern provinces, particularly those along the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz”, similar to the US attacks during a recent 13-day campaign.
Iranian officials say a residential building on Qeshm Island was hit, with three people trapped under the rubble, and two injured people taken to hospital.
The explosions were heard as far as the port city of Bandar Abbas in Hormozgan province, leading to initial reports that the port was hit.
The island has experienced power outages, and authorities are working to restore electricity and remove debris, the officials said.
A deputy security minister in Khuzestan province told Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB that US forces targeted “some locations in Abadan”.
Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported US strikes on the outskirts of the city of Kazerun in the southwestern Fars province, as well as two loud explosions on the island of Kish in the Gulf.
Authorities say operations at Kish island’s airport and passenger ferry services remain unaffected.
The IRGC said that as long as Washington’s threats continue, Tehran’s resistance will also continue.
Ryan Bohl, a senior Middle East analyst with RANE network, says the US has two likely escalation options.
“The first is the repeat of what America was doing prior to last Friday, which is focusing on targets and infrastructure related to Iran’s blockade of Hormuz,” he said.
“Or it could be an escalation towards the bridges and power plant strategy that President Trump has repeatedly threatened over and over again.”
The US is eager to end Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a large percentage of global oil shipping passes.
Earlier, Iran rejected an Omani proposal on co-managing shipping routes through the strait.
The US Treasury Department announced new sanctions on Wednesday on two Iranian firms it said are integral to an IRGC-backed “scheme” that forces commercial vessels to buy insurance to transit Hormuz.
“The United States will not allow Iran to hold global commerce hostage or use international shipping to finance the IRGC’s terrorism, aggression, and repression,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wrote on X.
CENTCOM claimed the latest strikes aimed to “further diminish threats posed by Iran and its proxies to American forces, commercial shipping, and neighboring Gulf nations”.
Former Pentagon official David Des Roches told Al Jazeera that the latest US strikes were “not a very overwhelming attack”, adding that Trump is perhaps, “trying to keep things proportionate, or to keep things open for diplomacy”.

title: Why did Anthony Fauci invoke the Fifth Amendment? Senate hearing explained
summary: The former top US health official invoked the amendment as Republicans questioned him over COVID-19.
full_text:
Why did Anthony Fauci invoke the Fifth Amendment? Senate hearing explained
The former top US health official invoked the amendment as Republicans questioned him over COVID-19.
Dr Anthony Fauci pleads the Fifth at Covid hearing
Dr Anthony Fauci, a former top United States public health official, has declined to answer questions at a Republican-led Senate committee hearing into the origins of COVID-19 and the handling of the pandemic.
The former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination on Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 1 itemend of listFauci was called to testify by Republican Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, who accuses him of misleading Congress and questions whether US-funded research in China played a role in the pandemic, allegations Fauci denies.
Although former President Joe Biden granted Fauci a preemptive pardon in 2025, Republicans claim it does not protect him from any alleged crimes committed after it was issued, such as perjuring himself at a Senate hearing.
Fauci’s lawyers advised him not to testify, arguing that anything he said under oath could expose him to new legal risks.
Here is what to know:
Who is Anthony Fauci?
Fauci, 85, is a physician and immunologist who led the US NIAID for 38 years, advising seven presidents, both Republican and Democratic.
He became the public face of the US response to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, after helping lead the country’s response to health crises including HIV/AIDS, Ebola and the 2001 anthrax attacks.
He became a target of conservative criticism over pandemic policies, including mask recommendations, vaccines and school closures.
During his last year in government, Fauci was also chief medical adviser to Biden until he retired in 2022.
During the pandemic, between 2019 and 2022, he kept more than 1,000 pages of diary entries documenting his work advising the White House and responding to the pandemic.
The notes chronicle his interactions with senior officials and the media.
Why is Fauci being questioned?
He was subpoenaed to testify over his handling of the pandemic and its origins before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
The hearing, led by Paul, focused on several issues:
- COVID-19’s origins: Paul has long argued that the coronavirus that causes COVID may have leaked from a laboratory in Wuhan, China, and questioned whether US-funded research played a role in the outbreak.
- Gain-of-function research: Republicans say Fauci misled Congress about whether the National Institutes of Health (NIH) funded gain-of-function research at the Wuhan Institute of Virology, involving modifying viruses to understand how they evolve and assess pandemic risks. Fauci says the NIH did not fund research that caused COVID-19.
- Allegations of a cover-up: Paul accused Fauci of making false statements to Congress and concealing the NIH’s involvement in research in Wuhan. Fauci denies that.
- Fauci’s diary: Before the hearing, Paul released more than 1,100 pages of Fauci’s typewritten diary. Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr said the notes were government record because they were written by a federal employee on a government computer during a public health emergency and they were found on government property.
- Paul said the diary showed differences between Fauci’s private discussions and his public statements. Fauci’s supporters say the entries reflect the uncertainty scientists faced as they learned more about a new virus.
What happened at the hearing?
The tense hearing lasted about three hours.
After a brief opening statement, Fauci repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination and declined to answer more than 100 questions.
He accused committee chairman Paul of having an “obsession” with prosecuting him.
The hearing included several tense moments:
- Contempt vote: Paul said the committee would vote next week on whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress over his refusal to answer questions, threatening “consequences for refusing to answer”.
- Lawyer removed: Paul directed Capitol Police to remove Fauci’s lawyer, David Schertler, after he tried to speak without being recognised by the committee. “This testimony is from Anthony Fauci. This is not a game with his lawyers,” Paul said. Schertler later described the hearing as an “obsessive vendetta”.
- Democrats defend Fauci: Democratic senators said the hearing was politically motivated. Senator Gary Peters called it “a partisan exercise” designed to support “a predetermined conclusion” rather than offering legitimate oversight.
Closing the hearing, Paul asked rhetorically: “Did [Fauci’s] actions lead to the largest man-made plague in history?”
Why did Fauci invoke the Fifth Amendment?
Fauci said he invoked the Fifth Amendment on the advice of his lawyers because he believed his answers could expose him to new legal risks.
He argued that Paul was trying to build a criminal case against him rather than conduct legitimate congressional oversight.
Although Biden’s pardon protects Fauci from prosecution for actions before January 2025, Republicans say any false statements made under oath during this hearing could still expose him to perjury charges.
The Fifth Amendment protects people from being forced to give evidence that could incriminate them in a criminal case. Invoking it is a constitutional right and does not imply guilt.
What do scientists believe about COVID-19’s origins?
Most scientists believe COVID-19 likely spread naturally from animals to humans, known as zoonotic spillover, pointing to a wildlife market in Wuhan as the most likely place where it first spread.
Fauci has consistently said he believes that scientific evidence points to a natural origin, while remaining open to other possibilities.
Notes from his diary detail a January 2020 call with 11 top virologists and evolutionary biologists – only two were convinced the virus had a natural origin, while the rest debated whether it could have been engineered.
Today, most scientists favour a natural origin, while the US intelligence community is divided.
The FBI said in 2023 that a laboratory-related incident is the most likely origin of the pandemic. The CIA reached the same conclusion in 2025, but with low confidence. Other agencies and the National Intelligence Council continue to favour a natural origin or remain undecided.
Does Biden’s pardon protect Fauci?
Yes, but only what happened before the pardon was issued.
On January 19, 2025, Biden granted Fauci a full and unconditional pardon covering any federal offences he may have committed since 2014, saying the move aimed to protect Fauci from “politically motivated prosecutions”.
The pardon does not cover actions taken after it was issued. Fauci could face legal consequences if he were accused of committing a new crime, such as making false statements under oath during Wednesday’s Senate hearing.
Paul and other Republicans also argue that because Biden’s pardon shields Fauci from criminal liability for his past actions, he can no longer claim that his testimony about those actions would incriminate him and should not be able to invoke his Fifth Amendment.
The legal standing of this argument is not clear, and Paul has acknowledged that it is a novel “legal question that the courts may have to decide”.
Can Fauci be held in contempt or prosecuted?
Potentially, but it remains unclear whether either will happen.
Paul said the Senate committee will vote next week on whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress after he refused to answer more than 100 questions.
Being held in contempt means lawmakers believe a witness has refused to cooperate with a lawful investigation. It does not automatically lead to criminal charges, but can trigger further legal action.
If the committee approves the measure, it could refer the case to the Justice Department for possible criminal prosecution,

title: Man convicted in terrorism trial over the 2022 stabbing of author Salman Rushdie
summary: A man was convicted of federal terrorism charges in the 2022 stabbing of Salman Rushdie, the author who has faced a decades-old death threat over his novel "The Satanic Verses."
full_text:
Man convicted in terrorism trial over the 2022 stabbing of author Salman Rushdie
A man was convicted Wednesday of federal terrorism charges in the 2022 stabbing of Salman Rushdie, the author who has faced a decades-old death threat over his novel "The Satanic Verses."
After just a couple of hours of deliberations, a jury found Hadi Matar guilty of all the charges against him, including engaging in an act of transnational terrorism.
Rushdie, who was about to speak on writers' safety, was slashed 15 times on an amphitheater stage in 2022. He was gravely wounded and lost the sight in his right eye.
Prosecutors asserted that Matar was motivated by the late Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini 's 1989 call for Rushdie's death because of "The Satanic Verses."
"His brutal attack on Mr. Rushdie during a peaceful speaking event is a chilling reminder of the global reach of Iranian terrorism," Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg said in a statement after the verdict, adding that "justice has been done." Iran's government has denied involvement in the attack.
Matar's defense: No evidence of his state of mind
Messages seeking comment on the verdict were sent to Matar's attorneys and Rushdie's assistant. During the trial, defense lawyer Nathaniel Barone said the government had no proof of what was in Matar's head.
Matar himself declined to testify. Rushdie did, telling jurors: "I can't say what his ambitions or his aim was, but the wounds were dispersed across my body."
Matar, 28, is already serving a 25-year New York state prison sentence on an attempted murder conviction in the stabbing. His federal sentencing is set for Nov. 3, when he faces a potential life term.
Rushdie won Britain's prestigious Booker Prize for his 1981 novel "Midnight's Children," about his native India. "The Satanic Verses," a novel of magical realism about the lives and dreams of two actors who survive a plane explosion, followed in 1988.
It drew critical acclaim in the United Kingdom but engendered protests around the Muslim world over what some believers saw as blasphemous suggestions about Islam's Prophet Muhammad, particularly in a dream sequence. Over the ensuing years, at least 45 people were killed in riots over the book, a Japanese translator was stabbed to death, and an Italian translator and Norwegian publisher were attacked.
Rushdie, who was born into a Muslim family, has said the dream sequence was just that. But he went into hiding for years, gradually emerging after Iran's government distanced itself in 1998 from Khomeini's fatwa, or religious edict.
"For two decades or more, I led a public life without a hint of trouble," Rushdie testified at the trial in Buffalo, New York.
Yet the fatwa was never rescinded; indeed, Khomenei's successor, the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, indicated in 2017 that it remained in effect. An Iranian foundation has offered a more than $3 million bounty for killing Rushdie.
Prosecutors: Matar's messages showed him zeroing in on Rushdie
Matar broached the fatwa with contacts in messaging apps in 2021 and 2022, according to exhibits shown in court. The messages showed Matar fuming that he felt Rushdie had attacked Islam and, by surviving, emboldened others to insult the faith. Matar alluded to a 2006 comment along those lines by the late Hezbollah militant group leader Hassan Nasrallah, the messages showed.
Born in the U.S., Matar also holds citizenship in Lebanon, where Hezbollah is based. Prosecutors said that photos in Matar's New Jersey bedroom and on his computer indicated his support for Hezbollah, which the U.S. has designated a terrorist organization.
Matar "spent months planning and preparing to carry out what he hoped would be the execution of Salman Rushdie," U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo said in a statement Wednesday.
The messages showed Matar initially talked about wanting to "expose" Rushdie, then about taking his life. In a private note to himself, he wrote: "We need to kill him ASAP," Assistant U.S. Attorney Timothy Lynch said in an opening statement on July 22. The prosecutor said Matar framed the planned killing as part of what he considered a jihad, or holy war.
By spring 2022, the electronic chats showed, Matar wrote that he had discerned where Rushdie lived and was tracking his public appearances, eventually pointing out his scheduled August 2022 talk at the Chautauqua Institution, a western New York arts and intellectual center.
As Rushdie was being introduced, his attacker climbed on stage behind him, then stabbed him as the audience gasped. Spectators and another speaker, Henry Reese, scrambled to aid Rushdie. Law enforcement officers, assigned to the event, arrested the attacker — soon identified as Matar — after civilians restrained him.
Rushdie published a 2024 memoir about the attack, then returned to fiction with last year's "The Eleventh Hour." The author, who was knighted by Britain's late Queen Elizabeth II, received a Dayton Literary Peace Prize lifetime achievement award in November.

title: Hope dwindles for rescue in southwestern Japan quake as death toll climbs to 23
summary: Time was running out to find survivors, as rescuers continued to work in the Kumamoto area on Japan 's southern main island of Kyushu, where the magnitude 7.1 earthquake hit Tuesday.
full_text:
Hope dwindles for rescue in southwestern Japan quake as death toll climbs to 23
KUMAMOTO, Japan — Rural communities in southwestern Japan were struggling to get their lives back to normal Thursday, two days after a powerful earthquake set off an explosion at a mall, toppled a factory chimney and flattened homes, killing at least 23 people.
Time was running out to find survivors, as rescuers continued to work in the Kumamoto area on Japan 's southern main island of Kyushu, where the magnitude 7.1 earthquake hit Tuesday.
The number of those missing was unclear. The quake left at least 63 people injured, five of them seriously, the Kumamoto prefectural government said.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara, speaking to reporters Thursday, gave a higher number for the death toll at 28. That came from a police tally, he said, which includes cases still under investigation. Some of those cases may later turn out to be unrelated to the earthquake.
Survivors spoke about coming home and desperately pulling family members out of the wreckage. Some had suffered injuries and were rushed to the hospital.
Thousands of people spent another night at evacuation centers set up throughout the area in gymnasiums and other big spaces. Some homes were still without water or electricity, while others were simply afraid to go back.
Nearly 23,000 homes were still without electricity and more than 10,000 people were staying in the roughly 400 shelters, where power sources were being added to provide air conditioning.
Concerns were growing about illness, including from the sweltering heat. The Ministry of Environment sent out a heat stroke alert for the Kumamoto area, with temperatures expected to reach as high as 33 C (91 F) Thursday.
Although Japan boasts strict building codes because of the frequency of quakes in the country, some homes in the area are in the older style of Japanese housing, making them relatively fragile.
The most serious damage was at the Aeon Mall shopping center in the town of Kashima, which was bustling with thousands of people when the quake struck in the late afternoon.
The company said some 3,000 customers were evacuated to a parking lot before the explosion happened in another part of the mall, where some people were still working. The mall's second floor collapsed, trapping people.
As of early Thursday, six people were confirmed to have died at the mall site among the 11 people pulled out of the wreckage, according to Kumamoto authorities.
Family members of those still missing could be seen wandering helplessly near the wrecked mall, waiting for word, despite the sweltering weather.
In the Yatsushiro area, where a chimney collapsed at a Nippon Paper Industries factory, 10 people were rescued, but eight others died, and one remained missing, according to the Kumamoto prefectural government disaster team.

full_text:
Why did an Okinawan delegation visit a Beijing cemetery amid China-Japan tensions?
The trip highlights historical ties between China and the Ryukyu Islands that Beijing is leveraging as a counterweight in its row with Tokyo
During the visit in June – first made public by the Global Times on Sunday – about a dozen delegates travelled to the site southeast of Beijing, which honours six centuries of ties between China and the former island nation later annexed by Japan.
During the memorial ceremony, the delegation members paid tribute with traditional rituals, incense and liquor. Some members also wore traditional attire, according to the Global Times.
Among the visitors was Tetsumi Takara, a former Japanese lawmaker who told the newspaper that historical ties between China and Ryukyu “should not be forgotten, distorted, or hijacked by politics”.
The Beijing site holds the graves of more than 10 Ryukyu Kingdom officials and envoys from the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), including an envoy who objected to Japan’s 1879 annexation of the kingdom, and a student who took his own life to protest against the islands’ loss of independence, according to state news agency Xinhua.

title: A quarter of young Africans believe USAID cuts could be positive, survey finds
summary:
Losing funds should force leaders to confront their own challenges, they said, while many voiced concerns over increasing foreign influence

A quarter of young Africans believe aid cuts by the US could have a positive impact, saying that losing foreign money will force leaders to confront and solve their own challenges, according to a new survey.

In Ghana and Nigeria, almost half (41% and 40% respectively) of young people aged 18 to 24 were optimistic, with Liberia not far behind (37%). A further one in 10 (11%) young people were uncertain about the impact, according to the African Youth Survey, which interviewed almost 5,000 people across 16 of the continent’s 54 recognised countries.

full_text:
A quarter of young Africans believe aid cuts by the US could have a positive impact, saying that losing foreign money will force leaders to confront and solve their own challenges, according to a new survey.
In Ghana and Nigeria, almost half (41% and 40% respectively) of young people aged 18 to 24 were optimistic, with Liberia not far behind (37%). A further one in 10 (11%) young people were uncertain about the impact, according to the African Youth Survey, which interviewed almost 5,000 people across 16 of the continent’s 54 recognised countries.
The Trump administration announced in early 2025 that it was eliminating more than 90% of USAID’s foreign contracts and $60bn in overall US assistance around the world. US foreign aid had been designed to play a critical role in tackling poverty, hunger and inequality worldwide.
Other countries, including Britain, France and Germany, have also been slashing aid budgets. The UK announced in February 2025 that the aid budget would be cut from 0.5% of gross national income to 0.3% in 2027, its lowest level as a percentage of national income since records began. The UN target is 0.7%.
Ivor Ichikowitz, whose South African family foundation commissioned the report, said: “The big picture [from the survey] is that the youth is concerned about governments that are overly influenced by foreign powers. What they’re saying is that African governments need to take agency and responsibility for their own reality.”
Africa has the youngest population in the world, with 70% of sub-Saharan Africa under the age of 30, according to the UN. The median age of the continent is 19 years and six months. By 2030, Africa will be home to more than 40% of the world’s youth.
The sudden USAID cuts were met with public outrage and pushback from development and humanitarian organisations. They caused the closure of vital services, including maternity clinics, and medicine shortages at a time when UN agencies are struggling to find money for their humanitarian work and food insecurity has been worsened by the climate crisis.
According to the survey, nearly half of African youth (46%) did believe the closure of USAID would have a damaging impact on their countries, with healthcare services and disease prevention seen as the areas most affected. This anxiety is highest in Mozambique (76%), followed by Kenya (63%) and Rwanda (63%), where youth feel the cuts will disproportionately affect the most vulnerable members of society.
Degan Ali, executive director of Adeso, an African non-profit incubating ideas and enterprises to lower aid dependency, said that while the cuts were carried out in a “hugely irresponsible and inhumane” manner, she was not surprised that a significant proportion of young people saw positivity there. “I think it’s a reflection of the general feeling. A lot of people find aid very demeaning,” she said. “They didn’t feel that the aid was being used for the right things and there is a sense of ‘We can do this for ourselves’. The younger generation feel like our leaders are the duty bearers and are supposed to be handling the needs of our communities.”
She said people believed that the aid that comes into a country is not going to the right causes or the right people. “There’s all this money going into the development sector, but they’re not really seeing major changes on the ground,” she said. “The younger generation is very politically active and more savvy. They are pushing back and trying to hold their leaders accountable.”
She also said that the youth was looking towards African role models on the continent, a move exemplified by the popularity of Burkina Faso’s military leader, Ibrahim Traoré, who portrays himself as a pan-Africanist figure leading his nation out of the clutches of western imperialism and neocolonialism.
“He is one of the more popular leaders across the entire continent of Africa,” said Ali. “There are matatus (minibus taxis) that have his name on in Nairobi, Kenya. The youth see that he is turning around a very poor country and that he really cares about his people. That further motivates young people to protest and say, ‘We don’t need aid, we have enough resources in our country and we need our leaders to behave differently.’”
Hibak Kalfan, executive director of Near, a network of civil society organisations from the global south, said the shuttering of USAID had led to the closure of initiatives and organisations across the whole continent, but had also created the opportunity to reconsider resources and sustainability. “It has put a real light on the fact that [organisations] have been highly dependent on bilateral external funding for years, and the future of aid will depend on a diversity of resources,” she said.

title: NSW to send paramedics not police to some mental health emergencies after multiple deaths
summary:
Mental health experts to triage triple zero calls, but not all of the changes will be implemented 24/7 or statewide

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

New South Wales will send specialist nurses rather than police to some mental health emergencies after the state announced long-fought-for reform in the wake of multiple deaths at the hands of police.

Rose Jackson and Yasmin Catley, the mental health and police ministers, announced on Thursday a statewide change to how triple 0 calls are triaged, with a new team of mental health experts assessing mental health calls 24/7 in a bid to provide better support.

full_text:
New South Wales will send specialist nurses rather than police to some mental health emergencies after the state announced long-fought-for reform in the wake of multiple deaths at the hands of police.
Rose Jackson and Yasmin Catley, the mental health and police ministers, announced on Thursday a statewide change to how triple 0 calls are triaged, with a new team of mental health experts assessing mental health calls 24/7 in a bid to provide better support.
The change, funded by $270m over ten years, will also establish a hub providing real-time clinical advice to NSW Ambulance first responders and assisting them in making safer decisions.
This will be bolstered by eight new mental health teams that will provide a health-led response to call-outs and include a paramedic and specialist mental health nurse. But this initiative will only operate 12 hours a day and won’t be statewide.
Outside those 12 hours, police or existing responses such as the co-response model known as Police Ambulance and Clinical Early Response (Pacer) – which has been criticised by advocates for not operating 24/7 and statewide – will respond.
The mental health minister, Rose Jackson, said reform, which was shaped by the UK’s “right person, right care” model, was “only the beginning” and could be scaled statewide.
“We’re committing $270m as a first step. But I recognise that mental health crises don’t happen within neat 12-hour windows. They’re things that can occur any time of day, any day of the week,” she said.
Police and government had been under pressure to enact reforms after fatalities while people were in mental health distress. This included 42-year-old Jesse Deacon, who lived with schizophrenia and was fatally shot by police at his home in a public housing estate after he was reported to be self-harming in July 2023.
Deacon’s mother, 82-year-old Judy Deacon, has since become one of the state’s loudest voices for change in pushing for change, and has called for mental health experts to triage Triple 0 calls.
Deacon welcomed the change as an important first step that might have saved her son’s life.
“I think the outcome might have been different,” she said. “Me and other victims’ families will be closely watching and making sure it will end up making a difference.”
Police will continue to be the lead responder in instances where there’s a risk to safety, such as if someone is armed with a knife.
Grace Cameron-Lee, a senior solicitor in the police accountability practice at Redfern Legal Centre, welcomed the change but said NSW police training and operational changes that prioritise de-escalation techniques “remains critical”.
Asked on Thursday if the reform would include more training for police, Catley said: “Police are trained in mental health. That’s a component of their training in Goulburn now, but … they are not mental health clinicians, and that has to be recognised.
“This model is exactly what we need to ensure that those people who are experiencing a mental health incident get the right care.”
Dr Pramudie Gunaratne, the chief executive of the Australian Society of Psychiatrists, also welcomed the reform, describing it as “a stronger front door into the mental health system”.
But, she said, “a front door is only useful if there’s a house behind it” and urged more funding for community mental health support.
“Without enough community mental health services, people will still find themselves stuck in the cycle of crisis, emergency response and discharge, instead of receiving the sustained care they need to recover,” she said.
Jackson has been under pressure to release analysis into the mental health system which is expected to have outlined the resource gaps in the system.
She said on Thursday she planned to release the report publicly but didn’t give a timeline.
“There are gaps in the system, particularly in community mental health care. And yes, this is about a different response for crisis and emergency … It’s obviously preferable if we can invest earlier so that we don’t get to that crisis point.”

title: ‘Warring kingdoms’: cofounder of religious Reformers compares NSW Liberal party factionalism to Braveheart
summary:
Robert Assaf tells Icac that Angus Taylor wasn’t ‘that involved’ but the federal opposition leader ‘definitely wasn’t opposed’ to work of conservative group

A member of a group of young conservative Liberal power brokers being investigated for allegedly soliciting illegal donations has compared their factional work to Mel Gibson’s Braveheart – and said they “didn’t think the law applied to us” when it came to political funding.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Thursday heard from Robert Assaf, the first witness from the conservative right Liberal factional group the Reformers to give evidence.

full_text:
A member of a group of young conservative Liberal power brokers being investigated for allegedly soliciting illegal donations has compared their factional work to Mel Gibson’s Braveheart – and said they “didn’t think the law applied to us” when it came to political funding.
The Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Thursday heard from Robert Assaf, the first witness from the conservative right Liberal factional group the Reformers to give evidence.
Icac is investigating whether Liberal figures, including Assaf, “solicited or accepted” donations, including from prohibited donors, in amounts which were undeclared or exceeded caps, to recruit or renew members to the party – a practice known as “branch-stacking”. The Reformers allegedly wanted more conservative policies on issues including same-sex marriage, transgender rights, abortion and euthanasia.
Assaf, 30, who admitted to being one of two founding members of the Reformers in 2017, said the group was started in the context of a factional split in the Liberal party between the religious conservative hard right and the centre-right.
“My observations at the time were, the right faction was like – I’m not sure if you’ve seen Braveheart – but like these warring kingdoms, and they would slaughter each other, and then every now and then they’d come together for a big fight,” Assaf said.
While branch-stacking is not of itself illegal, Icac is investigating whether the alleged conduct of the Reformers involved possible offences under NSW’s Electoral Funding Act. Asked about his knowledge of the laws governing donations, Assaf told Icac that the group “didn’t think the law applied to us”.
“Because it was an electoral law, we’re not campaigning in elections in that sense,” he told counsel assisting peggy Dwyer SC.
“We’re internal Liberal party machinations. My understanding the whole way through was, until very recently … was it’s internal. It doesn’t count as anything to do with electoral laws or any other law.”
He defended the Reformers, which includes members being investigated over a second allegation: that they took $2m in payments from the fugitive property developer Jean Nassif in exchange for outcomes sought by Nassif.
“The Reformers sound really spooky in the media right now, but it was just a bunch of 20-year-old people trying to figure things out,” Assaf said.
Assaf appeared after two days of evidence from former Liberal staffer Dylan Whitelaw, who was associated with the group but has not been named in allegations against the Reformers.
After being mentioned during Whitelaw’s examination on Tuesday and Wednesday, the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, dodged further questions on Thursday after denying he had ever donated to the Reformers.
“I’ve answered these questions yesterday. I’m not going to give a running commentary on it,” Taylor said. The federal Liberal leader is not accused of wrongdoing.
On Thursday, Assaf claimed Taylor was one of several state and federal Liberal politicians who were aware of and supported the Reformers’ work.
“Angus was around it, but I don’t think he was really that involved,” Assaf said. “He definitely wasn’t opposed.”
He said the former NSW Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet, whose brothers Jean-Claude and Charles Perrottet are named in the Icac allegations, was “pretty absent in the whole thing, but supportive from what I understood”. Dominic Perrottet is not accused of wrongdoing.
The commission heard Assaf went to the same independent Catholic schoolas Jean-Claude and Charles Perrottet, as well as another member of the Reformers, Jeremy Greenwood.
After spending a year in a Catholic seminary, Assaf later worked in federal parliament for various ministers, senators and MPs, including Tony Abbott, who the commission heard gave talks at recruitment events hosted by the Reformers.
He described having an “icky feeling” about getting involved in politics, but said he was convinced to join the Liberal party after attending a 2015 talk at the Sydney University Liberal club by NSW upper house member Damien Tudehope, against the Safe Schools program, whose stated aim was to keep gay and transgender students safe.
Assaf, who described Tudehope as “a warrior for the values that he cared about”, said the politician subsequently gave numerous talks at events hosted by the Reformers.
Tudehope, who is not accused of wrongdoing, stepped aside from his role as shadow attorney general and Liberal upper house leader after being called as a witness by Icac.
The inquiry heard that Assaf and fellow Reformer, Christian Ellis, started the group in 2017, after forming a strong friendship while working together on the No campaign for the same-sex marriage plebiscite.
The inquiry heard that adopting the model that had seen Assaf recruited, the group began to organise talks on conservative issues, aiming to sign up new members afterwards.
Dwyer on Thursday showed Assaf a draft document sent to him by Ellis which detailed a plan to recruit 5,000 Christian conservative members to the party to take control of the NSW division of the Liberal party, which had 4,000 members at the time.
Assaf said the main aim of the Reformers was “policy change” but increasing the number of members in the Liberal party was “certainly part of the process”.
Asked about a stated aim “to take over left-wing branches through stealth”, Assaf said “ideally, we would not want to take branches through stealth”.
“I prefer to be a front stabber than a back stabber,” he added, stating the group’s intention was to create a “broad church” within the party. Assaf said they wanted to “change the terrible situation of factionalism”.
“Christians obviously don’t like lying,” he said. “But there was a strategy to it, and some people needed to be more comfortable with that than others.”
Icac’s inquiry continues.

full_text:
Dr Anthony Fauci, the US’s chief medical adviser at the start of the pandemic, has described a book by News Corp investigative journalist Sharri Markson backing the “lab leak” theory of Covid-19’s origins as a “bunch of nonsense” in his newly released diaries.
This week, Fauci, 85, was subpoenaed by the Republican senator Rand Paul to appear at a Senate hearing into Covid-19 and his handling of the pandemic.
The physician and veteran former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, who retired in 2022, accused Paul of an “unhinged” campaign lobbying for his imprisonment and refused to answer questions at Wednesday’s hearing.
The hearing was a continuation of Paul’s years-long support of the lab leak theory, or the idea that the Covid-19 pandemic began as a release from the Wuhan Institute of Virology.
Ahead of his appearance, Paul published 1,141 pages of Fauci’s pandemic-era journal entries. In the entries, Fauci criticised reporting in The Australian newspaper and a book by Markson that claimed a facility in Wuhan was “immersed in genetically manipulating bat-coronaviruses in perilous experiments”.
On 7 May 2021, Markson reported in The Australian that Chinese military scientists “discussed the weaponisation of Sars coronaviruses five years before the Covid-19 pandemic” and predicted a third world war would be fought with biological weapons.
Fauci, who served under seven US presidents but became a household name overnight in 2020, wrote in his private diary that the article “does not make any sense”.
“Why would someone want to make an agent that could equally infect your own population. Something is wrong with this report. I will have to follow up on it,” he wrote.
Guardian Australia later found the “chilling” document produced by Chinese military scientists in the article was based on a discredited 2015 book containing conspiracy theories about biological warfare which is freely available on the internet.
Markson’s story was criticised as misleading and alarmist by China analysts. A deputy editor of Foreign Policy magazine and China expert, James Palmer, said the article had links to conspiracy theories about the origins of the coronavirus which are popular with the political right.
The story was published to promote Markson’s debut book, What Really Happened in Wuhan, which argued there was “no scientific consensus that Covid-19 has a natural origin” and that China had conspired to cover up the truth.
Fauci also took aim at Markson’s book, writing in his diary that “the same old crap is going on with the far right continuing to attack me”.
“The latest written by an Australian person who says I’m the father of gain of function research quotes from the infamous Richard Ebright saying that I’m a liar and I have misled everybody about gain of function,” he wrote. “What a bunch of nonsense! The far right continues to try and discredit me.”
Ebright is an American molecular biologist and proponent of the lab leak theory.
Markson told Guardian Australia “the majority of the intelligence community now concludes that Covid-19 likely originated in a Wuhan laboratory”.
“I led the way internationally exposing the role of Anthony Fauci’s agency funding 65 projects at the Wuhan Institute of Virology, funnelling the money through EcoHealth Alliance,” she said on Thursday.
The origins of the Covid-19 pandemic remain the subject of intense debate among scientists and the wider public.
There are two competing theories – the natural-origins hypotheses, which suggests the pandemic began when a close relative of Sars-CoV-2 jumped from a wild animal to a human through the wildlife trade, and lab leak theories, which argue that the virus emerged when Chinese scientists became infected through research-associated activities.
News Corp was approached for comment.

title: ‘Lenin was an enemy of humanity’: Why Kyiv wants to put Cossack chief statue in place of Soviet leader
summary:
Removal of Soviet-era statues sped up when Russia seized Crimea in 2014, and since Putin’s 2022 invasion has moved at pace as Ukrainians question their identity

Since 2013 the plinth at the bottom of Taras Shevchenko Boulevard in Kyiv has been eerily empty. The scruffy monument is daubed in white paint and graffiti. Someone has stuck a Ukrainian trident where Lenin once stood, gazing down during the years of Soviet communism. A crowd toppled the sculpture during Ukraine’s Maidan revolution, which ousted the pro-Russian government, and smashed it with sledgehammers.

In June, Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed putting a new figure on the plinth: Ivan Mazepa, a Cossack military and political leader, who broke with Moscow and fought for Ukraine’s independence. “I am certain that where Lenin fell, Mazepa will stand firm,” Zelenskyy said. He spoke next to a bust of Mazepa in the Pechersk Lavra, an ancient Kyiv monastery hit by Russian missiles.

full_text:
Since 2013 the plinth at the bottom of Taras Shevchenko Boulevard in Kyiv has been eerily empty. The scruffy monument is daubed in white paint and graffiti. Someone has stuck a Ukrainian trident where Lenin once stood, gazing down during the years of Soviet communism. A crowd toppled the sculpture during Ukraine’s Maidan revolution, which ousted the pro-Russian government, and smashed it with sledgehammers.
In June, Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed putting a new figure on the plinth: Ivan Mazepa, a Cossack military and political leader, who broke with Moscow and fought for Ukraine’s independence. “I am certain that where Lenin fell, Mazepa will stand firm,” Zelenskyy said. He spoke next to a bust of Mazepa in the Pechersk Lavra, an ancient Kyiv monastery hit by Russian missiles.
The proposed swap of Lenin for Mazepa has triggered a lively debate about monuments and what they say about changing national identity. After winning independence in 1991, Ukraine removed large numbers of Soviet-era statues and renamed streets as part of “decommunisation”. The process sped up in 2014 when Russia seized Crimea and fighting began in the Donbas, and moved even faster after Vladimir Putin’s 2022 full-scale invasion that aimed to scrub Ukraine from Europe’s map.
Nataliia Kryvda, a professor of the history of culture at Taras Shevchenko National University in Kyiv, said Ukraine was going through an unfinished period of decolonisation. “The USSR absorbed national cultures. It tried to make a single nation of Soviet citizens. Russia today looks at Ukraine and says we are one people. It isn’t true. We have our own mindset, historical destiny, beliefs and dreams. Our identity is a dynamic process,” she said.
Standing next to the ex-Lenin plinth, Kryvda said she was in favour of a Mazepa monument. “Why not? He’s our leader. Each culture needs to mark its space with memorials. They objectify memory,” she said. She described Mazepa as a “contradictory personality” and not an “ideal hero”.
“He really was a friend and political partner of Russia, right up until the moment he dramatically changed his life and history,” she added.
As hetman, or head, of Cossack Ukraine, Mazepa sought to balance the demands of neighbouring Moscow and Warsaw. In 1708, the Russian emperor Peter the Great refused to protect Ukrainian territory from invading Swedes. Mazepa abandoned the tsar and formed an alliance with the Swedish King Charles XII, an act that ended in defeat and led the Bolsheviks to call modern Ukrainian patriots “Mazepists”.
“Mazepa was the architect of European Ukraine,” Kryvda said.
In his speech at the Pechersk Lavra, Zelenskyy said Russia had smeared Mazepa for centuries, depicting him as a traitor. Their goal, he said, was to make Ukrainians “view their own history through the eyes of others”.
Alim Aliev, a writer and Crimean Tatar campaigner, said Ukraine was belatedly recovering its identity. “We are reclaiming our own voices and names,” he said. He cited the example of the 20th-century Ukrainian poet and dissident Vasyl Stus, whose image will appear in September on a new 2,000 Hryvnia note. Stus studied in Donetsk, the eastern Donbas city occupied by Russia, and led Ukraine’s national revival. He died in 1985 in a Soviet prison camp.
In Aliev’s view, Ukraine was now speaking about its past “without mediators” and said it was appropriate that statues of the 19th-century Russian poet Pushkin had been taken down across the country. “He had a totally imperial view of Crimea,” Aliev said, citing Pushkin’s narrative poem, The Fountain of Bakhchisarai. “He exoticises Crimean Tatars and describes us from a colonial perspective.” Of the Mazepa statue, he added: “I don’t think it’s a controversial idea.”
Last month workmen took away a monument to another Russian literary giant Mikhail Bulgakov. It had stood since 2007 outside the house where Bulgakov lived, in one of Kyiv’s most attractive streets, St Andrew’s Descent. Kyiv’s city council voted to remove it. Other plaques to Bulgakov, born in Kyiv to a Russian family when it was part of the Russian empire, have already been taken down, including one outside the university where he studied medicine. Bulgakov’s museum – housed in the writer’s home – remains open.
The museum’s director, Liudmyla Habianuri, said she was not opposed to the sculpture’s removal and dismissed a petition to keep it as “bland”. She acknowledged that Bulgakov had written negatively about Ukrainian nationalist forces in his Kyiv novel The White Guard, set in the winter of 1918-19, amid revolution and war. She stressed, however: “Bulgakov was a witness to his times. And a satirist. He didn’t like anybody. That included communists and priests.”
Habianuri said Russia’s war had prompted Ukrainians to ask: “‘Who am I?’ It’s a very painful question,” she said. “If I speak Russian and watch Russian films and the Russians are killing me then I must give all that up. Then I’m Ukrainian. And if I’m Ukrainian, I must become Ukrainian as quickly as possible.”
This has led people to join the struggle for identity, she said, either via social media or by attacking monuments.
Bulgakov, she said, was a frequent subject of such struggles. “Right now there is a table with only two columns: plus or minus. As a Russian, who didn’t write from the perspective of Ukraine’s defenders, Bulgakov can’t get a plus sign.”
Habianuri said a process of “simplification” was under way but was delighted when demonstrators pulled down the Lenin statue, saying: “The man was an enemy of humanity itself.” Mazepa, she said, was a “unique person” who had inspired a notable poem by Lord Byron. But she questioned whether the plinth was a fitting spot for a memorial.
“I understand it’s a quick jab at Russia. But it’s not the right place for a hero,” she said. “The Germans hanged people there during the second world war.”
Unlike Lenin, the Bulgakov statue was carefully packed up and returned to the family of its late sculptor, Mykola Rapay. His daughter, Kateryna, declined a request from the Guardian for the work to be photographed at its new location. She said she had given official guarantees that the monument would remain “out of public space”.
“These are not my whims,” she said. “The sculpture is not my property. I am the guarantor of its preservation.”
Over at the Pechersk Lavra tourists walked past the new Mazepa bust, which has been erected in front of a fountain and a pleasant shady garden. It sits next to the complex’s 11th-century Dormition Cathedral, used in medieval times for the burial of prominent figures. Last week a boy photographed his father next to the new monument.
Mazepa, a patron of the arts, donated money to pay for the cathedral’s baroque renovation. In June, a Russian drone crashed into its roof, causing a fire, and blackening external pictures of saints. Other icons and religious artefacts were rescued.
One Ukrainian visitor, Olena Polishchuk, said she had come to the Lavra from the UK, where she has lived since Putin’s big invasion. What did she think of Mazepa? “He’s a famous man. I’m glad he’s being commemorated. He’s an important part of our history,” she said.

title: Deadly strikes on Ukrainian cities after Zelenskyy warns of ‘massive’ Russian attack
summary:
Six dead in Kryvi Rih including two children and fires in Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, after wave of ballistic missile launches

A Russian missile strike killed at least six people in central Ukraine, including two girls, the head of Kryvyi Rih’s military administration said, while at least one person died in Kyiv, after the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warned the country hours in advance of Moscow launching another massive attack.

“In a village on the outskirts of Kryvyi Rih, a direct strike by an Iskander-M ballistic missile, launched from Voronezh, hit a private house where a large family lived, killing girls aged five and 12 and four adults,” said Oleksandr Vilkul, adding that a further eight people were wounded and that the death toll may rise.

full_text:
A Russian missile strike killed at least six people in central Ukraine, including two girls, the head of Kryvyi Rih’s military administration said, while at least one person died in Kyiv, after the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warned the country hours in advance of Moscow launching another massive attack.
“In a village on the outskirts of Kryvyi Rih, a direct strike by an Iskander-M ballistic missile, launched from Voronezh, hit a private house where a large family lived, killing girls aged five and 12 and four adults,” said Oleksandr Vilkul, adding that a further eight people were wounded and that the death toll may rise.
In Kyiv, “sadly, one death has been confirmed” the military administration for the capital city announced. The Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko, reported fires in several districts. Earlier, he posted: “The enemy is attacking the capital with ballistic weapons. The threat of further attack remains present. Stay in shelters!”
Elsewhere, residential buildings in the western city of Lviv were damaged by Russian air attacks, mayor Andriy Sadovyi said on Telegram, citing preliminary reports and asking people to seek shelter.
Late on Wednesday, Zelenskyy had posted: “The Russians prepared a massive attack several days ago, and there is a high probability that the strike will be carried out tonight … Please, in all regions of Ukraine, pay attention to air raid alerts today and stay safe.”
As the attacks took place, Poland, which shares a border with Ukraine, protectively scrambled fighter jets to protect its airspace, its armed forces said.
“Fighter aircraft and an early warning aircraft have begun operations while ground-based air defence systems and radar reconnaissance systems have reached a state of readiness.”
Zelenskyy also repeated his request to Ukraine’s allies to supply Kyiv with the missiles its air defence system lacks. “It is important that our partners fully understand what is happening and that the protection of people’s lives depends directly on their willingness, or lack of willingness, to provide air defence missiles.”
Meanwhile in Russia, a warehouse of online retailer Wildberries in the western city of Penza caught fire from a Ukrainian drone attack, said the regional governor, Oleg Melnichenko. One person was injured and around 200 people were evacuated from the site, he added.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

title: US launches fresh strikes on Iran after days-long pause, amid fears the war is widening
summary:
Trump vowed to hit Iran ‘very hard’ after it targeted a base in Jordan that hosts US troops, a day after joint US-Saudi strikes on militants in Iraq

  • Middle East crisis – live updates

The US military has launched strikes on Iranian targets in response to Tehran’s attack on American forces in Jordan on Wednesday, raising the risk of a return to all-out-war in the region.

The new strikes were launched hours after president Donald Trump vowed to hit Iran “very hard” after it targeted a base in Jordan that hosts US troops, and comes after a days-long pause in violence between the two sides.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The US military has launched strikes on Iranian targets in response to Tehran’s attack on American forces in Jordan on Wednesday, raising the risk of a return to all-out-war in the region.
The new strikes were launched hours after president Donald Trump vowed to hit Iran “very hard” after it targeted a base in Jordan that hosts US troops, and comes after a days-long pause in violence between the two sides.
Iranian state media said two people were injured in attacks on the island of Qeshm in the strait of Hormuz and that explosions were also reported in Khuzestan province to the north-west.
US central command said in a social media post that over the span of two hours they struck “dozens” of targets belonging to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corp, including military command centres as well as missile and drone facilities, and coastal surveillance and defence sites.
The barrage came after the US partnered with Saudi Arabia to strike Iran-backed militias in neighbouring Iraq on Wednesday, killing at least 20 fighters and six Iranian advisers.
Elsewhere, drone strikes ignited fires on two natural gas vessels at the Egyptian port of Damietta, according to British maritime security firm Ambrey. It was not immediately clear who was responsible for the strikes on a US-owned floating storage facility and a Greek-owned tanker. No injuries were reported.
Asked during an Oval Office event if Iran was responsible for the strikes on the natural gas vessels, Trump responded: “It’s a little more of the same.”
“In the meantime, we’re going to be hitting them very hard because it’s our turn to hit them,” he added.
Analysts said the flare-ups on multiple fronts after several days of relative calm pushed the region into “uncharted territory”. It also underscored the difficulty of winding down a five-month conflict that has jolted the world economy and which remains unpopular among Americans.
The fighting was also likely to add to concerns that the US is further drawing down already diminished stockpiles of sophisticated munitions needed to defend its bases and allies.
Wednesday’s joint US-Saudi strikes on Iraq came after Riyadh had accused Iraqi militias of firing drones against its oil facilities. An umbrella group of Iraqi militias initially denied the allegations.
The Popular Mobilization Forces, a coalition of primarily Shiite Iranian-backed armed groups that is officially under the command of the Iraqi military, said at least 20 fighters were killed and 32 wounded in the overnight strikes.
Iran’s deputy governor for political, security and social affairs in Markazi province told Iranian state media that four advisers from Tehran were also killed.
The coalition joined the fight against the Islamic State group after it seized large sections of Iraq in 2014. The Iraqi government later designated the coalition as an “independent military formation” within the armed forces, but the militias have significant autonomy and some have attacked US facilities.
Before the latest eruption, mediators had expressed optimism about bringing the US and Iran back to the negotiating table. An interim agreement collapsed in recent weeks over renewed fighting in the strait of Hormuz.
A regional official said mediators are “still trying with both sides” to restore calm and get the ceasefire back on track. He gave no details on whether progress was being made and spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door diplomacy.
The renewed hostilities sent oil prices spiking. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 7.3% to over $88 a barrel.
Saudi Arabia is also locked in a renewed conflict with the Houthis. The Iran-backed militants have declared a blockade of Saudi shipping that could choke off another crucial Middle East trade route, the Bab el-Mandeb strait from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden.

title: Bitcoin, ether whipsaw wipes out $286 million in leveraged bets
full_text:
Bitcoin, ether whipsaw wipes out $286 million in leveraged bets
Price volatility around the Federal Reserve's rate decision cleared positions for roughly 90,000 traders, with unusually equal losses for bulls and bears.
- Nearly $286 million in crypto derivatives positions were liquidated over 24 hours, even as bitcoin traded roughly flat around $63,900 and ether slipped modestly to $1,900.
- Liquidations were split between longs and shorts in major coins, with about $57 million in bitcoin and $58 million in ether positions wiped out amid price swings of less than 2%.
- Equity perpetuals on crypto exchanges saw heavy, mostly long-side losses tied to the AI chip trade, as leveraged bets on SanDisk, Micron, SK Hynix and a semiconductor ETF were hit by the sharpest chip selloff of the year.
Major cryptocurrencies are unchanged over 24 hours. But masking the calm are erratic back-and-forth price swings around the Fed meeting that flushed out leveraged futures bets, triggering heavy liquidations.
About $286 million in positions were liquidated across 87,294 traders in 24 hours, according to CoinGlass. Longs accounted for $186 million of the damage and shorts $100 million, the signature of a market that moved hard in both directions and settled back where it started.
Bitcoin’s data show that both bulls and bears have borne the brunt of liquidations. Roughly $57 million in bitcoin positions were cleared, and the balance was nearly even, with about $28 million in longs against $29 million in shorts. The price swung between $63,247 and $64,660 during the window, a range of barely 2%, which was enough to clear traders positioned either way.
The single biggest liquidation was a $2.9 million bitcoin position on Binance.
Ether recorded the largest total at about $58 million, tilted toward longs, as prices ranged between $1,850 and $1,920. As of this writing, bitcoin 
The bulk of the damage happened around Wednesday’s Fed rate decision as the widely-watched event led to erratic price movements, triggering $188 million in liquidations, with longs alone accounting for $130 million of that tally.
A more unusual wreckage was in equity futures listed on crypto exchanges. About $19 million in SanDisk positions were liquidated on crypto derivatives venues, along with $10 million in Micron, $7 million in SK Hynix and $7 million in SOXL, a leveraged semiconductor ETF. These are perpetual futures on stocks and funds, listed on crypto exchanges and traded with the same leverage as bitcoin.
Almost all of it was long. Micron’s liquidations split roughly seven to one in favor of longs, $9 million against $1 million, and SanDisk’s ran two to one. Traders were using crypto rails to bet on the AI memory trade going up, and they were positioned that way heading into the sharpest chip selloff of the year.
But the timing turned out unfortunate. SK Hynix fell 17% on Wednesday after reporting profit up 557%, short of expectations. Korea’s Kospi has dropped more than 40% from its June peak.
It is the second time this week that equity perpetuals on crypto venues have caused real losses. On Monday, a single trade on a thin Korean pre-market venue dropped Trade.xyz’s SK Hynix contract 19% and triggered $60 million liquidations, which the exchange has since agreed to reimburse.

title: Bitcoin analysts agree the Fed's hold was hawkish. They are split on what happens next.
full_text:
Bitcoin analysts agree the Fed's hold was hawkish. They are split on what happens next.
Four analysts agree the Fed's hawkish hold changes the calculus for risk assets, but they split on whether bitcoin's real test is already here or still six weeks away.
- The Fed held rates at 3.5%-3.75% for a fifth straight meeting, but a 9-3 vote and Warsh's hawkish tone caught some off guard.
- Analysts agree the tone was hawkish but split on what it means next.
- Bitcoin held near $64,000 through the decision, even as stocks slid and Treasury yields rose.
The Fed held interest rates steady Wednesday, in a decision shadowed by unusual uncertainty after several prominent voices had called for a hike. Bitcoin 
Despite the calm, analysts appear divided on the post-Fed outlook for BTC.
Some are calling the Fed’s decision the least favorable outcome for digital assets, while others are taking a more constructive view. Others emphasize that bitcoin’s outlook depends on what happens with other assets, with some saying the real test for bitcoin still lies ahead at the September Fed meeting.
Andrei Grachev, managing partner at DWF Labs, is worried about what Wednesday's hold, delivered with a hawkish tone, signals about the Fed's tolerance for pain.
The hawkishness wasn't subtle. The Federal Open Market Committee held rates at 3.5%-3.75%, but three policymakers – Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, Minneapolis Fed president Neel Kashkari, and Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan – dissented in favor of a hike, pushing the decision through on a 9-3 vote. Warsh then opened his press conference saying "there is no soft inflation target," reiterating that any inflation print above 2% is unacceptable to him.
"This is the Fed telling markets it will not tolerate inflation above target even at the cost of a growth scare," Grachev said. "For digital assets, that's the least favorable outcome on the table this cycle."
His reasoning simple. "Tighter policy, less liquidity, [means] more expensive carry." Tighter liquidity makes leveraged and carry-funded crypto positions more expensive to hold, which can pressure bitcoin's price. Grachev expects the shift in positioning to happen immediately, not gradually. "Institutional positioning should shift defensive immediately, and risk-on assets will take the biggest hit, he said.
He gave bitcoin some credit for resilience so far, but not much comfort looking ahead: "Bitcoin has held up through a hawkish stretch already, but a fresh hawkish surprise would negatively impact prices."
Can-Luca Köymen, investment strategist at Sygnum Bank, took a nearly opposite view, largely because he'd already priced in the hawkish hold.
"This was broadly the outcome we expected," he said. "Our base case was a hold, and hawkish language accompanying it is consistent with a committee that wants to preserve optionality while the energy picture remains unsettled."
For bitcoin specifically, Köymen stressed that a restrictive Fed isn't the same thing as a deteriorating backdrop.
"The signal is that the macro backdrop stays restrictive for a while longer rather than that it deteriorates," he said. His firm's constructive stance on crypto, he added, was never built on the Fed cutting rates soon in the first place, but rests “on inflationary pressure remaining manageable," and Wednesday didn't change that math.
“What we continue to watch is the oil path and whether the recent improvement in ETF flows and on-chain accumulation persists,” he said.
Bitget’s Chief analyst Ryan Lee’s comments center less on bitcoin directly and more on the assets he expects to absorb the immediate pressure: Nasdaq and gold.
Per Lee, the Fed's hawkish tone made sense once you account for oil. June's soft inflation print, he argued, "was flattered by energy prices that reversed hard on the Hormuz disruption, and the committee clearly knows the July data will carry that premium." In his view, the debate has already moved past whether the Fed cuts this year.
“The debate has shifted to whether the next move is a hike,” Lee said.
He offered some encouragement for the bulls too, saying buyers haven't disappeared.
"Institutional demand continued to absorb much of the initial volatility, suggesting investors are still willing to buy into weakness," he said, a sign that dip-buying discipline hasn't broken down. But he expected the pain, if it comes, to concentrate first in rate-sensitive tech.
"The Nasdaq 100 is likely to bear the brunt of that repricing as higher-for-longer yields continue to pressure growth valuations," he said, adding that gold "could also come under pressure if rising yields and a stronger dollar outweigh safe-haven demand" — a call that didn't play out Wednesday, when gold actually closed up 0.27% at $4,048.99.
Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, was the most forward-looking of the four, pointing to the September Fed meeting as the real risk.
"A sigh of relief from investors as the Fed shows patience once more," he said of Wednesday's outcome. But he was explicit that the relief is temporary: "It is, however, a gamble, as it sets up a potentially fraught September meeting should inflation remain uncomfortably high and the FOMC have to take a difficult decision in the heat of the Midterms political campaign."
The focus on September is not without reason. Fed funds futures are now pricing a 72% probability of a hike at the September meeting, and three sitting regional Fed presidents already dissented Wednesday in favor of hiking now.
Where that leaves bitcoin
None of the analysts are calling for a crash, and none are calling for a rally.
The split is really about things to watch next, such as tighter liquidity, oil and ETF flows, or September FOMC, and not whether bitcoin is in immediate danger.

title: Ostium blames off-chain breach for $24 million exploit, rules out smart contract flaw
summary: The team said trader collateral was unaffected and that it will release a recovery plan for liquidity providers.
full_text:
Ostium blames off-chain breach for $24 million exploit, rules out smart contract flaw
Quick Take
- Ostium said in a post-mortem that its $23.75 million exploit, which occurred on July 15, stemmed from a compromise of its off-chain infrastructure.
- The team said trader collateral was unaffected and that it will release a recovery plan for liquidity providers.
We'd love your feedback.
Onchain perpetuals exchange Ostium said its July 15 exploit, which drained 23.75 million USDC from its OLP vault, stemmed from a compromise of its off-chain infrastructure rather than vulnerability in its smart contracts or protocol multisigs.
In a post-mortem published Wednesday, Ostium wrote that the attacker leveraged unauthorized access to the protocol's off-chain infrastructure to submit fraudulent BTC-USD price reports. This enabled the attacker to generate artificial trading profits from the public OLP vault.
Ostium said that this initial unauthorized access occurred off-chain.
"Based on our investigation, we have no evidence this incident was a result of a vulnerability in Ostium's smart-contract code logic or a compromise of the multisigs that govern the protocol," the team said.
Specifically, the attacker used forwarder paths that were already recognized by the protocol. They first tested with a 100 USDC position to generate roughly 897.8 USDC of artificial profit.
The attacker then executed the main batch, resulting in 11.9 million USDC transferred to the beneficiary wallet, and later executed six further standalone cycles. In total, the attack drained 23.75 million USDC from the OLP vault.
The Ostium team noted that its automated monitoring detected the activity and ultimately prevented further withdrawals. The protocol has since migrated to a new production environment with updated security controls, and trading resumed on July 23.
Ostium also said that trader collateral was not affected and user margin remained in the protocol's trading contracts.
"A separate recovery plan for liquidity providers is being finalized and will be shared in a separate post," the team added.
The exploit came after Ostium partnered with Nasdaq in May to power equity perpetual products using the exchange operator's market data. At the time, the protocol said it had processed more than $50 billion in cumulative trading volume.

summary:
以太坊基金會（Ethereum Foundation）宣布安全研究員 Pascal Caversaccio 加 […]

〈以太坊基金會補進第四位董事 Pascal Caversaccio，密碼龐克宣言作者，一年任期不支薪〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
以太坊基金會（Ethereum Foundation）宣布安全研究員 Pascal Caversaccio 加入董事會，成為繼 Vitalik Buterin、Aya Miyaguchi 與 Patrick Storchenegger 之後的第四位董事，初始任期一年且不支薪。這是基金會董事會在 6 月縮編至三人後的首次補位，接手的人來自安全與隱私陣營。
（前情提要：半年抓 100 名北韓 IT 駭客、追回 580 萬美元，以太坊基金會安全計畫報告）
（背景補充：以太坊基金會拒絕透露「Vitalik投票權重」，治理透明度遭社群質疑：根本中心化）
重點摘要
- Pascal Caversaccio 出任以太坊基金會第四位董事，初始任期一年，無償擔任不領報酬
- 他是安全應變團隊 SEAL 911 共同創辦人，也是 2024 年《以太坊密碼龐克宣言》作者
- 這是董事會 6 月因共同執行董事王筱維請辭縮至三人後的首次擴編
以太坊基金會 7 月 29 日宣布，安全研究員 Pascal Caversaccio（社群多以帳號 pcaversaccio 稱呼）正式加入董事會。董事會成員因此增至四人，另外三席分別是主席 Aya Miyaguchi、以太坊共同創辦人 Vitalik Buterin，以及瑞士法律顧問 Patrick Storchenegger。
兩個條件值得先標出來，因為多數轉述都漏掉了。他的初始任期是一年，而且是無償擔任，不領任何報酬。
他是誰
Pascal Caversaccio 最為人知的身分是 SEAL 911 共同創辦人。這是一支 24 小時運作的加密資安緊急應變隊伍，透過 Telegram 提供免費熱線，當某個 DeFi 協議正在被即時抽乾時，由經過審核的安全研究員組成戰情室，分流漏洞、嘗試白帽救援、協調揭露。他同時是通用合約部署框架 CreateX 與 Vyper 安全函式庫 snekmate 的作者。
另一個身分是寫作者。他在 2024 年寫了《以太坊密碼龐克宣言》（The Ethereum Cypherpunk Manifesto），2025 年寫了《以太坊隱私：通往自我主權之路》。他原本就在基金會的 Silviculture Society 裡，那是一個關注抗審查、開源開發、隱私與安全的非正式顧問小組，這次等於從顧問席位被拉進董事會。
這是縮編後的第一次補人
以太坊基金會董事會在今年 6 月縮到三個人。原因是共同執行董事王筱維（Hsiao-Wei Wang）於 6 月 18 日請辭，同時卸下董事身分，她在基金會待了將近十年。
那次請辭並不是孤例。多家外媒統計，基金會在 2026 年累計約 19 人離職或被裁撤，其中資深層級的出走在五個月內就至少有八起。共同執行董事 Tomasz Stańczak 早在 2 月就已離開。
Vitalik Buterin 曾用「更小的船」形容基金會的未來，方向是收縮到安全、隱私與抗審查三件事。基金會這次的官方說法也一致，稱自己正在把角色重新定位為「長期的守護者，而不是生態發展的中心」。在這個定位底下，補進來的第一個人不是執行職，是一個不支薪的董事席位，而且找的是寫密碼龐克宣言的那個人。
基金會對董事會的職能定義，除了設定戰略願景與確保管理決策符合組織價值，還包括擔任守護使命與瑞士法律合規的「安全理事會」（security council）。
這個安全理事會總算坐了一個真的在做安全的人。
常見問題
Pascal Caversaccio 加入以太坊基金會董事會的條件是什麼？
初始任期為一年，屬於無償志願性質，不領取任何報酬。他成為第四位董事，與主席 Aya Miyaguchi、Vitalik Buterin 及瑞士法律顧問 Patrick Storchenegger 共同組成董事會。
SEAL 911 是什麼組織？
由 Pascal Caversaccio 共同創辦的加密資安緊急應變團隊，透過 Telegram 提供 24 小時免費熱線。協議遭遇即時攻擊時，經審核的安全研究員會組成戰情室，分流漏洞並協調白帽救援與揭露。

title: eBay 前執行長動用企業力量威脅自媒體，七年後以 5570 萬美元和解
summary:
麻州一對經營電商電子報的夫妻，在 2019 年被 eBay 安全部門寄送活蟑螂、豬胎兒與喪禮花圈進行威脅了三個 […]

〈eBay 前執行長動用企業力量威脅自媒體，七年後以 5570 萬美元和解〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
麻州一對經營電商電子報的夫妻，在 2019 年被 eBay 安全部門寄送活蟑螂、豬胎兒與喪禮花圈進行威脅了三個星期，起因是妻子算出了執行長的薪水有多少。七年後的現在，eBay 與四名前高層同意支付 5,570 萬美元和解，前執行長 Devin Wenig 個人掏出 300 萬美元。
（前情提要：被 AI 裁員的記者，發現公司還用自己名字發文章）
（背景補充：驚爆！Ripple董事、川普親信涉「網路跟蹤、騷擾」遭 FBI 逮補，受害者：如惡魔一般恐怖）
重點摘要
- eBay 與四名前高層 7 月 27 日以 5,570 萬美元和解，其中 4,870 萬為賠償、700 萬為慈善捐款
- 導火線是 Ina Steiner 在 2019 年 4 月報導執行長 Devin Wenig 薪酬為員工中位數的 152 倍
- 七名前 eBay 員工遭定罪，主謀 Jim Baugh 判刑 57 個月，但寫下「燒成灰燼」的高層從未被起訴
美國麻州一間郊區住宅，在深夜門鈴響起，門口站著陌生人，說是看到網路廣告，來參加這裡舉辦的性愛派對。住在裡面的夫妻非常沮喪，他們一開始不知道得罪了誰。
信箱被塞了活蟑螂，門外掛著喪禮花圈。收到包裹拆開，裡面是一個死掉的豬胎。另外的包裹裡是一本書，書名叫《失去配偶的生存指南》。
除了這些以外，他們還收到沾著血的萬聖節豬頭面具、活蜘蛛。還有寄到鄰居家、收件人寫著屋主名字的色情雜誌，還有沒人訂過的整車披薩。
訂購那個喪禮花圈的花店，離 eBay 位於加州 San Jose 的總部只有幾條街。
網拍賣家電子報被找麻煩
Ina Steiner 和 David Steiner 是一對夫妻，他們曾經經營一個叫 EcommerceBytes 的網站與電子報，讀者是靠 eBay、Amazon 這些平台吃飯的中小賣家。平台改了規則、調了費率、封了帳號，他們就寫。這種媒體在任何一個平台生態裡都存在，規模不大，但被鎖定的讀者非常忠實，因為那是這些賣家少數的資訊來源。
2019 年 4 月，Ina Steiner 寫了一篇文章，內容是當時的 eBay 執行長 Devin Wenig 的薪酬，換算下來是 eBay 員工薪資中位數的 152 倍。
這篇報導成了整件事的起點。
當時 eBay 內部的氣壓已經很低，因為 2019 年 1 月，激進投資機構 Elliott Management 入股 eBay 並公開要求改革，管理層被壓在績效與換人的雙重壓力下。一份專門盯著 eBay 挑毛病、還被賣家當聖經看的電子報，在那個時間點寫出執行長的薪水，變成了 eBay 高層的眼中釘。
一個前 CIA 探員負責出手
要負責處理這對夫妻「問題」的，是 eBay 的安全部門。
部門主管 Jim Baugh 是前 CIA 人員。根據法庭紀錄與後續報導，Jim Baugh 在部門內建立了一套近乎邪教的管理方式。他要求下屬觀看他認為有「教育意義」的電影片段，清單包括《華爾街之狼》裡員工拒絕配合聯邦執法人員的橋段、《門當父不對》的「信任圈」、影集《Billions》談忠誠的段落，以及《美國黑幫》裡 Denzel Washington 飾演的角色當著眾人的面處決一個人來立投名狀。
員工的證詞描述了安全部的氣氛，不照做的話，「你以後再也找不到別的工作」。
後來負責審理此案的聯邦法官 Patti Saris 用了兩個詞來形容這起案件，「難以想像」、「有毒文化」。
很難想像，這是一家美國 500 大企業。
從「幹掉她」到「燒成灰燼」
檢方掌握的通訊紀錄，從 eBay 高層下指令的訊息很清楚。
2019 年 4 月，薪酬報導刊出後，公關長 Steve Wymer 向 Devin Wenig 表態：「我們要碾碎這個女人。」
2019 年 5 月 31 日，Devin Wenig 傳給 Steve Wymer 三個字：「Take her down.」（幹掉她）
2019 年 8 月 1 日，EcommerceBytes 刊出一篇關於 eBay 控告 Amazon 挖角賣家的報導。報導上線半小時後，Devin Wenig 再次傳訊：「如果你打算搞掉她，現在就是時候。」
Steve Wymer 把這條訊息轉給 Jim Baugh，附上自己的意見，指出她是個「需要被燒毀的酸民」。他說他想看到「灰燼」，要求「不擇手段」。
2019 年 8 月 5 日到 8 月 23 日，那些包裹開始寄到自媒體夫妻的家裡。
同時進行的還有另外幾條戰線，eBay 安全團隊開始用假帳號在 Craigslist 論壇上，用 Steiner 夫婦的住家地址刊登性愛派對廣告，把陌生人一批批引到他們家門口。他們在 Twitter 上用匿名帳號騷擾這對夫妻；他們替他們訂閱大量從未申請過的郵件清單，讓信箱被垃圾郵件淹沒。
然後安全團隊買了機票，從加州飛到波士頓。
他們計畫是在 Steiner 夫婦的車上裝 GPS 追蹤器，並且進入他們家的車庫。這趟行動由當時的 eBay 執行長 Devin Wenig 和全球韌性總監 David Harville 親自執行。
他們以為自己是在演電影。
破案的是那對夫妻自己
Ina Steiner 和 David Steiner 察覺有車在跟蹤他們，記下了車牌，交給當地警方。
那是一輛租來的車。租車的人是一個住在加州、沒有任何前科紀錄的女性。到這裡線索看起來就斷了。
於是這對夫妻自己上網查，他們查出那個名字的職業，是 eBay 的情報分析師。他們接著發現，那個寄來的喪禮花圈，訂購地點就在 eBay 加州總部附近。
一個由前 CIA 探員領軍的企業情報團隊，被兩個寫電子報的人用車牌號碼和搜尋引擎反追蹤出來。
2020 年 6 月，六名前 eBay 員工遭到起訴。最終有七名前員工與一名約聘人員認罪。
- Jim Baugh（安全與安保資深總監）: 57 個月有期徒刑，罰金 4 萬美元
- David Harville（全球韌性總監）: 24 個月有期徒刑，罰金 2 萬美元
- Philip Cooke（安全營運資深經理）: 18 個月有期徒刑
- Stephanie Popp（全球情報資深經理）: 12 個月有期徒刑
- Stephanie Stockwell（全球情報經理）: 居家監禁 1 年
- Veronica Zea（約聘情報分析師）: 居家監禁 1 年
- Brian Gilbert（特別行動資深經理）: 緩刑，賠償被害人 2 萬美元
eBay 公司本身在 2021 年與司法部簽署緩起訴協議，承認六項重罪，繳交 300 萬美元刑事罰金，並接受三年強化合規監督。
驚人的和解金額
7 月 27 日公布的民事和解，總額 5,570 萬美元，拆開來是這樣：
- 賠償金 4,870 萬美元：eBay 4,615 萬、前執行長 Devin Wenig 200 萬、前高層 Wendy Jones 50 萬、前公關長 Steve Wymer 5 萬
- 慈善捐款 700 萬美元：eBay 600 萬、Devin Wenig 額外 100 萬，捐給一個以 Ina Steiner 命名、保護憲法第一修正案權利的組織
Devin Wenig 個人合計掏出 300 萬美元。2021 年美國司法部對 eBay 這家公司開出的刑事罰金，也是 300 萬美元。一整家公司承認六項重罪的刑事代價，和前執行長這次個人掏的錢，一樣多。
對 eBay 來說，這是九天的淨利
eBay 2025 年全年營收 111 億美元，淨利 20.31 億美元。
把 eBay 這次要付的 4,615 萬賠償加上 600 萬慈善，總共 5,215 萬美元，除以它每天約 556 萬美元的淨利，答案是 9.4 天。
2021 年那筆 300 萬美元的刑事罰金，換算下來是 13 個小時。
他們要的不是錢，是不用閉嘴
拿到 5,570 萬美元之後，David Steiner 被問到這份和解協議裡最重要的是什麼。他的回答不是任何一個數字。
「這份和解協議裡最重要的東西，是沒有保密條款。身為記者，我們可以自由談論這件事，沒有任何束縛。」
這句話需要一點背景才能聽懂它，企業和解通常買的就是當事人永遠沉默，付一筆錢，換一份保密協議把知道事實的人掩蓋起來，後來的人查不到，金額愈大，封口通常愈嚴。
但這次 eBay 的和解協議沒有這一條，eBay 另外還必須發出公開聲明，承認「2019 年前 eBay 員工對 Steiner 夫婦所做的事是錯的、可恥的，本來就不該發生」。
原告律師 Christopher Murphy 的說法是：「這個案子從一開始就不只是為了拿到賠償。我們的當事人想要的是把真相挖出來，保護記者和發行人。」
這件事在今年 2 月差點就以另一種方式結束。2 月 25 日雙方曾達成暫定和解，法院下了附條件的撤案裁定，但協議最終沒能定案。6 月，Steiner 夫婦要求聯邦法官重新開啟此案。7 月 27 日的版本，是重開之後才談成的。
Steiner 夫婦最後拿到的不是 5,570 萬美元，是繼續講話的權利，那本來就是他們原本就有的東西。
常見問題
eBay 為什麼要騷擾 Steiner 夫婦？
導火線是 Ina Steiner 在 2019 年 4 月報導執行長 Devin Wenig 薪酬為員工中位數的 152 倍。當時激進投資機構 Elliott Management 剛入股施壓，高層將這份長期批評 eBay 的電子報視為必須解決的問題。
這次 5,570 萬美元和解包含哪些項目？
賠償金 4,870 萬美元（eBay 4,615 萬、Devin Wenig 200 萬、Wendy Jones 50 萬、Steve Wymer 5 萬），加上 700 萬美元慈善捐款。協議沒有保密條款，eBay 另須發布公開聲明承認前員工的行為錯誤。

title: 你的Agent代表你嗎？「可信 AI 黑客松」開放單人報名，1.2 萬鎂獎金 8/5 截止
summary:
你的 Agent 替你查價、下單、送件、簽約，但沒有一筆紀錄能證明「這是你同意的」。聚焦這道信任缺口的「可信 […]

〈你的Agent代表你嗎？「可信 AI 黑客松」開放單人報名，1.2 萬鎂獎金 8/5 截止〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
你的 Agent 替你查價、下單、送件、簽約，但沒有一筆紀錄能證明「這是你同意的」。聚焦這道信任缺口的「可信 AI 黑客松」，8 月 29 日至 31 日在台北南港 N24 台北方舟登場，總獎金 12,000 美元起、最多錄取 20 隊，報名 8 月 5 日截止，本屆首度開放單人報名。
（前情提要：OpenAI 黑客松登陸台灣：北中南串連冠軍可拿 5,000 美元 API 額度（規則速看））
（背景補充：Visa 研究：AI 代理過去一年處理 1.1 億筆交易，微支付正崛起）
＊本文為新聞稿，由 台灣區塊鏈愛好者協會（TABEI） 提供
你的 Agent，其實不是你的 Agent。它替你查價、下單、送件、簽約，但全程沒有一筆紀錄能證明「這是你同意的」。唯一的憑據，是一串誰也驗不了的 API 金鑰。
在鏈上，這件事十年前就解決了。私鑰簽名就是授權，鏈上紀錄天生是稽核軌跡。但 AI Agent 沒有那個簽名視窗，而這正是它至今進不了金融、醫療與政府流程的原因。
聚焦這道缺口的「可信 AI 黑客松」，8 月 29 日至 31 日在台北南港 N24 台北方舟登場。由台灣區塊鏈愛好者協會（TABEI）主辦，總獎金 12,000 美元起，最多錄取 20 隊，報名至 8 月 5 日截止，本屆並首度開放單人報名。
幣圈的技術棧，正是 AI 缺的那塊拼圖
這個 Agent 代表誰？被授權做什麼？授權何時失效？出事後行為能否追溯？多數 AI 系統至今答不出這四個問題。而問題指向的解法，包括可驗證憑證（VC）、去中心化識別（DID）、選擇性揭露、零知識證明、聯邦學習與差分隱私，正是區塊鏈與隱私技術社群十年累積的主場。你在幣圈練的技能，不用轉行，可以直接平移到 AI 經濟最缺人的位置。
六道命題，出自兩場產業座談
TABEI 於 6 月 5 日召開第一場專家學者座談，將「AI 行為信任缺口」定位為跨產業共同痛點；7 月 16 日第二場產業需求座談於政大公企中心舉行，邀集製造貿易、電商電支、醫療保險、政府服務與移工數位信任等領域的業者與學者同桌，釐清哪些痛點產業可自行解決、哪些需要政策調整，以及哪些場景有機會接軌 GLEIF vLEI、W3C VC、FIDO 等國際標準。兩場座談的產出，即為本屆六道命題：
- 製造貿易｜碳足跡與 DPP: 只揭露碳排那一項，不外洩製程機密
- 電支金融｜開戶之後: 看見持續異常，又不看光交易明細
- 醫療保險｜理賠合作: 病人同意可被機器驗證，只交換最小必要資訊
- 政府服務｜跨機關代辦: 「代查」與「代送件」的授權邊界與即時撤銷
- 普惠金融｜移工與新住民: 逾 87 萬移工，被信任又不被冒用的數位身份
- 供應鏈合規｜國際稽核: 合規證明持續可驗證，而非稽核當天才生出來
單人可報名，書審不用原型
「湊不到隊」這個藉口，本屆直接拆掉，開放單人報名，先報名卡位，入選後由主辦方於賽前工作坊協助媒合，最終組成 3 至 5 人隊伍即可。報名也不需提交原型，書面初審只看兩段文字，你觀察到的痛點與解法構想（各 300 字內），8 月 7 日公布入選名單。
賽前設兩場工作坊：8/15 線上場講可驗證憑證、隱私計算與 Agent 工程；8/22 實體場由出題的產業方講解命題並進行逐隊 Clinic。活動全程免費、供餐，8/29 至 8/30 開放留宿；表現優異的作品，將有機會與命題方進行後續 PoC 對接。
TABEI 自 2016 年起舉辦台灣歷史最悠久的區塊鏈年會，並主辦過 WAGMI Battle、ZK BuidlArk 等技術賽事。
活動資訊
- 地點: N24 台北方舟（台北市南港區市民大道七段 100 號，台鐵／捷運松山站步行約 5 分鐘）

常見問題
可信 AI 黑客松要怎麼報名？一定要先組好隊嗎？
報名 8 月 5 日 23:59 截止，本屆首度開放單人報名，入選後由主辦方在賽前工作坊協助媒合，最終組成 3 至 5 人隊伍即可。書面初審不需提交原型，只看痛點觀察與解法構想各 300 字內。
這場黑客松想解決什麼問題？
AI Agent 缺少可被驗證的授權與稽核紀錄，因此進不了金融、醫療與政府流程。六道命題聚焦用可驗證憑證、去中心化識別與零知識證明等技術補上這道信任缺口，最多錄取 20 隊。

title: 美國制裁伊朗海運公司，比特幣成了過海收錢的秘密武器

〈美國制裁伊朗海運公司，比特幣成了過海收錢的秘密武器〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
美國財政部對兩家伊朗海運公司下手，指出荷姆茲海峽保險網路接受比特幣收取保險費，為革命軍團創收。8 家公司和 8 艘船隻同時遭列制裁名單。
（前情提要：伊朗推「荷姆茲安全」海事保險平台，接受比特幣、USDT 支付，美國財政部警告：誰敢就制裁）
（背景補充：美財政部點名「伊朗加密管道」列制裁清單，荷姆茲海峽船運崩跌 95%、USDT 灰色流通空間正在消失）
美國財政部週三宣布制裁兩家伊朗海運公司，指控其透過接受比特幣和其他數位資產收取航運保險費，為伊朗革命軍團（IRGC）創收。同時遭制裁的還有 8 家與伊朗影子艦隊相關的公司，以及 8 艘被列為財產的海上船隻。
財政部外資及匯率問題辦公室（OFAC）在 公告 中指出，波斯灣海事保險公司（Persian Gulf Marine Insurance Company）和荷姆茲海運服務管理局（HormuzSafe Marine Services Authority）構成了革命軍團後的海事保險網路，要求商業船隻在透過荷姆茲海峽前購買指定保險。
從提案到制裁：比特幣保險的實際運作
5 月 18 日，HormuzSafe 網站截圖曾在網上流傳，顯示海運貨物提供「數位保險」，保費可用比特幣支付。當時報導指出伊朗仍在考慮這種保險模式，該網站隨後一度無法存取。
伊朗國營媒體法爾斯通訊社（Fars News Agency）表示，該平台可簽發海事保險單和金融責任證明，預估能創造超過 10 億美元的收入。
這次制裁確認了該平台已進入實際運作階段。OFAC 指出 HormuzSafe 接受比特幣和其他加密貨幣以規避制裁，為革命軍團創收，同時幫助伊朗加強對海峽船運的控制。
財政部長：「不會讓伊朗攔截全球貿易」
財政部長斯科特·貝森特（Scott Bessent）表示：「美國不會讓伊朗劫持全球貿易。」他指控伊朗政權利用國際航運為革命軍團籌措資金。
荷姆茲海峽承載了全球約五分之一的原油貿易，任何控制或貨幣化透過該水道交通的舉措，都對國際能源市場有顯著影響。
比特幣的優勢：沒有中心化發行者
相較於穩定幣，比特幣對受制裁者有獨特優勢：沒有中心化發行者可以凍結資金。4 月，美國當局剛凍結了與伊朗相關的 3.44 億美元 USDT 穩定幣。
根據比特幣政策研究所的早期報告，伊朗接受人民幣、Tether USDT 和比特幣作為石油通行費，但當時尚未發現任何比特幣支付的上鏈證據。如今制裁公告證實了這些加密管道的存在。
臺灣航運的啟示
臺灣作為航運大國，全球前十大航運公司中有 4 家總部位在臺灣。若航運保險費用改用比特幣結算，對臺灣的航運產業鏈意味著什麼？比特幣支付基礎設施的普及可能比想像中更接近現實。
